“*Nothing!*” answered Lord Orville with a smile and a shrug.
“By Jove,” cried the man, “she is the most beautiful creature I ever saw in my life!”
Lord Orville, as he well might, laughed; but answered, “Yes, a pretty modest-looking girl.”
“O my Lord!” cried the madman, “she is an angel!”
“A *silent* one,” returned he.
“Why ay, my Lord, how stands she as to that? She looks all intelligence and expression.”
“A poor weak girl!” answered Lord Orville, shaking his head.
“By Jove,” cried the other, “I am glad to hear it!”
At that moment, the same odious creature who had been my former tormentor, joined them. Addressing Lord Orville with great respect, he said, “I beg pardon, my Lord﻿—if I was﻿—as I fear might be the case﻿—rather too severe in my censure of the lady who is honoured with your protection﻿—but, my Lord, ill-breeding is apt to provoke a man.”
“Ill-breeding!” cried my unknown champion, “impossible! that elegant face can never be so vile a mask!”
“O Sir, as to that,” answered he, “you must allow *me* to judge; for though I pay all deference to your opinion﻿—in other things﻿—yet I hope you will grant﻿—and I appeal to your Lordship also﻿—that I am not totally despicable as a judge of good or ill-manners.”
“I was so wholly ignorant,” said Lord Orville, gravely, “of the provocation you might have had, that I could not but be surprised at your singular resentment.”
“It was far from my intention,” answered he, “to offend your Lordship; but, really, for a person who is nobody, to give herself such airs﻿—I own I could not command my passion. For, my Lord, though I have made diligent enquiry﻿—I cannot learn who she is.”
“By what I can make out,” cried my defender, “she must be a country parson’s daughter.”

===Chinese===

第十二封 伊芙琳娜续
4月5日，星期二。
昨晚的麻烦没完没了。方才我连哄带笑，从玛丽亚嘴里掏出了一段我这辈子听过的最奇妙的对话。乍一听，您会被我的虚荣吓一跳；可是亲爱的先生，您要有耐心！
这必定是在我陪米尔文太太坐牌局那会儿。玛丽亚正在用茶点，看见奥维尔勋爵也自己走过来取点心；他不认得她，她却一眼认出了他。紧接着，一个满身轻狂气的男人急步凑上去，嚷道："咦，勋爵大人，您把您那位可爱的舞伴怎么发落啦？"
"*没怎么！*"奥维尔勋爵笑着耸耸肩。
"老天在上，"那人嚷道，"她是我平生所见最美的造物！"
奥维尔勋爵笑了——他尽可以笑；口里却说："是的，一个模样挺娴静的姑娘。"
"哦大人！"那疯子嚷道，"她是位天使！"
"一位*沉默的*天使。"他回敬。
"嘿，正是这话，大人，这方面她如何？她那一脸的灵秀和表情呀。"
"一个可怜的弱智姑娘罢了！"奥维尔勋爵答，摇着头。
"谢天谢地！"另一位喊，"听您这么说，我倒高兴！"
就在这时，先前折磨过我的那个可憎的东西也加入了他们。他毕恭毕敬地向奥维尔勋爵开口："乞恕罪，大人——倘若小人方才对这位荣蒙大人护佑的夫人责之过苛——只怕难免——可是大人，粗俗无礼最惹人火。"
"粗俗无礼！"我那位不知名的护主喊道，"断无此理！那样一张清雅的脸，断做不出这样卑俗的面具！"
"哦先生，这层嘛，"他答道，"总得容*小人*来判断；虽则在别的事上小人无不拜服尊见——可您总得恩准——小人也要向大人陈情——论鉴别举止的雅俗，小人也未必一无可取。"
"我全然不知，"奥维尔勋爵正色道，"您受过怎样的冒犯，所以您这份罕见的怨气，我不能不吃惊。"
"小人万不敢开罪大人，"他答，"可是说真格的，一个不知何许人的人物，也摆这样的谱——小人自认按捺不住。因为大人，小人明察暗访了一番——实在查不出她的来历。"
"依我看呐，"我的辩护人嚷道，"她多半是个乡下牧师的女儿。"

===Original===

“He! he! he! very good, ’pon honour!” cried the fop;﻿—“well, so I could have sworn by her manners.”
And then, delighted at his own wit, he laughed, and went away, as I suppose, to repeat it.
“But what the deuce is all this?” demanded the other.
“Why a very foolish affair,” answered Lord Orville; “your Helen first refused this coxcomb, and then﻿—danced with me. This is all I can gather of it.”
“O, Orville,” returned he, “you are a happy man!﻿—But *ill-bred*?﻿—I can never believe it! And she looks too sensible to be *ignorant*.”
“Whether ignorant or mischievous, I will not pretend to determine; but certain it is, she attended to all *I* could say to her, though I have really fatigued myself with fruitless endeavours to entertain her, with the most immovable gravity; but no sooner did Lovel begin his complaint, than she was seized with a fit of laughing, first affronting the poor beau, and then enjoying his mortification.”
“Ha! ha! ha! why there is some *genius* in that, my Lord, perhaps rather﻿—*rustic*.”
Here Maria was called to dance, and so heard no more.
Now, tell me, my dear Sir, did you ever know anything more provoking? “*A poor weak girl!*” “*ignorant or mischievous!*” What mortifying words! I am resolved, however, that I will never again be tempted to go to an assembly. I wish I had been in Dorsetshire.
Well, after this, you will not be surprised that Lord Orville contented himself with an enquiry after our healths this morning, by his servant, without troubling himself to call, as Miss Mirvan had told me he would; but perhaps it may be only a country custom.
I would not live here for the world. I care not how soon we leave town. London soon grows tiresome. I wish the Captain would come. Mrs. Mirvan talks of the opera for this evening; however, I am very indifferent about it.
Wednesday Morning.
Well, my dear Sir, I have been pleased against my will, I could almost say; for I must own I went out in very ill humour, which I think you cannot wonder at: but the music and the singing were charming; they soothed me into a pleasure the most grateful, the best suited to my present disposition in the world. I hope to persuade Mrs. Mirvan to go again on Saturday. I wish the opera was every night. It is, of all entertainments, the sweetest and most delightful. Some of the songs seemed to melt my very soul.

===Chinese===

"咭！咭！咭！妙极，凭良心说！"纨袴子喊；——"着啊，凭她那做派，我也敢赌咒。"
接着他为自己的机智大乐，笑着走了——多半是到处复述去了。
"可这到底都是怎么一回事？"另一位追问。
"一桩蠢事罢了，"奥维尔勋爵答，"您的海伦先回绝了那个自负鬼，随后——又同我跳了舞。我所知道的就这些。"
"哦，奥维尔，"他回道，"你是个幸福的人！——可是*没教养*？——我永远不信！她瞧着也太明白事理，不会*无知*。"
"是无知还是促狭，我不敢断；可有一件事千真万确：*我*对她说的话，她无不全听在耳里——我实在费尽力气逗她说话，都说乏了，她只报以一成不变的端凝；可洛弗尔（Lovel）一开口抱怨，她便发作般大笑起来，先触怒那可怜的花花公子，再欣赏他的难堪。"
"哈！哈！哈！这里头可有点*才情*呢，大人——只是未免——*土气*。"
讲到这里，玛丽亚被唤去跳舞，后面就没听见了。
怎么样，亲爱的先生，您还知道比这更气人的事么？"*一个可怜的弱智姑娘！*""*无知还是促狭！*"多伤人的字眼！我已拿定主意，再也不受人诱去什么舞会了。我但愿自己在多塞特郡。
好吧，往后奥维尔勋爵今晨只遣仆人问了个安、没屈尊登门，您不会再奇怪了——米尔文小姐原同我说过他会来的；不过这兴许只是乡下的礼数。
给我全世界我也不愿在此长住。我们多早晚离城我都不嫌快。伦敦很快就叫人腻了。但愿舰长快来。米尔文太太说今晚去看歌剧；不过我去不去都无所谓。
星期三早晨。
亲爱的先生，我几乎是违着自己的心意又受了次用；因为我得承认，出门时我一肚子不痛快——您想这也不奇怪——可是那音乐、那歌声实在迷人；它们把我抚慰进一种最熨帖的欢愉，恰是世上最合我此刻心绪的一种。我巴不得劝动米尔文太太星期六再去。但愿歌剧夜夜都演。在一切消遣里，它最甜美、最悦人。有几支歌，简直把我的魂都融了。

===Original===

It was what they call a *serious* opera, as the *comic* first singer was ill.
Tonight we go to Ranelagh. If any of those three gentlemen who conversed so freely about me should be there﻿—but I won’t think of it.
Thursday Morning.
Well, my dear Sir, we went to Ranelagh. It is a charming place; and the brilliancy of the lights, on my first entrance, made me almost think I was in some enchanted castle or fairy palace, for all looked like magic to me.
The very first person I saw was Lord Orville. I felt so confused!﻿—but he did not see me. After tea, Mrs. Mirvan being tired, Maria and I walked round the room alone. Then again we saw him, standing by the orchestra. We, too, stopped to hear a singer. He bowed to me; I courtesied, and I am sure I coloured. We soon walked on, not liking our situation; however, he did not follow us; and when we passed by the orchestra again, he was gone. Afterwards, in the course of the evening, we met him several times; but he was always with some party, and never spoke to us, though whenever he chanced to meet my eyes, he condescended to bow.
I cannot but be hurt at the opinion he entertains of me. It is true my own behaviour incurred it﻿—yet he is himself the most agreeable, and, seemingly, the most amiable man in the world, and therefore it is that I am grieved to be thought ill of by him: for of whose esteem ought we to be ambitious, if not of those who most merit our own?﻿—But it is too late to reflect upon this now. Well I can’t help it.﻿—However, I think I have done with assemblies.
This morning was destined for *seeing sights*, auctions, curious shops, and so forth; but my head ached, and I was not in a humour to be amused, and so I made them go without me, though very unwillingly. They are all kindness.
And now I am sorry I did not accompany them, for I know not what to do with myself. I had resolved not to go to the play tonight; but I believe I shall. In short, I hardly care whether I do or not.
---
I thought I had done wrong! Mrs. Mirvan and Maria have been half the town over, and so entertained!﻿—while I, like a fool, stayed at home to do nothing. And, at the auction in Pall Mall, who should they meet but Lord Orville. He sat next to Mrs. Mirvan, and they talked a great deal together; but she gave me no account of the conversation.

===Chinese===

那是一出他们所谓的*正*歌剧，因为唱*谐*剧的头牌角儿病了。
今晚我们去拉内拉夫。要是那三位这样随意议论过我的先生有谁在场——不，我不去想它了。
星期四早晨。
亲爱的先生，我们去拉内拉夫了。那是个迷人的地方；一进门，满眼灯彩的辉煌，几乎叫我以为置身什么中了魔的城堡、仙人的宫殿——在我眼里，处处都像魔法。
我头一个看见的人就是奥维尔勋爵。我那样心慌！——可他没看见我。茶后，米尔文太太乏了，玛丽亚同我自绕着大厅散步。又看见了他，正站在乐池边。我们也停下来听歌。他向我致意；我屈了屈膝，脸肯定红了。我们很快走开了——那个位置叫人发窘；他倒也没有跟来；等我们再经过乐池，他已不在。其后一晚又遇见他几回，可他总有同伴，从不曾同我们说话——只是每当偶然接上我的目光，总肯屈尊颔首。
他心里那样看我，我不能不难过。这原是我自家的举止招来的——可他本人是世上最可亲、看来也最可爱的人；正因如此，被他看轻才叫我伤心：倘若连最配受我们敬重的人的敬重都不图，我们还图谁的？——可现在想这些太迟了。罢，我拗不过它。——不过，舞会的事，我想我是从此洗手了。
今天上午原定去*看景致*：拍卖行、稀奇铺子，等等；可我头疼，也没心思寻乐，就央他们自己去——他们好不情愿。一家人待我都是这样好。
这会儿我又后悔没同去了，一个人不知拿自己怎么办。本打定今晚不去看戏了；可我想我还是去。说真的，去不去我几乎无所谓。
---
我就知道做错了！米尔文太太和玛丽亚逛了半个城，可乐坏了！——而我像个傻子，闷在家里干坐。在蓓尔美尔街的拍卖行里，你猜她们遇见了谁——奥维尔勋爵。他坐在米尔文太太旁边，两人谈了很久；可她一句也没向我转述那场谈话。

===Original===

I may never have such another opportunity of seeing London; I am quite sorry that I was not of the party; but I deserve this mortification, for having indulged my ill-humour.
Thursday Night.
We are just returned from the play, which was King Lear, and has made me very sad. We did not see anybody we knew.
Well, adieu, it is too late to write more.
Friday.
Captain Mirvan is arrived. I have not spirits to give an account of his introduction, for he has really shocked me. I do not like him. He seems to be surly, vulgar, and disagreeable.
Almost the same moment that Maria was presented to him, he began some rude jests upon the bad shape of her nose, and called her a tall ill-formed thing. She bore it with the utmost good humour; but that kind and sweet-tempered woman, Mrs. Mirvan, deserved a better lot. I am amazed she would marry him.
For my own part, I have been so shy, that I have hardly spoken to him, or he to me. I cannot imagine why the family was so rejoiced at his return. If he had spent his whole life abroad, I should have supposed they might rather have been thankful than sorrowful. However, I hope they do not think so ill of him as I do. At least, I am sure they have too much prudence to make it known.
Saturday Night.
We have been to the opera, and I am still more pleased than I was on Tuesday. I could have thought myself in Paradise, but for the continual talking of the company around me. We sat in the pit, where everybody was dressed in so high a style, that if I had been less delighted with the performance, my eyes would have found me sufficient entertainment from looking at the ladies.
I was very glad I did not sit next the Captain; for he could not bear the music or singers, and was extremely gross in his observations of both. When the opera was over, we went into a place called the coffee room where ladies, as well as gentlemen, assemble. There are all sorts of refreshments, and the company walk about, and *chat* with the same ease and freedom as in a private room.
On Monday we go to a ridotto, and on Wednesday we return to Howard Grove. The Captain says he won’t stay here to be *smoked with filth* any longer; but, having been seven years *smoked with a burning sun*, he will retire to the country, and sink into a *fair weather chap*.
Adieu, my dear Sir.

===Chinese===

再看一眼伦敦，这样的机会我未必再有；没能同行，我好懊悔；可这份羞也该我受，谁叫我由着坏脾气。
星期四夜。
刚看完戏回来，演的是《李尔王》，看得我心里好惨。没遇见一个熟人。
好吧，再会，太晚了，不多写了。
星期五。
米尔文舰长到了。我没心思细写他被引见的情形——他实在叫我吃惊。我不喜欢他。他瞧着乖戾、粗鄙、讨人嫌。
玛丽亚被引见给他的那一刻还没过完，他就拿她鼻子的形状不好开始开粗俗的玩笑，叫她"高高的一个畸玩意儿"。她极有涵养地受了；可米尔文太太那样一位仁厚和婉的女人，实在配得好一点的命。她怎么会嫁他，我诧异极了。
我自己呢，一直怯生生的，几乎没同他讲过话，他也几乎没同我讲过。我想不通，这一家子怎么这样欢天喜地迎他回来。他若一辈子待在外洋，我原以为这一家该庆幸而不该伤心呢。不过，但愿他们不至把他看得像我这样坏。至少，他们准是太过审慎，决不说破。
星期六夜。
我们又去了歌剧，比星期二更中我的意。我简直要当自己进了天堂——若不是身旁的看客说个不停。我们坐在正厅，人人衣饰之盛，哪怕演出不那样中意，光看看太太们，我的眼睛也不愁没有消遣。
幸而我没挨着舰长坐；他受不了那音乐和歌手，对两样都出言极其粗鄙。歌剧散场后，我们进了一处叫咖啡室的地方，男女宾客杂聚。各样茶点齐备，宾客往来散步，*闲谈*得同在自家客厅里一样自在随便。
星期一我们去参加一场里多托，星期三就回霍华德林苑。舰长说，他不肯再待在这儿受*烟尘熏烤*了；他在外洋被*烈日熏烤*了七年，这就要退居乡间，做一个*好天气的老伙计*。
再会，亲爱的先生。

## Letter / 书信
===Original===

XIII Evelina in Continuation
Tuesday, April 12.
My dear Sir,
We came home from the ridotto so late, or rather so early that it was not possible for me to write. Indeed, we did not *go*﻿—you will be frightened to hear it﻿—till past eleven o’clock: but nobody does. A terrible reverse of the order of nature! We sleep with the sun, and wake with the moon.
The room was very magnificent, the lights and decorations were brilliant, and the company gay and splendid. But I should have told you, that I made many objections to being of the party, according to the resolution I had formed. However, Maria laughed me out of my scruples, and so once again I went to an assembly.
Miss Mirvan danced a minuet; but I had not the courage to follow her example. In our walks I saw Lord Orville. He was quite alone, but did not observe us. Yet, as he seemed of no party, I thought it was not impossible that he might join us; and though I did not wish much to dance at all﻿—yet, as I was more acquainted with him than with any other person in the room, I must own I could not help thinking it would be infinitely more desirable to dance again with him than with an entire stranger. To be sure, after all that had passed, it was very ridiculous to suppose it even probable that Lord Orville would again honour me with his choice; yet I am compelled to confess my absurdity, by way of explaining what follows.
Miss Mirvan was soon engaged; and presently after a very fashionable gay looking man, who seemed about thirty years of age, addressed himself to me, and begged to have the honour of dancing with me. Now Maria’s partner was a gentleman of Mrs. Mirvan’s acquaintance; for she had told us it was highly improper for young women to dance with strangers at any public assembly. Indeed it was by no means my wish so to do: yet I did not like to confine myself from dancing at all; neither did I dare refuse this gentleman as I had done Mr. Lovel, and then, if any acquaintance should offer, accept him: and so, all these reasons combining, induced me to tell him﻿—yet I blush to write it to you!﻿—that I was *already engaged*; by which I meant to keep myself at liberty to a dance, or not, as matters should fall out.

===Chinese===

第十三封 伊芙琳娜续
4月12日，星期二。
亲爱的先生：
从里多托回来得太晚——不如说太早——我没法写信。说真的，我们出门时——您听了要吃惊——已过十一点：可人人都这样。大自然秩序的大颠倒！我们随太阳入睡，随月亮醒来。
大厅极尽壮丽，灯彩装饰一片辉煌，宾客欢盛华美。不过我该先告诉您：按先前下的决心，我本推三阻四不想入伙。玛丽亚却把我的顾虑笑掉了，于是我又进了一回舞会。
米尔文小姐跳了小步舞；我没有胆量学她。散步时我看见了奥维尔勋爵。他独自一人，没留意我们。可他既不属于任何一伙，我想他来加入我们也不是全无可能；虽然我本不大想跳舞，可这满场里我认得的只有他一个，我得承认，我禁不住想：若再跳，同他跳总比同全然的生人跳可取得多。当然，经过那一切之后再这样想，荒唐得很；可为了解释后文，我只好招认我这份荒唐。
米尔文小姐很快有了舞伴；随后一位看去三十上下、一脸时髦轻狂的先生朝我走来，求我赏光同他跳舞。玛丽亚的舞伴是米尔文太太的熟人；她早告诫过我们：年轻女子在公共舞会上同生人跳舞，极不合适。同生人跳本就全然非我所愿；可我也不愿因此就整晚枯坐；我又不敢像回绝洛弗尔先生那样回绝这位先生、回头再有熟人相邀又应下——这几层顾虑合在一处，竟诱我告诉他——给您写这个我脸红！——说我*已有约在先*；我的意思是给自己留着可跳可不跳的自由，看事态再说。

I suppose my consciousness betrayed my artifice, for he looked at me as if incredulous; and, instead of being satisfied with my answer and leaving me, according to my expectation, he walked at my side, and, with the greatest ease imaginable, began a conversation in the free style which only belongs to old and intimate acquaintance. But, what was most provoking, he asked me a thousand questions concerning *the partner to whom I was engaged*. And at last he said, “Is it really possible that a man whom you have honoured with your acceptance can fail to be at hand to profit from your goodness?”
I felt extremely foolish; and begged Mrs. Mirvan to lead to a seat; which she very obligingly did. The Captain sat next her; and to my great surprise, this gentleman thought proper to follow, and seat himself next to me.
“What an insensible!” continued he; “why, Madam, you are missing the most delightful dance in the world!﻿—The man must be either mad or a fool﻿—Which do you incline to think him yourself?”
“Neither, Sir,” answered I, in some confusion.
He begged my pardon for the freedom of his supposition, saying, “I really was off my guard, from astonishment that any man can be so much and so unaccountably his own enemy. But where, Madam, can he possibly be!﻿—has he left the room!﻿—or has not he been in it?”
“Indeed, Sir,” said I peevishly, “I know nothing of him.”
“I don’t wonder that you are disconcerted, Madam; it is really very provoking. The best part of the evening will be absolutely lost. He deserves not that you should wait for him.”
“I do not, Sir,” said I, “and I beg you not to﻿—”
“Mortifying, indeed, Madam,” interrupted he, “a lady to wait for a gentleman!﻿—O fie!﻿—careless fellow!﻿—What can detain him?﻿—Will you give me leave to seek him?”
“If you please, Sir,” answered I; quite terrified lest Mrs. Mirvan should attend to him; for she looked very much surprised at seeing me enter into conversation with a stranger.
“With all my heart,” cried he; “pray, what coat has he on?”
“Indeed I never looked at it.”
“Out upon him!” cried he; “What! did he address you in a coat not worth looking at?﻿—What a shabby wretch!”
How ridiculous! I really could not help laughing, which I fear encouraged him, for he went on.
“Charming creature!﻿—and can you really bear ill usage with so much sweetness? Can you, *like patience on a monument*, smile in the midst of disappointment?

For my part, though I am not the offended person, my indignation is so great, that I long to kick the fellow round the room!﻿—unless, indeed﻿—(hesitating and looking earnestly at me), unless, indeed﻿—it is a partner of your own *creating*?”
I was dreadfully abashed, and could not make an answer.
“But no!” cried he (again, and with warmth), “It cannot be that you are so cruel! Softness itself is painted in your eyes.﻿—You could not, surely, have the barbarity so wantonly to trifle with my misery.”
I turned away from this nonsense with real disgust, Mrs. Mirvan saw my confusion, but was perplexed what to think of it, and I could not explain to her the cause, lest the Captain should hear me. I therefore proposed to walk; she consented, and we all rose; but, would you believe it? this man had the assurance to rise too, and walk close by my side, as if of my party!
“Now,” cried he, “I hope we shall see this ingrate.﻿—Is that he?”﻿—pointing to an old man who was lame, “or that?” And in this manner he asked me of whoever was old or ugly in the room. I made no sort of answer: and when he found that I was resolutely silent, and walked on as much as I could without observing him, he suddenly stamped his foot, and cried out in a passion, “Fool! idiot! booby!”
I turned hastily toward him: “O, Madam,” continued he, “forgive my vehemence; but I am distracted to think there should exist a wretch who can slight a blessing for which I would forfeit my life!﻿—O that I could but meet him, I would soon﻿—But I grow angry: pardon me, Madam, my passions are violent, and your injuries affect me!”
I began to apprehend he was a madman, and stared at him with the utmost astonishment. “I see you are moved, Madam,” said he; “generous creature!﻿—but don’t be alarmed, I am cool again, I am indeed﻿—upon my soul I am;﻿—I entreat you, most lovely of mortals! I entreat you to be easy.”
“Indeed, Sir,” said I very seriously, “I must insist upon your leaving me; you are quite a stranger to me, and I am both unused, and averse to your language and your manners.”
This seemed to have some effect on him. He made me a low bow, begged my pardon, and vowed he would not for the world offend me.
“Then, Sir, you must leave me,” cried I. “I am gone, Madam, I am gone!”

One dance is all I solicit. Permit me, Madam, the honour of this young lady’s hand; it will be a favour I shall ever most gratefully acknowledge.”
“Sir,” answered she, “favours and strangers have with me no connection.”
“If you have hitherto,” said he, “confined your benevolence to your intimate friends, suffer me to be the first for whom your charity is enlarged.”
“Well, Sir, I know not what to say to you﻿—but﻿—”
He stopped her *but* with so many urgent entreaties that she at last told me, I must either go down one dance, or avoid his importunities by returning home. I hesitated which alternative to chose; but this impetuous man at length prevailed, and I was obliged to consent to dance with him.
And thus was my deviation from truth punished; and thus did this man’s determined boldness conquer.
During the dance, before we were too much engaged in it for conversation, he was extremely provoking about *my partner*, and tried every means in his power to make me own that I had deceived him; which, though I would not so far humble myself as to acknowledge, was indeed but too obvious.
Lord Orville, I fancy, did not dance at all. He seemed to have a large acquaintance, and joined several different parties: but you will easily suppose, I was not much pleased to see him, in a few minutes after I was gone, walk towards the place I had just left, and bow to and join Mrs. Mirvan!
How unlucky I thought myself, that I had not longer withstood this stranger’s importunities! The moment we had gone down the dance, I was hastening away from him; but he stopped me, and said, that I could by no means return to my party without giving offence, before we had *done our duty of walking up the dance*. As I know nothing at all of these rules and customs I was obliged to submit to his directions; but I fancy I looked rather uneasy, for he took notice of my inattention, saying, in his free way, “Whence that anxiety?﻿—Why are those lovely eyes perpetually averted?”
“I wish you would say no more to me, Sir,” cried I peevishly; “you have already destroyed all my happiness for this evening.”
“Good Heaven! What is it I have done?﻿—How have I merited this scorn?”
“You have tormented me to death; you have forced me from my friends, and intruded yourself upon me, against my will, for a partner.”

“To your *partner*, I presume, Madam?” said he, very gravely.

"在我此刻最诚心希望自己在的地方！"

"先生的放肆，用在相熟的人身上，或许没那么讨厌；可对*我*——"
"您真公道，"他打断我喊道，"是，我这个人处熟了确实可爱；往后您会完全被我迷住的。"
"往后，先生，我但愿永远不——"
"哦嘘！——嘘！——您忘了我发现您时的处境了？——您忘了，人弃您而去时，是我追的您——人负您时，是我崇拜的您？——若不是我这——"
"若不是您，先生，我兴许还是快乐的呢。"
"那么，我是否可以推定：*若不是有我*，您那位*舞伴*早出现了？——可怜的家伙！——我的在场吓着他了？"
"我倒巴望*他的*在场，先生，能吓着*您*！"
"他来了！——这么说，您看见他了？"
"或许，先生，我看见了。"我叫道，实在听腻了他的打趣。
"在哪儿？在哪儿？——看老天爷份上，指给我看那个可怜虫！"
"可怜虫，先生！"
"哦，一头野蛮畜生！——一个鬼祟、没脸、可鄙的幼犬！"
我不知道是什么迷了我——自尊受了伤，心也乏了——总而言之，我一时糊涂，望着奥维尔勋爵，应了一句："*可鄙的*，您说？"
他的目光立刻追上我的："怎么，*那位*就是那位先生？"
我不答；我不能认，也不肯否：——我指望他认错了人，好把我从他的纠缠里解出来。
刚刚做完他所谓的礼数，我便急不可待地要回米尔文太太那边去。
"回您*舞伴*那边去，我猜，夫人？"他极郑重地说。
这话把我窘坏了。我怕这个捣乱的人不知他的身份，径直找上奥维尔勋爵，说出什么来拆穿我的把戏。傻呀，把自己卷进这样的难局！

===Original===

I now feared what I had before wished; and therefore, to avoid Lord Orville, I was obliged myself to *propose* going down another dance, though I was ready to sink with shame while I spoke.
“But your *partner*, Ma’am?” said he, affecting a very solemn air, “perhaps he may resent my detaining you: if you will give me leave to ask his consent﻿—”
“Not for the universe.”
“Who is he, Madam?”
I wished myself a hundred miles off. He repeated his question, “What is his name?”
“Nothing﻿—nobody﻿—I don’t know﻿—”
He assumed a most important solemnity: “How!﻿—not know?﻿—Give me leave, my dear Madam, to recommend this caution to you: Never dance in public with a stranger﻿—with one whose name you are unacquainted with﻿—who may be a mere adventurer﻿—a man of no character, consider to what impertinence you may expose yourself.”
Was ever anything so ridiculous? I could not help laughing, in spite of my vexation.
At this instant, Mrs. Mirvan, followed by Lord Orville, walked up to us. You will easily believe it was not difficult for me to recover my gravity; but what was my consternation, when this strange man, destined to be the scourge of my artifice, exclaimed, “Ha! My Lord Orville!﻿—I protest I did not know your Lordship. What can I say for my usurpation?﻿—Yet, faith, my Lord, such a prize was not to be neglected.”
My shame and confusion were unspeakable. Who could have supposed or foreseen that this man knew Lord Orville? But falsehood is not more unjustifiable than unsafe.
Lord Orville﻿—well he might﻿—looked all amazement.
“The philosophic coldness of your Lordship,” continued this odious creature, “every man is not endowed with. I have used my utmost endeavours to entertain this lady, though I fear without success; and your Lordship will not be a little flattered, if acquainted with the difficulty which attended my procuring the honour of only one dance.” Then, turning to me, who was sinking with shame, while Lord Orville stood motionless, and Mrs. Mirvan astonished﻿—he suddenly seized my hand, saying, “Think, my Lord, what must be my reluctance to resign this fair hand to your Lordship!”
In the same instant, Lord Orville took it of him; I coloured violently, and made an effort to recover it.

===Chinese===

此刻我怕的正是我先前盼的；于是为了避开奥维尔勋爵，我竟不得不*主动*提议再跳一支——说话时我羞得几乎要沉到地底。
"可是您那位*舞伴*呢，夫人？"他装出一副顶郑重的神气说，"他或许要怪我扣住您了；您若肯容我去征求他的同意——"
"万万不可。"
"他是谁，夫人？"
我恨不得自己在百里之外。他又问一遍："他姓甚名谁？"
"没什么——没人——我不知道——"
他摆出一副了不得的庄严："怎么！——不知道？——容小人进一言，亲爱的夫人：劝您一条——今后切莫在公共场合同生人跳舞——同一个您连姓名都不知道的人跳——他没准儿是个纯粹冒险家——一个没有品行的人；想想您可能把自己暴露给怎样的纠缠。"
世上还有比这更可笑的事么？尽管一肚子恼，我还是没忍住笑。
正在这时，米尔文太太朝我们走来，奥维尔勋爵随在身后。您想得到，我恢复端凝并不难；可当我这个命中注定来惩罚我狡计的怪人喊出——"哈！奥维尔勋爵！——我竟没认出大人您。我的僭越，可怎么说呢？——不过说真的，大人，这样的猎物可不能错过。"——这时我的羞与慌真没法说了。谁能料到、谁能预见这人竟认识奥维尔勋爵？可见假话不但不该，而且不安全。
奥维尔勋爵——也难怪——满脸惊愕。
"大人您那哲人般的冷静，"这个可憎的东西接下去，"并非人人禀赋。小人已竭尽所能娱这位夫人，只怕白费；大人您若知道，小人仅仅为求执手一舞之荣，曾经历怎样的艰难，您必定大为受用。"说着，他转向我——我正羞得往下沉，奥维尔勋爵僵立着，米尔文太太惊得说不出话——他突然抓住我的手，说："想想，大人，把这双玉手奉还大人，小人是多么不舍！"
就在同一瞬，奥维尔勋爵从他手里把我的手接了过去；我满脸通红，用力想抽回。

===Original===

“You do me too much honour, Sir,” cried he, (with an air of gallantry, pressing it to his lips before he let it go); “however, I shall be happy to profit by it, if this lady,” turning to Mrs. Mirvan, “will permit me to seek for her party.”
To compel him thus to dance, I could not endure; and eagerly called out, “By no means﻿—not for the world!﻿—I must beg﻿—”
“Will you honour *me*, Madam, with your commands,” cried my tormentor; “may *I* seek the lady’s party?”
“No, Sir,” answered I, turning from him.
“What *shall* be done, my dear?” said Mrs. Mirvan.
“Nothing, Ma’am;﻿—anything, I mean﻿—”
“But do you dance, or not? you see his Lordship waits.”
“I hope not﻿—I beg that﻿—I would not for the world﻿—I am sure I ought to﻿—to﻿—”
I could not speak; but that confident man, determining to discover whether or not I had deceived him, said to Lord Orville, who stood suspended, “My Lord, this affair, which at present seems perplexed, I will briefly explain:﻿—this lady proposed to me another dance﻿—nothing could have made me more happy﻿—I only wished for your Lordship’s permission; which, if now granted, will, I am persuaded, set everything right.”
I glowed with indignation. “No, Sir﻿—it is your absence, and that alone, can set everything right.”
“For Heaven’s sake, my dear,” cried Mrs. Mirvan, who could no longer contain her surprise, “what does all this mean?﻿—were you pre-engaged?﻿—had Lord Orville﻿—”
“No, Madam,” cried I, “only﻿—only I did not know that gentleman﻿—and so﻿—and so I thought﻿—I intended﻿—I﻿—”
Overpowered by all that had passed, I had not strength to make my mortifying explanation;﻿—my spirits quite failed me, and I burst into tears.
They all seemed shocked and amazed.
“What is the matter, my dearest love?” cried Mrs. Mirvan, with kindest concern.
“What have I done!” exclaimed my evil genius, and ran officiously for a glass of water.
However, a hint was sufficient for Lord Orville, who comprehended all I would have explained. He immediately led me to a seat, and said in a low voice, “Be not distressed, I beseech you: I shall ever think my name honoured by your making use of it.”
This politeness relieved me. A general murmur had alarmed Miss Mirvan, who flew instantly to me; while Lord Orville the moment Mrs. Mirvan had taken the water, led my tormentor away.
“For Heaven’s sake, dear Madam,” cried I, “let me go home;﻿—indeed I cannot stay here any longer.”

===Chinese===

"先生，您太抬举我了，"他喊（带着一股献殷勤的气派，把它按到唇边才放手）；"不过，倘若这位夫人，"他转向米尔文太太，"肯容我去寻她的一伙，我乐意叨光。"
这样逼他跳舞，我怎么受得了；急忙喊道："使不得——万万使不得！——我必须求——"
"夫人可肯赏*我*脸面，"我的折磨者喊，"可否由*我*去寻这位夫人的一伙？"
"不，先生。"我扭开脸答。
"那可怎么办呢，亲爱的？"米尔文太太说。
"不怎么办，夫人；——我是说，随便怎么办——"
"可你到底跳还是不跳？勋爵大人等着呢。"
"我但愿不跳——我求——我死也不肯——我确实应该——应该——"
我说不下去；可那个厚脸的人存心要查个明白，我究竟骗没骗他，便对僵立着的奥维尔勋爵说："大人，这桩眼下看似纠结的事，小人三言两语便可讲明：——是这位夫人向小人提议再跳一舞的——小人再快活不过——只求大人恩准；您此刻点了头，小人相信，一切便都顺了。"
我气得满脸发烫。"不，先生——要一切顺，唯有您走开。"
"看在老天份上，亲爱的，"米尔文太太再按捺不住惊讶，"这都是怎么一回事？——你先有约了？——是不是奥维尔勋爵——"
"没有，夫人，"我叫道，"只是——只是我不认识那位先生——所以——所以我想到——我本想——我——"
经过的一切压倒了我，我没了力气作这丢人的解释；——心气一泄，眼泪夺眶而出。
他们全都惊呆了。
"怎么了，我最亲爱的宝贝？"米尔文太太最关切地喊。
"我闯了什么祸呀！"我的凶神喊，慌忙殷勤地跑去取一杯水。
不过，一点就透——奥维尔勋爵全明白了我想要解释的一切。他立刻领我入座，低声说："请别难过，我求您：您肯用我的名字，我永远引以为荣。"
这份体面解脱了我。一阵低低的骚动惊动了米尔文小姐，她立刻飞到我身边；米尔文太太一接过水，奥维尔勋爵便把我的折磨者引开了。
"看老天份上，亲爱的夫人，"我叫道，"让我回家吧；——我实在不能再待在这儿了。"

===Original===

“Let us all go,” cried my kind Maria.
“But the Captain, what will he say﻿—I had better go home in a chair.”
Mrs. Mirvan consented, and I rose to depart. Lord Orville and that man both came to me. The first, with an attention I but ill-merited from him, led me to a chair; while the other followed, pestering me with apologies. I wished to have made mine to Lord Orville, but was too much ashamed.
It was about one o’clock. Mrs. Mirvan’s servants saw me home.
And now﻿—what again shall ever tempt me to an assembly? I dread to hear what you will think of me, my most dear and honoured Sir: you will need your utmost partiality to receive me without displeasure.
This morning Lord Orville has sent to enquire after our health; and Sir Clement Willoughby, for that, I find, is the name of my persecutor, has called; but I would not go downstairs till he was gone.
And now, my dear Sir, I can somewhat account for the strange, provoking, and ridiculous conduct of this Sir Clement last night; for Miss Mirvan says he is the very man with whom she heard Lord Orville conversing at Mrs. Stanley’s, when I was spoken of in so mortifying a manner. He was pleased to say he was glad to hear I was a fool; and therefore, I suppose, he concluded he might talk as much nonsense as he pleased to me: however, I am very indifferent as to his opinion;﻿—but for Lord Orville﻿—if then he thought me an idiot, now, I am sure, he must suppose me both bold and presuming. Make use of his name!﻿—what impertinence﻿—he can never know how it happened﻿—he can only imagine it was from an excess of vanity;﻿—well, however, I shall leave this bad city tomorrow, and never again will I enter it.
The Captain intends to take us tonight to the fantoccini. I cannot bear that Captain; I can give you no idea how gross he is. I heartily rejoice that he was not present at the disagreeable conclusion of yesterday’s adventure, for I am sure he would have contributed to my confusion; which might, perhaps, have diverted him, as he seldom or never smiles but at some other person’s expense.
And here I conclude my London letters﻿—and without any regret; for I am too inexperienced and ignorant to conduct myself with propriety in this town, where everything is new to me, and many things are unaccountable and perplexing.
Adieu, my dear Sir; Heaven restore me safely to you!

===Chinese===

"咱们都走。"我好心的玛丽亚喊。
"可舰长会怎么说——我还是单坐一顶轿椅回去的好。"
米尔文太太应了，我起身告辞。奥维尔勋爵同那个人都走了过来。前者以一种我全然不配得的体贴，扶我上轿椅；后者跟在后头，一路拿告罪烦我。我本想向奥维尔勋爵致歉，实在羞得开不了口。
那时约莫一点钟。米尔文太太的仆人送我回的家。
如今——还有什么能再诱我去舞会？我最亲爱、最敬爱的先生，我怕听您怎么想我：要您不带着不快收下我，得用上您全部的偏心才行。
今晨奥维尔勋爵遣人来问安；克莱门特·威洛比爵士（Sir Clement Willoughby）——我发现这正是那位纠缠我的人的姓名——也来访过；我躲着不肯下楼，直到他走了。
而现在，亲爱的先生，我多少能解释昨晚克莱门特爵士那奇怪、气人、可笑的行径了：米尔文小姐说，斯坦利夫人家那晚——就是说我被人那样难堪地议论的那晚——同奥维尔勋爵交谈的，正是此人。他既爱说"听说她是傻瓜，我很高兴"，想必便断定：同我讲多少浑话都不妨。不过，他怎么看我，我全无所谓；——至于奥维尔勋爵——他那时既当我是白痴，如今，我确信，他必以为我又胆大又狂妄。用他的名字！——好大的唐突——他永远无从知道其中原委——只能想象是出于虚荣的过分。——罢了，反正明天我就离开这座坏城，永不再来。
舰长今晚要带我们去看木偶戏。那个舰长，我受不了；他有多粗鄙，我没法向您形容。昨夜那桩不愉快的收场他幸而不在，我真是由衷庆幸；他若在场，准会火上浇油；说不定还会引为笑乐——他不取笑别人，就几乎从不笑。
我的伦敦书简到此为止——毫无遗憾；我太无知太不懂事，在这样的城里举止无法得体：这里于我样样新鲜，许多事无从解释、无从捉摸。
再会，亲爱的先生；愿上天保我平安回到您身边！

===Original===

I wish I was to go immediately to Berry Hill; yet the wish is ungrateful to Mrs. Mirvan, and therefore I will repress it. I shall write an account of the fantoccini from Howard Grove. We have not been to half the public places that are now open, though I dare say you will think we have been to all. But they are almost as innumerable as the persons who fill them.

===Chinese===

我但愿这就直奔贝里山；可这念头亏负了米尔文太太，我只好把它按下。木偶戏的观后感，我从霍华德林苑写给您。眼下开着的公共场所，我们连一半都没去到——虽然我敢说您已当我们全去遍了。可它们几乎同填满它们的人头一样数不清。

## Letter / 书信
===Original===

XIV Evelina in Continuation
Queen Ann Street, April 13.
How much will you be surprised, my dearest Sir, at receiving another letter, from London, of your Evelina’s writing! But, believe me, it was not my fault, neither is it my happiness, that I am still here: our journey has been postponed by an accident equally unexpected and disagreeable.
We went last night to see the fantoccini, where we had infinite entertainment from the performance of a little comedy in French and Italian, by puppets, so admirably managed, that they both astonished and diverted us all, except the Captain, who has a fixed and most prejudiced hatred of whatever is not English.
When it was over, while we waited for the coach, a tall elderly woman brushed quickly past us, calling out, “My God, what shall I do?”
“Why, what *would* you do?” cried the Captain.
“*Ma foi, Monsieur*,” answered she, “I have lost my company, and in this place I don’t know nobody.”
There was something foreign in her accent, though it was difficult to discover whether she was an English or a French woman. She was very well dressed; and seemed so entirely at a loss what to do, that Mrs. Mirvan proposed to the Captain to assist her.
“Assist her!” cried he, “ay, with all my heart;﻿—let a linkboy call her a coach.”
There was not one to be had, and it rained very fast.
“*Mon Dieu!*” exclaimed the stranger, “what shall become of me? *Je suis au désespoir!*”
“Dear Sir,” cried Miss Mirvan, “pray let us take the poor lady into our coach. She is quite alone, and a foreigner﻿—”
“She’s never the better for that,” answered he: “she may be a woman of the town, for anything you know.”
“She does not appear such,” said Mrs. Mirvan; “and indeed she seems so much distressed, that we shall but follow the golden rule, if we carry her to her lodgings.”
“You are mighty fond of new acquaintance,” returned he; “but first let us know if she be going our way.”
Upon enquiry, we found that she lived in Oxford Road; and, after some disputing, the Captain surlily, and, with a very bad grace, consented to admit her into his coach; though he soon convinced us, that he was determined she should not be too much obliged to him, for he seemed absolutely bent upon quarrelling with her: for which strange inhospitality I can assign no other reason, than that she appeared to be a foreigner.

===Chinese===

第十四封 伊芙琳娜续
女王安妮街，4月13日。
最亲爱的先生，再收到一封您伊芙琳娜从伦敦写来的信，您要多吃惊！可是请相信：人还在这里，既不是我的错，也不是我的福：我们的行程被一件又意外又糟糕的事故搁下了。
昨晚我们去看木偶戏，一出自法文和意大利文改编的小喜剧，由木偶演出，演得那样精妙，我们人人又惊又乐——只除舰长，凡不是英国的，他一律抱着一份死心眼的仇恨。
散场后我们等马车时，一个高个子老太太匆匆擦过我们身边，嘴里嚷着："我的天，这可怎么好？"
"嗬，您想*怎么*好？"舰长喊。
"*真的，先生*，"她答，"我同我的伴儿走散了，这地方我谁也不认得。"
她的口音里有股外国味，可她是英国人还是法国人，又难以断定。她穿得很好；那副全然没了主意的样子，叫米尔文太太提议舰长去帮帮她。
"帮她！"他喊，"行啊，乐意之至——叫个火把童儿去给她叫辆车。"
一辆也雇不着，雨又下得急。
"*我的天！*"那位陌生太太喊，"我可怎么办呀？*我急死了！*"
"亲爱的先生，"米尔文小姐喊，"求求您，让这位可怜的太太搭我们的车吧。她孤身一人，又是外国人——"
"沾这个光不成，"他答，"谁知道呢，她兴许还是个窑姐儿呢。"
"她不像那样的人，"米尔文太太说；"再说她实在窘得很，我们送她回住处，不过是行那条金律。"
"你可真爱结新交，"他回嘴；"不过先得弄清，她顺不顺路。"
一问，她住在牛津路；争了几句，舰长悻悻地、老大不情愿地同意让她上车；不过他随即就让我们看明白了：他打定主意不叫她受他太多恩——他简直存心同她吵架；这份奇怪的怠客，我猜不出别的缘故，只因她看着是个外国人。

===Original===

The conversation began, by her telling us, that she had been in England only two days; that the gentlemen belonging to her were Parisians, and had left her to see for a hackney-coach, as her own carriage was abroad; and that she had waited for them till she was quite frightened, and concluded that they had lost themselves.
“And pray,” said the Captain, “why did you go to a public place without an Englishman?”
“*Ma foi*, Sir,” answered she, “because none of my acquaintance is in town.”
“Why then,” said he, “I’ll tell you what, your best way is to go out of it yourself.”
“*Pardi, Monsieur*,” returned she, “and so I shall; for, I promise you, I think the English a parcel of brutes; and I’ll go back to France as fast as I can, for I would not live among none of you.”
“Who wants you?” cried the Captain: “do you suppose, Madam French, we have not enough of other nations to pick our pockets already? I’ll warrant you, there’s no need for you for to put in your oar.”
“Pick your pockets, Sir! I wish nobody wanted to pick your pockets no more than I do; and I’ll promise you you’d be safe enough. But there’s no nation under the sun can beat the English for ill-politeness: for my part, I hate the very sight of them; and so I shall only just visit a person of quality or two of my particular acquaintance, and then I shall go back again to France.”
“Ay, do,” cried he; “and then go to the devil together, for that’s the fittest voyage for the French and the quality.”
“We’ll take care, however,” cried the stranger with great vehemence, “not to admit none of your vulgar unmannered English among us.”
“O never fear,” returned he, coolly, “we shan’t dispute the point with you; you and the quality may have the devil all to yourselves.”
Desirous of changing the subject of a conversation which now became very alarming, Miss Mirvan called out, “Lord, how slow the man drives!”
“Never mind, Moll,” said her father, “I’ll warrant you he’ll drive fast enough tomorrow, when you are going to Howard Grove.”
“To Howard Grove!” exclaimed the stranger, “why, *mon Dieu*, do you know Lady Howard?”
“Why, what if we do?” answered he; “that’s nothing to you; she’s none of *your* quality, I’ll promise you.”
“Who told you that?” cried she; “you don’t know nothing about the matter!

===Chinese===

话是这样开的头：她告诉我们，她来英格兰才两天；随行的那几位先生是巴黎人，出去雇街车去了——她自家的马车没运到；她等他们直等到心里发毛，断定他们迷了路。
"请问，"舰长说，"您去公共场合，怎么不带个英国人？"
"*真的，先生*，"她答，"因为我的相识一个也不在城里呀。"
"那好，"他说，"我告诉你，您最好的法子，就是自己出城去。"
"*说真话，先生*，"她回敬，"我正要这样呢；因为我告诉你，我把英国人当作一帮畜生；我多快回法国就多快回去，我决不同你们哪个人住在一处。"
"谁稀罕你？"舰长喊；"法国太太，您以为我们不趁别的国的人来掏我们腰包么？我保准，用不着您来插一杠子。"
"掏腰包，先生！我巴不得人人都不想掏您的腰包，像我一样；那您保险得很。不过论无礼，天下没有一个国家赛得过英国人；拿我说，我看都懒得看他们一眼；我不过拜访一两位我的私交叉贵人，就回法国去。"
"好啊，去呀，"他喊，"然后同他们一齐见魔鬼去，那才是配法国人和贵人的航程。"
"我们倒要小心，"那位陌生太太火气十足地喊，"不放进你们任何粗俗没规矩的英国人。"
"哦，放心，"他冷冷地回，"这一点我们不同你们争；魔鬼你们同贵人独享就是了。"
眼看话头越来越吓人，米尔文小姐想岔开，喊道："天哪，这车夫赶得多慢！"
"别忙，小妞，"她父亲说，"保准明天你去霍华德林苑时，他赶得够快。"
"去霍华德林苑！"那位太太喊道，"怎么，*我的天*，你们认识霍华德夫人？"
"认识又怎样？"他答；"与你何干；她可不是*你们那种*贵人，我担保。"
"谁告诉你的？"她喊；"这事你一概不知！

===Original===

besides, you’re the ill-bredest person ever I see: and as to your knowing Lady Howard, I don’t believe no such a thing; unless, indeed, you are her steward.”
The Captain, swearing terribly, said, with great fury, “*You* would much sooner be taken for her washwoman.”
“Her washwoman, indeed?﻿—Ha, ha, ha, why you han’t no eyes; did you ever see a washwoman in such a gown as this?﻿—Besides, I’m no such mean person, for I’m as good as Lady Howard, and as rich too; and besides, I’m now come to England to visit her.”
“You may spare yourself that there trouble,” said the Captain, “she has paupers enough about her already.”
“Paupers, Mister!﻿—no more a pauper than yourself, nor so much neither;﻿—but you are a low, dirty fellow, and I shan’t stoop to take no more notice of you.”
“Dirty fellow!” exclaimed the Captain, seizing both her wrists, “hark you, Mrs. Frog, you’d best hold your tongue; for I must make bold to tell you, if you don’t, that I shall make no ceremony of tripping you out of the window, and there you may lie in the mud till some of your *Monseers* come to help you out of it.”
Their increasing passion quite terrified us; and Mrs. Mirvan was beginning to remonstrate with the Captain, when we were all silenced by what follows.
“Let me go, villain that you are, let me go, or I’ll promise you I’ll get you put to prison for this usage. I’m no common person, I assure you; and, *ma foi*, I’ll go to Justice Fielding about you; for I’m a person of fashion, and I’ll make you know it, or my name a’n’t Duval.”
I heard no more: amazed, frightened, and unspeakably shocked, an involuntary exclamation of *Gracious Heaven!* escaped me, and, more dead than alive, I sunk into Mrs. Mirvan’s arms. But let me draw a veil over a scene too cruel for a heart so compassionately tender as yours; it is sufficient that you know this supposed foreigner proved to be Madame Duval﻿—the grandmother of your Evelina!
O, Sir, to discover so near a relation in a woman, who had thus introduced herself!﻿—what would become of me, were it not for you, my protector, my friend, and my refuge?
My extreme concern, and Mrs. Mirvan’s surprise, immediately betrayed me. But, I will not shock you with the manner of her acknowledging me, or the bitterness, the *grossness*﻿—I cannot otherwise express myself﻿—with which she spoke of those unhappy past transactions you have so pathetically related to me.

===Chinese===

再说，你是我平生所见最没教养的人；至于你说认识霍华德夫人，我才不信呢——除非，你当真是她的管家。"
舰长恶狠狠咒骂着，怒气冲冲地说："*你*倒更像个给她洗衣服的。"
"洗衣服的，是么？——哈，哈，哈，你眼珠子都没长；你见过穿这样袍子的洗衣妇么？——再说，我才不是那样下贱的人：我同霍华德夫人一样好，一样阔；况且我这回上英格兰，就是来看她的。"
"那您不妨省下这个麻烦，"舰长说，"她手边的穷亲戚够多的了。"
"穷亲戚，先生！——你不比我穷才怪，还赶不上我呢；——你是个下流胚、脏东西，我犯不上再理你。"
"脏东西！"舰长喊，一把攫住她两腕，"你听好，青蛙太太，你最好住嘴；我索性告诉你，你再不住口，我就不客气，把你从车窗里扔出去，叫你躺在泥里，等你的哪位*法国爷*来捞你。"
两人火气越蹿越高，吓坏了我们；米尔文太太正要劝舰长，接下来的一幕，把我们都镇住了。
"放开我，你这个恶棍，放开我，不然我保准叫人为这一顿好进监狱。我不是平头百姓，我告诉你；*真的*，我要到菲尔丁法官那里告你去；我是有身份的人，我非叫你知道不可，不然我就不姓杜瓦尔。"
后面的话我没听见：惊讶、惊吓、说不出的震惊之中，一声"慈悲的天哪！"不由自主地冲出我口，我半死不活地倒进米尔文太太怀里。可是，这样一幕太残酷了，不宜呈给您那样慈悲柔软的心，且让我拉一幅幕把它遮住；您只需知道：这位假定外邦人，原来是杜瓦尔夫人——您伊芙琳娜的外祖母！
哦，先生，这样一个近亲，竟以这副样子自己登场！——若不是有您，我的保护人、我的朋友、我的避难所，我可怎么办？
我的极度失态同米尔文太太的惊讶，立刻把我出卖了。可她认下我的那一幕，她提起那些不幸往事时的刻毒、*粗恶*——我找不到别的字眼——我不忍转述给您，您早已那样哀婉地讲给我听过的往事。

===Original===

All the misery of a much injured parent, dear, though never seen, regretted, though never known, crowded so forcibly upon my memory, that they rendered this interview﻿—one only excepted﻿—the most afflicting I can ever know.
When we stopped at her lodgings, she desired me to accompany her into the house, and said she could easily procure a room for me to sleep in. Alarmed and trembling, I turned to Mrs. Mirvan. “My daughter, Madam,” said that sweet woman, “cannot so abruptly part with her young friend; you must allow a little time to wean them from each other.”
“Pardon me, Ma’am,” answered Madame Duval, (who, from the time of her being known, somewhat softened her manners) “Miss can’t possibly be so nearly connected to this child as I am.”
“No matter for that,” cried the Captain, (who espoused my cause to satisfy his own pique, though an awkward apology had passed between them) “she was sent to us; and so, dy’e see, we don’t choose for to part with her.”
I promised to wait upon her at what time she pleased the next day; and, after a short debate, she desired me to breakfast with her, and we proceeded to Queen Ann Street.
What an unfortunate adventure! I could not close my eyes the whole night. A thousand times I wished I had never left Berry Hill: however, my return thither shall be accelerated to the utmost of my power; and, once more in that abode of tranquil happiness, I will suffer no temptation to allure me elsewhere.
Mrs. Mirvan was so kind as to accompany me to Madame Duval’s house this morning. The Captain, too, offered his service; which I declined, from a fear she should suppose I meant to insult her.
She frowned most terribly upon Mrs. Mirvan; but she received me with as much tenderness as I believe she is capable of feeling. Indeed, our meeting seems really to have affected her; for when, overcome by the variety of emotions which the sight of her occasioned, I almost fainted in her arms, she burst into tears, and said, “let me not lose my poor daughter a second time!” This unexpected humanity softened me extremely; but she very soon excited my warmest indignation, by the ungrateful mention she made of the best of men, my dear and most generous benefactor. However, grief and anger mutually gave way to terror, upon her avowing the intention of her visiting England was to make me return with her to France.

===Chinese===

一位深受伤害的母亲的全部苦楚——亲爱的、却从未谋面，追念的、却从不相识——一齐涌上我的心头，逼得这场会面——除一场外——成了我此生最刺痛的一场。
车停在她寓所门前，她要我陪她进屋，说她不难替我张罗一间过夜的屋子。我惊慌发抖，转向米尔文太太。"我的女儿，夫人，"那位可亲的太太说，"不能这样突然地同她年轻的朋友分手；您得容一点工夫，让她们慢慢分开。"
"恕我直言，太太，"杜瓦尔夫人答（自被认出之后，她的做派略软了些），"小姐同这孩子的亲分，怎么也近不过我。"
"那管不着，"舰长喊（他站在我这边，只为出自己那口气；两人之间虽已草草道过歉），"她是送到我们这里的；所以，你瞧，我们不乐意放人。"
我答应翌日她什么时候方便，什么时候去拜望她；短促一番争执后，她约我同她共进早餐，然后我们回到女王安妮街。
多倒霉的一场奇遇！我一夜没能合眼。一千次地懊悔当初不该离开贝里山：不过，我的归期要竭力提前；一旦回到那宁静幸福之所，任什么诱惑也休想再引我出门。
今晨，米尔文太太好意陪我去了杜瓦尔夫人府上。舰长也要效劳；我谢绝了，怕她疑心我存心辱她。
她朝米尔文太太皱了顶凶的眉；接待我，却带着她这人想必仅有的那点温情。说真的，我们的见面像是真动了她；当我被见到她所激起的重重情绪压倒、几乎晕在她怀里时，她竟落下泪来，说："别让我第二次失去我可怜的女儿！"这份出乎意料的仁慈把我大大软化了；可她很快又提起那位最好的人——我亲爱的、最慷慨的恩主——所用的那些忘恩负义的字眼，把我最热的义愤激了起来。然而，等她宣布：她此番访英，为的是带我一同回法国——悲愤又一同让位于恐惧。

===Original===

This, she said, was a plan she had formed from the instant she had heard of my birth; which, she protested, did not reach her ears till I must have been twelve years of age; but Monsieur Duval, who she declared was the worst husband in the world, would not permit her to do anything she wished: he had been dead but three months; which had been employed in arranging certain affairs, that were no sooner settled, than she set off for England. She was already out of mourning, for she said nobody here could tell how long she had been a widow.
She must have been married very early in life: what her age is I do not know; but she really looks to be less than fifty. She dresses very gaily, paints very high, and the traces of former beauty are still very visible in her face.
I know not when, or how, this visit would have ended, had not the Captain called for Mrs. Mirvan, and absolutely insisted upon my attending her. He is become, very suddenly, so warmly my friend, that I quite dread his officiousness. Mrs. Mirvan, however, whose principal study seems to be healing those wounds which her husband inflicts, appeased Madame Duval’s wrath, by a very polite invitation to drink tea and spend the evening here. Not without great difficulty was the Captain prevailed upon to defer his journey some time longer; but what could be done? It would have been indecent for me to have quitted town the very instant I discovered that Madame Duval was in it; and to have stayed here solely under her protection﻿—Mrs. Mirvan, thank Heaven, was too kind for such a thought. That she should follow us to Howard Grove, I almost equally dreaded. It is therefore determined, that we remain in London for some days, or a week: though the Captain has declared that the *old French hag*, as he is pleased to call her, shall fare never the better for it.
My only hope is to get safe to Berry Hill; where, counselled and sheltered by you, I shall have nothing more to fear. Adieu, my ever dear and most honoured Sir! I shall have no happiness till I am again with you.

===Chinese===

她说，这是她一听说我的出世就定下的计划；她赌咒说，那消息传到她耳朵时，我必定已有十二岁了；可杜瓦尔先生——她一口咬定是天下最坏的丈夫——不许她做任何她想做的事：他死了才三个月；这三个月用来料理几件事务，一了结，她就动身来了英格兰。她的丧服已经脱了，她说，反正这儿没人知道她守寡多久。
她一定嫁得很早：她的年纪我不知道；可她看上去实在不到五十。她穿得极艳，粉搽得极厚，当年姿色的痕迹，在她脸上还看得很清楚。
这一场拜访何时、怎样收的场，我不得而知，幸而舰长来接米尔文太太，一口咬定要我随她回去。他一下子变得这样起劲地做我的朋友，那份殷勤倒叫我发怵。米尔文太太呢——她的主修课仿佛就是医治丈夫砍下的伤口——用一份极其客气的邀请，请杜瓦尔夫人来喝茶、共度今晚，把她的怒火平息了。又费了好大的劲，才劝得舰长把行期再推些时候；可又有什么法子呢？我刚发现杜瓦尔夫人在城里，掉头就走，于礼不合；可单单留在她的护翼下——感谢上天，米尔文太太没有那样狠心。至于她跟到霍华德林苑去，我也几乎一样怕。于是议定：我们在伦敦再留几天，或一个星期：虽说舰长已放话，那个*法国老妖婆*——他偏这样叫她——休想因此得半点便宜。
我唯一的指望，是平安回到贝里山；有您指教、有您庇护，我就再没什么可怕的了。再会，我永远亲爱、最敬重的先生！不到您身边，我没有幸福可言。

## Letter / 书信
===Original===

XV Mr. Villars to Evelina
Berry Hill, April 16.
In the belief and hope that my Evelina would, ere now, have bid adieu to London, I had intended to have deferred writing, till I heard of her return to Howard Grove; but the letter I have this moment received, with intelligence of Madame Duval’s arrival in England, demands an immediate answer.
Her journey hither equally grieves and alarms me. How much did I pity my child, when I read of a discovery at once so unexpected and unwished! I have long dreaded this meeting and its consequence; to claim you seems naturally to follow acknowledging you. I am well acquainted with her disposition, and have for many years foreseen the contest which now threatens us.
Cruel as are the circumstances of this affair, you must not, my love, suffer it to depress your spirits: remember, that while life is lent me, I will devote it to your service; and, for future time, I will make such provisions as shall seem to me most conducive to your future happiness. Secure of my protection, and relying on my tenderness, let no apprehensions of Madame Duval disturb your peace: conduct yourself towards her with all the respect and deference due to so near a relation, remembering always, that the failure of duty on her part, can by no means justify any neglect on yours. Indeed, the more forcibly you are struck with improprieties and misconduct in another, the greater should be your observance and diligence to avoid even the shadow of similar errors. Be careful, therefore, that no remissness of attention, no indifference of obliging, make known to her the independence I assure you of; but when she fixes the time for her leaving England, trust to me the task of refusing your attending her: disagreeable to myself, I own, it will be; yet to you it would be improper, if not impossible.
In regard to her opinion of me, I am more sorry than surprised at her determined blindness; the palliation which she feels the want of, for her own conduct, leads her to seek for failings in all who were concerned in those unhapppy transactions which she has so much reason to lament. And this, as it is the cause, so we must in some measure consider it as the excuse of her inveteracy.
How grateful to me are your wishes to return to Berry Hill! Your lengthened stay in London, and the dissipation in which I find you are involved, fill me with uneasiness.

===Chinese===

第十五封 维拉尔斯先生致伊芙琳娜
贝里山，4月16日。
我本相信、也盼望我的伊芙琳娜此刻早已辞别伦敦，故打算等闻她回到霍华德林苑再写信；可方才接到的信，带来杜瓦尔夫人到英格兰的消息，不能不作速回复。
她这趟来，叫我一样地忧、一样地惊。读到那样一场既意外又非所愿的相认时，我多么怜我的孩子！这场会面同它的后果，我忌惮已久；认了你，接下来自然便是要索你。她的性子我深知，今日威胁着我们的这场争执，我多年前便已预见。
事情的情由虽残酷，我的爱，你却不可任它压垮你的心气：记住，只要我一息尚存，这条命便献给你效力；至于将来，我会作那样的安排，在我看来最能助你日后的幸福。有我的保护作倚靠，有我的慈爱可信赖，任凭杜瓦尔夫人，也不许她搅扰你的安宁：对她，你要拿出对这样一位近亲应尽的全部敬重与顺从，并且永远记住：她那一头失了本分，断不能成为你这一头怠慢的借口。恰恰相反：旁人的失检失德，在你眼前映照得越分明，你越该勤勉自守，连类似过错的影子也避开。因此千万留意，莫让一丝懈怠、一点不情愿的淡漠，把我向你担保的那份独立，泄露给她；等她定下离英的日子，把"拒绝你随行"这桩差事，交给我：我自己承认，那于我是苦差；可于你，则是不当，甚至不可能。
至于她对我的看法，我对她这份死心眼的偏执，与其说惊讶，不如说难过；她既需要为自己当年的行事寻找开脱，便不免向那桩她大有理由哀恸的不幸往事里、所有相关的人身上去寻过错。这既是她的病根，我们也只好多少当作她的托词。
你想回贝里山的那些话，于我多么可感！你在伦敦盘桓这许久，又——据我所知——陷在那样多的消遣里，叫我好不安。

===Original===

I mean not, however, that I would have you sequester yourself from the party to which you belong, since Mrs. Mirvan might thence infer a reproof which your youth and her kindness would render inexcusable. I will not, therefore, enlarge upon this subject; but content myself with telling you, that I shall heartily rejoice when I hear of your safe arrival at Howard Grove, for which place I hope you will be preparing at the time you receive this letter.
I cannot too much thank you, my best Evelina, for the minuteness of your communications. Continue to me this indulgence, for I should be miserable if in ignorance of your proceedings.
How new to you is the scene of life in which you are engaged!﻿—balls﻿—plays﻿—operas﻿—ridottos!﻿—Ah, my child! At your return hither, how will you bear the change? My heart trembles for your future tranquility.﻿—Yet I will hope everything from the unsullied whiteness of your soul, and the native liveliness of your disposition.
I am sure I need not say, how much more I was pleased with the mistakes of your inexperience at the private ball, than with the attempted adoption of more fashionable manners at the ridotto. But your confusion and mortifications were such as to entirely silence all reproofs on my part.
I hope you will see no more of Sir Clement Willoughby, whose conversation and boldness are extremely disgustful to me. I was gratified by the good nature of Lord Orville, upon your making use of his name; but I hope you will never again put it to such a trial.
Heaven bless thee, my dear child! And grant that neither misfortune nor vice may ever rob thee of that gaiety of heart, which, resulting from innocence, while it constitutes your own, contributes also to the felicity of all who know you!
Arthur Villars.

===Chinese===

不过我并非要你从你那一伙里自我幽闭；那样，米尔文太太会以为受了责备，以你的年轻同她的厚待，这是说不过去的。这个题目我就不多说了；只告诉你一句：闻你平安抵霍华德林苑之时，便是我衷心欢庆之时——我盼你读到这封信时，已在作回程的准备。
我最亲爱的伊芙琳娜，你通信的这样细，叫我感激不尽。请继续这样恩待我：你的行止我若一无所知，我是要苦坏的。
你正投身其中的人生的场景，于你多么新鲜！——舞会——戏剧——歌剧——里多托！——啊，我的孩子！待你回到这里，这落差你可怎么受？我的心为你将来的安宁发颤。——可是，凭你灵魂那未染的白，凭你天生的那股活泼，我什么都盼得。
用不着说：私家舞会上你不谙世事出的那些错，同里多托上你学时髦腔的那次尝试之间，前者给了我多少欢喜，比后者多得多。可你那时的惶乱与羞愧，早已把我这边的一切责备堵得无声了。
但愿你不再见到克莱门特·威洛比爵士，他的言谈同他的大胆，都叫我极其厌恶。你借用奥维尔勋爵之名时，他的厚道叫我心感；可我希望，你再不要把那个名字置于那样的试炼。
上天保佑你，我亲爱的孩子！愿灾殃与恶行，都永远夺不走你心头那份快活——它生自纯真，既成全你自己，也给一切识得你的人添福！
阿瑟·维拉尔斯。

## Letter / 书信
===Original===

XVI Evelina to the Rev. Mr. Villars
Queen Ann Street, Thursday morning, April 14.
Before our dinner was over yesterday Madame Duval came to tea; though it will lessen your surprise, to hear that it was near five o’clock, for we never dine till the day is almost over. She was asked into another room while the table was cleared, and then was invited to partake of the dessert.
She was attended by a French gentleman, whom she introduced by the name of Monsieur Du Bois: Mrs. Mirvan received them both with her usual politeness; but the Captain looked very much displeased; and after a short silence, very sternly said to Madame Duval, “Pray who asked you to bring that there spark with you?”
“O,” cried she, “I never go nowhere without him.”
Another short silence ensued, which was terminated by the Captain’s turning roughly to the foreigner, and saying, “Do you know, *Monseer*, that you are the first Frenchman I ever let come into my house?”
Monsieur Du Bois made a profound bow. He speaks no English, and understands it so imperfectly, that he might possibly imagine he had received a compliment.
Mrs. Mirvan endeavourd to divert the Captain’s ill-humour, by starting new subjects: but he left to her all the trouble of supporting them, and leant back in his chair in gloomy silence, except when any opportunity offered of uttering some sarcasm upon the French. Finding her efforts to render the evening agreeable were fruitless, Mrs. Mirvan proposed a party to Ranelagh. Madame Duval joyfully consented to it; and the Captain though he railed against the dissipation of the women, did not oppose it; and therefore Maria and I ran upstairs to dress ourselves.
Before we were ready, word was brought us that Sir Clement Willoughby was in the drawing room. He introduced himself under the pretence of enquiring after all our healths, and entered the room with the easy air of an old acquaintance; though Mrs. Mirvan confessed that he seemed embarrassed when he found how coldly he was received, not only by the Captain, but by herself.
I was extremely disconcerted at the thoughts of seeing this man again, and did not go downstairs till I was called to tea. He was then deeply engaged in a discourse upon French manners with Madame Duval and the Captain; and the subject seemed so entirely to engross him, that he did not, at first, observe my entrance into the room.

===Chinese===

第十六封 伊芙琳娜致尊敬的维拉尔斯牧师先生
女王安妮街，星期四早晨，4月14日。
昨日我们饭还没吃完，杜瓦尔夫人就来喝茶了；不过听说已近五点，您就不会那么吃惊了——我们开饭，总在白昼将尽的时候。收拾餐桌时，她被让进另一间屋，随后应邀入席用果点。
她带着一位法国先生，她介绍说叫杜布瓦先生（Monsieur Du Bois）：米尔文太太以她惯常的客气接待了他们两位；舰长却一脸不豫；短暂沉默之后，他硬邦邦地问杜瓦尔夫人："请问，谁请您带那位花花公子来的？"
"哦，"她喊，"我出门从不离他。"
又一阵短沉默，还是舰长粗声打破的：他转向那位外国人："您可知道，*法国爷*，您是我头一个让进家门的法国人？"
杜布瓦先生深深一躬。他不会英语，听也听不大懂，说不定还当自己领了夸奖。
米尔文太太想引新话题，岔开舰长的火气；可支撑话题的麻烦全落在她一人身上，舰长往椅背上一靠，阴沉地沉默，只在有机会损法国人一句时才开腔。她见把这一晚变得愉快的努力全归无效，便提议同去拉内拉夫。杜瓦尔夫人欢天喜地应了；舰长虽然骂太太小姐们荒唐，倒也没有反对；于是玛丽亚同我上楼更衣。
我们还没收拾停当，下人上来说克莱门特·威洛比爵士在客厅。他托词来问候全家的安康，自己引荐自己，进屋时一副老相识的随便派头；可米尔文太太承认，他发觉自己受到的冷遇——不但来自舰长，也来自她——之后，显得颇为尴尬。
一想到要再见这个人，我就心慌意乱，直到唤我喝茶才下去。他正同杜瓦尔夫人和舰长谈得起劲，谈的是法国风俗；这题目像是占了他全副心神，起初竟没留意我进屋。

===Original===

Their conversation was supported with great vehemence; the Captain roughly maintaining the superiority of the English in every particular, and Madame Duval warmly refusing to allow of it in any; while Sir Clement exerted all his powers of argument and of ridicule, to second and strengthen whatever was advanced by the Captain: for he had the sagacity to discover, that he could take no method so effectual for making the master of the house his friend, as to make Madame Duval his enemy; and indeed, in a very short time, he had reason to congratulate himself upon his successful discernment.
As soon as he saw me, he made a most respectful bow, and hoped I had not suffered from the fatigue of the ridotto: I made no other answer than a slight inclination of the head, for I was very much ashamed of that whole affair. He then returned to the disputants; where he managed the argument so skilfully, at once provoking Madame Duval, and delighting the Captain, that I could not forbear admiring his address, though I condemned his subtlety. Mrs. Mirvan, dreading such violent antagonists, attempted frequently to change the subject; and she might have succeeded, but for the interposition of Sir Clement, who would not suffer it to be given up, and supported it with such humour and satire, that he seems to have won the Captain’s heart; though their united forces so enraged and overpowered Madame Duval, that she really trembled with passion.
I was very glad when Mrs. Mirvan said it was time to be gone. Sir Clement arose to take leave; but the Captain very cordially invited him to join our party: he *had* an engagement, he said, but would give it up to have that pleasure.
Some little confusion ensued in regard to our manner of setting off. Mrs. Mirvan offered Madame Duval a place in her coach, and proposed that we four females should go all together; however, this she rejected, declaring she would by no means go so far without a gentleman, and wondering so polite a lady could make *so English* a proposal. Sir Clement Willoughby said, his chariot was waiting at the door, and begged to know if it could be of any use. It was at last decided, that a hackney-coach should be called for Monsieur Du Bois and Madame Duval, in which the Captain, and, at his request, Sir Clement, went also; Mrs. and Miss Mirvan and I had a peaceful and comfortable ride by ourselves.

===Chinese===

那场谈话吵得火热：舰长粗声粗气，坚称英国人样样都强；杜瓦尔夫人怒气冲冲，一样也不肯认；克莱门特爵士则施展他辩才与讥诮的全部本事，凡是舰长抛出来的，一概帮腔加固：因为他够精明，看得出：要讨这家主人的好，再没有比同杜瓦尔夫人结仇更灵的法子了。果然，没过多久，他就有理由庆幸自己眼力成功了。
他一见我，便毕恭毕敬一躬，问我可曾被里多托那晚的劳累累着了：我微微点头，别无回答，因为那桩事我羞还羞不过来。他便回到论战双方那里；他把仗打得那样巧，一面撩火杜瓦尔夫人，一面取悦舰长，叫我虽鄙他的狡狯，却不能不服他的手段。米尔文太太怕这两位对手闹起来，屡屡想换题目；若非克莱门特爵士作梗，本也可成——他偏不肯撒手，又拿幽默和讽刺撑着，看去竟赢得了舰长的心；他们合力把杜瓦尔夫人气得、压得真发抖。
米尔文太太说该动身了，我暗暗叫好。克莱门特爵士起身告辞；舰长却热诚地邀他同行：他*本来*有个约，他说，但为这份乐趣，愿意舍了。
出发时又起了一场小小的混乱。米尔文太太让杜瓦尔夫人坐自家的车，提议我们四个女眷同乘；她却回绝了，声明没绅士同行，万万不走这么远的路，还奇怪这样有礼的太太竟提出*这么英国*的提议。克莱门特·威洛比爵士说他的马车就在门口候着，问能否效力。最后议定：给杜布瓦先生和杜瓦尔夫人叫一辆街车，舰长——又应他自己之请——偕克莱门特爵士同坐；米尔文太太母女同我，自自在在、舒舒服服地坐了一路。

===Original===

I doubt not but they quarrelled all the way; for when we met at Ranelagh everyone seemed out of humour; and though we joined parties, poor Madame Duval was avoided as much as possible by all but me.
The room was so very much crowded, that but for the uncommon assiduity of Sir Clement Willoughby, we should not have been able to procure a box (which is the name given to the arched recesses that are appropriated for tea parties) till half the company had retired. As we were taking possession of our places, some ladies of Mrs. Mirvan’s acquaintance stopped to speak to her, and persuaded her to *take a round* with them. When she returned to us, what was my surprise, to see that Lord Orville had joined her party! The ladies walked on: Mrs. Mirvan seated herself, and made a slight, though respectful, invitation to Lord Orville to drink his tea with us; which, to my no small consternation, he accepted.
I felt a confusion unspeakable at again seeing him, from the recollection of the ridotto adventure: nor did my situation lessen it; for I was seated between Madame Duval and Sir Clement, who seemed as little as myself to desire Lord Orville’s presence. Indeed, the continual wrangling and ill-breeding of Captain Mirvan and Madame Duval made me blush that I belonged to them. And poor Mrs. Mirvan and her amiable daughter had still less reason to be satisfied.
A general silence ensued after he was seated: his appearance, from different motives, gave an universal restraint to everybody. What his own reasons were for honouring us with his company, I cannot imagine; unless, indeed, he had a curiosity to know whether I should invent any new impertinence concerning him.
The first speech was made by Madame Duval, who said, “It’s quite a shocking thing to see ladies come to so genteel a place as Ranelagh with hats on; it has a monstrous vulgar look: I can’t think what they wear them for. There is no such a thing to be seen in Paris.”
“Indeed,” cried Sir Clement, “I must own myself no advocate for hats; I am sorry the ladies ever invented or adopted so tantalizing a fashion: for, where there is beauty, they only serve to shade it; and, where there is none, to excite a most unavailing curiosity. I fancy they were originally worn by some young and whimsical coquette.”

===Chinese===

他们一路上准是吵过来的；因为在拉内拉夫碰头时，个个面带愠色；虽然合为一伙，可怜的杜瓦尔夫人人人躲着，只我不躲。
大厅里那样拥挤，若非克莱门特·威洛比爵士出奇地殷勤张罗，只怕等到人散了一半，我们也占不到一个包厢（就是那专用作茶会的拱形凹座）。我们刚落座，米尔文太太的几位相识的太太过来寒暄，劝她同去*绕一圈*。待她回到我们这里，叫我多么吃惊——奥维尔勋爵竟与她同行！太太们往前走了；米尔文太太落座，客气而淡然地邀奥维尔勋爵同我们用茶——他竟应了，叫我好不心慌。
一想起里多托那桩事，再见他，我就慌得说不出话；我的座位更不帮我——我夹坐在杜瓦尔夫人同克莱门特爵士中间，而这两位，看去同我一样，都不盼奥维尔勋爵在场。说真的，米尔文舰长同杜瓦尔夫人那没完没了的吵闹和无礼，叫我为同他们沾亲而脸红。可怜的米尔文太太和她那可爱女儿，就更没有满意的了。
他落座后，一阵全体的沉默：各怀各的心思，他的在场给了人人一层拘束。他究竟为何赏光同我们坐，我猜不出；除非——当真是好奇，想看看我还会编出什么关于他的新唐突。
头一句话是杜瓦尔夫人开的："瞧着太太们戴帽子来拉内拉夫这样体面的地方，真叫人惊心；俗气得吓人：我想不出她们戴它做什么。巴黎可见不着这种东西。"
"说真的，"克莱门特爵士喊，"我得自认，帽子的辩护士我是不做的；太太们发明、采纳这样磨人的时髦，我实在惋惜：有姿色的地方，帽子只会遮了它；没有的地方，只挑起一场全然无用的好奇。我猜，这东西起初总是一位又年轻又古怪的交际花戴出来的。"

===Original===

“More likely,” answered the Captain, “they were invented by some wrinkled old hag, who’d a mind for to keep the young fellows in chase, let them be never so weary.”
“I don’t know what you may do in England,” cried Madame Duval, “but I know in Paris no woman needn’t be at such a trouble as that to be taken very genteel notice of.”
“Why, will you pretend for to say,” returned the Captain, “that they don’t distinguish the old from the young there as well as here?”
“They don’t make no distinguishments at all,” said she; “they’re vastly too polite.”
“More fools they!” cried the Captain, sneeringly.
“Would to Heaven,” cried Sir Clement, “that, for our own sakes, we Englishmen too were blest with so accommodating a blindness!”
“Why the devil do you make such a prayer as that?” demanded the Captain: “them are the first foolish words I’ve heard you speak; but I suppose you’re not much used to that sort of work. Did you ever make a prayer before, since you were a sniveler?”
“Ay, now,” cried Madame Duval, “that’s another of the unpolitenesses of you English, to go to talking of such things as that: now in Paris nobody never says nothing about religion, no more than about politics.”
“Why then,” answered he, “it’s a sign they take no more care of their souls than of their country, and so both one and t’other go to old Nick.”
“Well, if they do,” said she, “who’s the worse, so long as they don’t say nothing about it? It’s the tiresomest thing in the world to be always talking of them sort of things, and nobody that’s ever been abroad troubles their heads about them.”
“Pray then,” cried the Captain, “since you know so much of the matter, be so good as to tell us what they *do* trouble their heads about?﻿—Hey, Sir Clement! han’t we a right to know that much?”
“A very comprehensive question,” said Sir Clement, “and I expect much instruction from the lady’s answer.”
“Come, Madam,” continued the Captain, “never flinch; speak at once; don’t stop for thinking.”
“I assure you I am not going,” answered she; “for as to what they *do* do, why they’ve enough to do, I promise you, what with one thing or another.”
“But *what, what* do they do, these famous *Monseers*?” demanded the Captain; “can’t you tell us? do they game?﻿—or drink?﻿—or fiddle?﻿—or are they jockeys?﻿—or do they spend all their time in flummering old women?”

===Chinese===

"多半，"舰长答，"是哪个满脸皱的老妖婆发明的，存心叫小伙子们追个没完，追得再累也不撒手。"
"你们英国人怎么样我不管，"杜瓦尔夫人喊，"可我知道，在巴黎，女人用不着费这份神，自然有人十分体面地青眼有加。"
"嗬，您倒想说，"舰长回，"他们那儿分不出老少，不像我们这儿？"
"他们根本不做区分，"她说；"他们客气透了。"
"傻得好！"舰长讥笑着喊。
"但愿老天，"克莱门特爵士喊，"看在我们自己份上，也给我们英国人这样随和的眼盲！"
"你干吗求这种愿？"舰长质问；"这是你说的头一句蠢话；不过你大概不常干这个。你自打脱了开裆裤，求过愿没有？"
"哎，来了，"杜瓦尔夫人喊，"这又是你们英国人的一样无礼：张口就谈这种事：在巴黎，谁也不谈教门，同不谈政治一样。"
"那好啊，"他答，"可见他们照管灵魂，同照管国家一样不上心，两头就一齐下了地狱。"
"好嘛，就算下了，"她说，"只要不说出口，碍着谁了？一天到晚讲这些，是天底下最腻人的事；凡是出过洋的人，谁都不为这个伤脑筋。"
"那么请问，"舰长喊，"您既这样内行，劳驾告诉我们：他们伤脑筋的*究竟*是什么？——呃，克莱门特爵士！这一层我们总该有权知道吧？"
"一个面面俱到的问题，"克莱门特爵士说，"我静候这位夫人的回答，必获教益。"
"来吧，夫人，"舰长接着说，"别缩；痛快说；别想。"
"我告诉你们，我才不说呢，"她答；"至于他们*究竟*干什么——嘿，他们够忙的，我担保，这事一件那件的。"
"可*到底、到底*干什么，这些大名鼎鼎的*法国爷*？"舰长逼问；"说不上来吧？他们赌钱？——灌酒？——拉提琴？——做马贩子？——还是把光阴全花在糊弄老太太上头？"

===Original===

“As to that, Sir﻿—but indeed I shan’t trouble myself to answer such a parcel of low questions, so don’t ask me no more about it.” And then, to my great vexation, turning to Lord Orville, she said, “Pray, Sir, was you ever in Paris?”
He only bowed.
“And pray, Sir, how did you like it?”
This *comprehensive* question, as Sir Clement would have called it, though it made him smile, also made him hesitate; however, his answer was expressive of his approbation.
“I thought you would like it, Sir, because you look so like a gentleman. As to the Captain, and as to that other gentleman, why they may very well not like what they don’t know: for I suppose, Sir, you was never abroad?”
“Only three years, Ma’am,” answered Sir Clement, drily.
“Well, that’s very surprising! I should never have thought it: however, I dare say you only kept company with the English.”
“Why, pray, who *should* he keep company with?” cried the Captain: “what I suppose you’d have him ashamed of his own nation, like some other people not a thousand miles off, on purpose to make his own nation ashamed of him?”
“I’m sure it would be a very good thing if you’d go abroad yourself.”
“How will you make out that, hey, Madam? come, please to tell me, where would be the good of that?”
“Where! why a great deal. They’d make quite another person of you.”
“What, I suppose you’d have me to learn to cut capers?﻿—and dress like a monkey?﻿—and palaver in French gibberish?﻿—hey, would you?﻿—And powder, and daub, and make myself up, like some other folks?”
“I would have you learn to be more *politer*, Sir, and not to talk to ladies in such a rude, old-fashion way as this. You, Sir, as have been in Paris,” again addressing herself to Lord Orville, “can tell this English gentleman how he’d be despised, if he was to talk in such an ungenteel manner as this before any foreigners. Why, there isn’t a hairdresser, nor a shoemaker, nor nobody, that wouldn’t blush to be in your company.”
“Why, look ye, Madam,” answered the Captain, “as to your hair-pinchers and shoeblacks, you may puff off their manners, and welcome; and I am heartily glad you like ’em so well: but as to me, since you must needs make so free of your advice, I must e’en tell you, I never kept company with any such gentry.”
“Come, ladies and gentlemen,” said Mrs. Mirvan, “as many of you as have done tea, I invite to walk with me.”

===Chinese===

"这个嘛，先生——说真的，这一堆下三烂的问题，我犯不着答，别再问我了。"接着，叫我大为难堪的是，她转向奥维尔勋爵："请问，先生，您去过巴黎么？"
他只一躬。
"那么请问，先生，您喜欢它么？"
这个——照克莱门特爵士的说法——*面面俱到*的问题，叫他失笑，也叫他踌躇；不过他的回答，表达了赞许。
"我就知道您会喜欢，先生，因为您看着像位绅士。至于舰长，还有那边那位先生，他们不喜欢的，多半因为他们不懂：我想先生您没出过洋吧？"
"统共三年，夫人。"克莱门特爵士干巴巴地答。
"哎哟，这可怪了！我怎么也想不到：不过我敢说，您只同英国人来往。"
"嗬，请问，他*该*同谁来往？"舰长喊；"我猜，您是要他羞于自己的国家，像离这儿不远某位那样，好叫自己的国家羞于他，是么？"
"我确信，你自己出国走走才好呢。"
"那怎么见得，嗬，夫人？来，请说说，好处在哪儿？"
"在哪儿！多着呢。他们准把你改造成另一个人。"
"什么，你要我去学蹦高？——穿得像猴儿？——满嘴法国呱嗒？——嗬，是不是？——还要扑粉、涂抹、把自己收拾起来，学某些人那样？"
"我要你学的，是更*客气*些，先生，别这样粗鲁地、老古董式地同太太们说话。您，先生，您到过巴黎，"她又转向奥维尔勋爵，"可以告诉这位英国先生：他若当着外邦人这样不体面地讲话，会被人怎样看轻。嗐，随便哪个梳头的、擦鞋的、随便什么人，同您作伴都要臊红脸。"
"听我说，夫人，"舰长答，"您那几位掐头发的、擦黑鞋的，您只管夸他们的规矩，欢迎之至；您这样喜欢他们，我由衷高兴：至于我，您既然非送忠告不可，我索性告诉您：这路贵人，我从来没同他们作过伴。"
"来吧，诸位女士先生，"米尔文太太说，"喝完茶的，都请陪我散步。"

===Original===

Maria and I started up instantly; Lord Orville followed; and I question whether we were not half round the room ere the angry disputants knew that we had left the box.
As the husband of Mrs. Mirvan had borne so large a share in the disagreeable altercation, Lord Orville forbore to make any comments upon it; so that the subject was immediately dropt, and the conversation became calmly sociable, and politely cheerful, and, to everybody but me, must have been highly agreeable:﻿—but, as to myself, I was so eagerly desirous of making some apology to Lord Orville, for the impertinence of which he must have thought me guilty at the ridotto, and yet so utterly unable to assume sufficient courage to speak to him, concerning an affair in which I had so terribly exposed myself, that I hardly ventured to say a word all the time we were walking. Besides, the knowledge of his contemptuous opinion haunted and dispirited me, and made me fear he might possibly misconstrue whatever I should say. So that, far from enjoying a conversation which might, at any other time, have delighted me, I continued silent, uncomfortable, and ashamed. O, Sir, shall I ever again involve myself in so foolish an embarrassment? I am sure that, if I do, I shall deserve greater mortification.
We were not joined by the rest of the party till we had taken three or four turns around the room; and then they were so quarrelsome, that Mrs. Mirvan complained of being fatigued and proposed going home. No one dissented. Lord Orville joined another party, having first made an offer of his services, which the gentlemen declined, and we proceeded to an outward room, where we waited for the carriages. It was settled that we should return to town in the same manner we came to Ranelagh; and, accordingly, Monsieur Du Bois handed Madame Duval into a hackney coach, and was just preparing to follow her, when she screamed, and jumped hastily out, declaring she was wet through all her clothes. Indeed, upon examination the coach was found to be in a dismal condition; for the weather proved very bad, and the rain had, though I know not how, made its way into the carriage.
Mrs.

===Chinese===

玛丽亚同我立刻起身；奥维尔勋爵随在后面；我疑心我们绕出半间屋子了，那几位吵红了眼的还没发觉我们已离开包厢。
因为米尔文太太的丈夫在那场难堪的口角里占了那样大的一份，奥维尔勋爵忍住不置一词；于是这题目随即撂下，谈话变得平静而随和、客气而愉快，除我以外，想必人人如沐春风：——至于我，我一心想为里多托那桩冒失——他必以为我犯下的冒失——向奥维尔勋爵道个歉，却又全然鼓不起勇气，去谈那件叫我出尽了丑的事，一路几乎不敢开口。况且，他心里那份轻蔑的看法，我知道得清清楚楚，它一直缠着我、压着我，怕自己说什么都要被他错解。于是，这场换在任何时候都会叫我快乐的谈话，我只落得沉默、难受、羞愧。哦，先生，我还会再陷进这样蠢的窘境里去么？我知道，若是再陷，再重的羞辱也是我活该。
我们绕完三四圈，其余的人才加入；他们那样好斗，米尔文太太直嚷乏了，提议回家。无人异议。奥维尔勋爵先是表示愿效犬马，先生们谢绝了，他便加入了另一伙；我们走进外厅等候马车。说定按来时的方式回城；于是杜布瓦先生扶杜瓦尔夫人上了街车，正要跟着上去，她一声尖叫，慌忙跳下车，嚷嚷浑身衣裳都湿透了。一查，那车果然惨不忍睹：天很坏，雨不知怎么竟渗进了车厢。
米尔文

===Original===

and Miss Mirvan, and myself, were already disposed of as before; but no sooner did the Captain hear this account, than, without any ceremony, he was so civil as to immediately take possession of the vacant seat in his own coach, leaving Madame Duval and Monsieur Du Bois to take care of themselves. As to Sir Clement Willoughby, his own chariot was in waiting.
I instantly begged permission to offer Madame Duval my own place, and made a motion to get out; but Mrs. Mirvan stopped me, saying, that I should then be obliged to return to town with only the foreigner, or Sir Clement.
“O never mind the old beldame,” cried the Captain, “she’s weatherproof, I’ll answer for her; and besides, as we are all, I hope, *English*, why she’ll meet with no worse than she expects from us.”
“I do not mean to defend her,” said Mrs. Mirvan; “but indeed, as she belongs to our party, we cannot, with any decency, leave the place till she is, by some means, accommodated.”
“Lord, my dear,” cried the Captain, whom the distress of Madame Duval had put into very good humour, “why, she’ll break her heart if she meets with any civility from a filthy Englishman.”
Mrs. Mirvan, however, prevailed; and we all got out of the coach, to wait till Madame Duval could meet with some better carriage. We found her, attended by Monsieur Du Bois, standing amongst the servants, and very busy in wiping her negligee, and endeavouring to save it from being stained by the wet, as she said it was a new Lyons silk. Sir Clement Willoughby offered her the use of his chariot, but she had been too much piqued by his raillery to accept it. We waited some time, but in vain; for no hackney-coach could be procured. The Captain, at last, was persuaded to accompany Sir Clement himself, and we four females were handed into Mrs. Mirvan’s carriage, though not before Madame Duval had insisted upon our making room for Monsieur Du Bois, to which the Captain only consented in preference to being incommoded by him in Sir Clement’s chariot.
Our party drove off first. We were silent and unsociable; for the difficulties attending this arrangement had made everyone languid and fatigued. Unsociable, I must own, we continued; but very short was the duration of our silence, as we had not proceeded thirty yards before every voice was heard at once﻿—for the coach broke down!

===Chinese===

太太母女同我，依旧照先前坐定；可舰长一听这情形，二话不说，竟那样"客气"，径自一屁股占了他自家马车里空出的座位，把杜瓦尔夫人同杜布瓦先生撂下，随他们自理。至于克莱门特·威洛比爵士，他自己的马车正候着。
我立刻请求把我的座位让给杜瓦尔夫人，起身要下车；米尔文太太拦住我，说那样我就只好单同那位外国人、或者同克莱门特爵士回城了。
"哦，别理那老虔婆，"舰长喊，"她是风吹雨打不透的，我担保；再说，咱们既然全是——我希望——*英国人*，她从我们这儿受的，超不出她的预想。"
"我不是要替她辩护，"米尔文太太说，"可她既是我们一伙的，不到她设法有了安置，我们就这样走，实在失体统。"
"老天，亲爱的，"舰长喊——杜瓦尔夫人的狼狈叫他心情大好，"嗐，她要是从一个脏英国人手里得了半点客气，心都要碎了。"
然而米尔文太太胜了；我们全下车站着，等杜瓦尔夫人寻到一辆好些的车。我们看见她由杜布瓦先生陪着，站在仆役堆里，正忙着揩她那件晨衣，尽力不让雨渍浸坏——她说那是里昂新绸。克莱门特·威洛比爵士提出借他的马车，可她被他先前那些打趣刺得太狠，不肯领受。我们等了好一阵，徒劳；街车一辆也雇不到。最后，说动舰长去陪克莱门特爵士同坐；我们四位女眷被扶进米尔文太太的马车——不过此前杜瓦尔夫人非逼我们给杜布瓦先生腾个座不可，舰长之所以点头，只是两害相权：总好过同他挤在克莱门特爵士的马车里。
我们这一路先行。人人无言，闷闷不乐；安排的种种周折，把大家熬得恹恹无力。闷，我承认，是闷到底了；可沉默极短——出不了三十码，人人一齐开了腔——马车翻了！

===Original===

I suppose we concluded, of course, that we were all half killed, by the violent shrieks that seemed to come from every mouth. The chariot was stopped, the servants came to our assistance, and we were taken out of the carriage, without having been at all hurt. The night was dark and wet; but I had scarce touched the ground when I was lifted suddenly from it by Sir Clement Willoughby, who begged permission to assist me, though he did not wait to have it granted, but carried me in his arms back to Ranelagh.
He enquired very earnestly if I was not hurt by the accident? I assured him I was perfectly safe, and free from injury; and desired he would leave me, and return to the rest of the party, for I was very uneasy to know whether they had been equally fortunate. He told me he was happy in being honoured with my commands, and would joyfully execute them; but insisted upon first conducting me to a warm room, as I had not wholly escaped being wet. He did not regard my objections; but made me follow him to an apartment, where we found an excellent fire, and some company waiting for carriages. I readily accepted a seat, and then begged he would go.
And go, indeed, he did; but he returned in a moment, telling me that the rain was more violent than ever, and that he had sent his servants to offer their assistance, and acquaint *the Mirvans* of my situation. I was very mad that he would not go himself; but as my acquaintance with him was so very slight, I did not think proper to urge him contrary to his inclination.
Well, he drew a chair close to mine; and, after again enquiring how I did, said, in a low voice, “You will pardon me, Miss Anville, if the eagerness I feel to vindicate myself, induces me to snatch this opportunity of making sincere acknowledgments for the impertinence with which I tormented you at the last ridotto. I can assure you, Madam, I have been a true and sorrowful penitent ever since; but﻿—shall I tell you honestly what encouraged me to﻿—”
He stopped, but I said nothing; for I thought instantly of the conversation Miss Mirvan had overheard, and supposed he was going to tell me himself what part Lord Orville had borne in it; and really I did not wish to hear it repeated. Indeed, the rest of his speech convinces me that such was his intention; with what view I know not, except to make a merit of his defending me.

===Chinese===

听那四面八方齐发的尖叫，我们多半都当自己摔死了半截。那辆双轮马车停下，仆人们赶来相救，我们被从车厢里搀出来，居然毫发无伤。夜又黑又湿；可我脚还没沾地，就被克莱门特·威洛比爵士猛地抱离了地面：他求准许他援手——却根本不等批准，就把我一路抱回了拉内拉夫。
他急切地问我可曾摔伤？我向他担保安然无恙，请他放下我回去照应其余的人，我不放心，急于知道她们是否同样走运。他说，承蒙吩咐，荣幸之至，乐于照办；只是坚持先引我进一间暖屋，因为我多少淋湿了。他不理会我的异议，径自领我进了一个房间：炉火正好，还有几拨宾客在等车。我欣然落座，又请他去。
去，他倒真去了；可转眼又回来，说雨下得比先前更凶，他已派仆人们前去效力，并把你*米尔文一家*我的处境告知。他不肯亲自去，我气极了；可我同他交情这样浅，不便违着他的意思强劝。
好吧，他把椅子拖到我身边；又问候了一番我的情形，低声说："安维尔小姐，倘若我为洗刷自己心切，趁这个机会，为上回里多托纠缠您的那番唐突作个真诚的告罪，请您恕我。我向您担保，夫人，打那以后，我一直是个又真心又悲伤的悔罪人；不过——要不要我老老实实告诉您，是什么给了我胆子——"
他顿住了；我一言不发；因为我立刻想到米尔文小姐偷听到的那场谈话，猜他就要亲口告诉我奥维尔勋爵在其中的一份；说真的，我不愿听人重述。果然，他后面的话叫我确信，他正是这个意思；用意何在，我不知道——除非是拿"替我辩护"来居功。

===Original===

“And yet,” he continued, “my excuse may only expose my own credulity, and want of judgment and penetration. I will, therefore, merely beseech your pardon, and hope that some future time﻿—”
Just then the door was opened by Sir Clement’s servant, and I had the pleasure of seeing the Captain, Mrs. and Miss Mirvan, enter the room.
“O ho!” cried the former, “you have got a good warm berth here; but we shall beat up your quarters. Here, Lucy, Moll, come to the fire, and dry your trumpery. But, heyday﻿—why, where’s old Madame French?”
“Good God,” cried I, “is not Madame Duval then with you?”
“With me! No﻿—thank God.”
I was very uneasy to know what might have become of her; and, if they would have suffered me, I should have gone in search of her myself; but all the servants were dispatched to find her; and the Captain said, we might be very sure her *French beau* would take care of her.
We waited some time without any tidings, and were soon the only party in the room. My uneasiness increased so much that Sir Clement now made a voluntary offer of seeking her. However, the same moment that he opened the door with this design, she presented herself at it, attended by Monsieur Du Bois.
“I was this instant, Madam,” said he, “coming to see for you.”
“You are mighty good, truly,” cried she, “to come when all the mischief’s over.”
She then entered﻿—in such a condition!﻿—entirely covered with mud, and in so great a rage, it was with difficulty she could speak. We all expressed our concern, and offered our assistance﻿—except the Captain, who no sooner beheld her than he burst out into a loud laugh.
We endeavoured, by our enquiries and condolements, to prevent her attending to him; and she was for some time so wholly engrossed by her anger and her distress, that we succeeded without much trouble. We begged her to inform us how this accident happened. “How!” repeated she﻿—“why it was all along of your all going away﻿—and there poor Monsieur Du Bois﻿—but it wasn’t his fault﻿—for he’s as bad off as me.”
All eyes were then turned to Monsieur Du Bois, whose clothes were in the same miserable plight with those of Madame Duval; and who, wet, shivering, and disconsolate, had crept to the fire.
The Captain laughed yet more heartily; while Mrs.

===Chinese===

"然而，"他接下去，"我的托词，说不定只暴露我自己的轻信，暴露我识力与眼力的欠缺。那么，我只求您饶恕，但愿来日——"
恰在此时，门被克莱门特爵士的仆人推开，我高兴地看见舰长同米尔文太太母女走了进来。
"哦嗬！"前头那位喊，"你们占了这么个暖和的好窝；可我们要来掏你们的窝了。来，露西，莫尔，到火边来，烤烤你们那些花哨货。可是——咦——法国老太太哪儿去了？"
"天哪，"我叫道，"杜瓦尔夫人不同你们在一起么？"
"同我！不——谢天谢地。"
我焦心她会出了什么事；他们若肯依我，我简直要亲自去找；可仆人们全被打发出去了；舰长说，尽管放心，她那位*法国相好*自会照管她。
我们等了一阵，杳无音信，屋里很快只剩我们一伙。我的不安越熬越重，克莱门特爵士便自告奋勇去找。然而，他为此开门的那一瞬，她本人恰在门口出现，杜布瓦先生陪着。
"夫人，"他说，"我正要去找您。"
"你倒真`好`，"她喊，"闯完了祸才来。"
她随即进屋——那副模样！——浑身是泥，怒得话都难连贯。我们人人表示关切，争相相助——只除舰长：他一见她，放声大笑。
我们连忙拿问询与慰问岔开她的注意；她一时全被怒气与狼狈占满，我们没费多大劲就成了。我们请她讲讲祸事怎么起的。"怎么起的！"她重复，——"还不是全怪你们一走了之——剩下可怜的杜布瓦先生——可那不怪他——他同我一样惨。"
众人的眼睛于是齐刷刷转向杜布瓦先生：他的衣裳同杜瓦尔夫人的一样凄惨；湿着、抖着、一脸绝望，缩到了火边。
舰长笑得更欢了；米尔文

===Original===
