霍华德夫人给我们的迎接亲热至极；她的仁厚与好客，凡愿意快活的人，没有不因之快活的。

再会，我最亲爱的先生。虽然我一直忘了提，我还是希望，凡有人问起我，您始终没有忘记替我问候。

## Letter / 书信
===Original===

XXVI Evelina to the Rev. Mr. Villars
Howard Grove, April 27.
O my dear Sir, I now write in the greatest uneasiness! Madame Duval has made a proposal which terrifies me to death, and which was as unexpected as it is shocking.
She had been employed for some hours this afternoon in reading letters from London: and, just about teatime, she sent for me into her room, and said, with a look of great satisfaction, “Come here, child, I’ve got some very good news to tell you: something that will surprise you, I’ll give you my word, for you ha’n’t no notion of it.”
I begged her to explain herself; and then, in terms which I cannot repeat, she said she had been considering what a shame it was to see me such a poor country, shamefaced thing, when I ought to be a fine lady; and that she had long, and upon several occasions, blushed for me, though she must own the fault was none of mine; for nothing better could be expected from a girl who had been so immured. However, she assured me she had, at length, hit upon a plan, which would make quite another creature of me.
I waited, without much impatience, to hear what this preface led to; but I was soon awakened to more lively sensations, when she aquainted me, that her intention was to prove my birthright, and to claim, by law, the inheritance of my real family!
It would be impossible for me to express my extreme consternation when she thus unfolded her scheme. My surprise and terror were equally great; I could say nothing: I heard her with a silence which I had not the power to break.
She then expatiated very warmly upon the advantages I should reap from her plan; talked in a high style of my future grandeur; assured me how heartily I should despise almost everybody and everything I had hitherto seen; predicted my marrying into some family of the first rank in the kingdom; and, finally, said I should spend a few months in Paris, where my education and manners might receive their last polish.
She enlarged also upon the delight she should have, in common with myself, from mortifying the pride of certain people, and showing them that she was not to be slighted with impunity.
In the midst of this discourse, I was relieved by a summons to tea. Madame Duval was in great spirits; but my emotion was too painful for concealment, and everybody enquired into the cause.

===Chinese===

第二十六封 伊芙琳娜致尊敬的维拉尔斯牧师先生

霍华德林苑，4月27日。

哦，亲爱的先生，我此刻是在极端的不安中给您写信！杜瓦尔夫人提出了一个主张，把我吓坏了——它来得意外，又叫人震惊。

今天下午，她读伦敦来信读了几个钟头；快到喝茶的时分，她打发人叫我进她的房间，一脸大大的得意：“过来，孩子，我有个天大的好消息告诉你：保管你想不到，我说话算数，你猜也没处猜。”

我求她说明白；随后，用一种我没法复述的字眼，她说，她一直在想：眼看我这样一个可怜巴巴、乡下气的、见人就脸红的东西，本该做位阔太太，多不像话；好几回了，她都替我脸红——虽然她承认这不怪我；一个这样圈禁大的姑娘，还能指望什么更好的呢。不过她要我放心，她终于想出了一个主意，管保叫我脱胎换骨、判若两人。

我不很性急地等着听这段开场白的下文；可她一说破——她的打算，是要证实我的出身权，依法认领我真正家族的产业——我立刻醒到了更剧烈的感觉里！

她这样摊开她的计划时，我的惊骇无法表达。惊与惧一样大；我说不出话：我听她说着，沉默得没力气打破。

接着她热烈地铺陈我将从她的计划里捞到的好处；高谈我日后的尊荣；担保我准会鄙视我迄今见过的一切人和一切东西；预言我嫁进王国里头一等的人家；末了说，我该去巴黎住上几个月，让我的教养和举止受一受最后的打磨。

她还大大渲染了她会同我共享的那份快意——杀一杀某些人的骄气，叫他们看看，轻慢她是要付代价的。

这篇宏论讲到一半，一声唤茶的铃救了我。杜瓦尔夫人兴致极高；可我的激动藏不住，人人都问缘故。

===Original===

I would fain have waived the subject, but Madame Duval was determined to make it public. She told them that she had it in her head to *make something* of me, and that they should soon call me by another name than that of Anville; and yet that she was not going to have the child married neither.
I could not endure to hear her proceed, and was going to leave the room; which, when Lady Howard perceived, she begged Madame Duval would defer her intelligence to some other opportunity; but she was so eager to communicate her scheme, that she could bear no delay; and therefore they suffered me to go without opposition. Indeed, whenever my situation or affairs are mentioned by Madame Duval, she speaks of them with such bluntness and severity, that I cannot be enjoined a task more cruel than to hear her.
I was afterwards accquainted with some particulars of the conversation by Miss Mirvan; who told me that Madame Duval informed them of her plan with the utmost complacency, and seemed to think herself very fortunate in having suggested it; but, soon after, she accidentally betrayed, that she had been instigated to the scheme by her relations the Branghtons, whose letters, which she received today, first mentioned the proposal. She declared that she would have nothing to do with any *roundabout ways*, but go openly and instantly to law, in order to prove my birth, real name, and title to the estate of my ancestors.
How impertinent and officious in these Branghtons, to interfere thus in my concerns! You can hardly imagine what a disturbance this plan has made in the family. The Captain, without enquiring into any particulars of the affair, has peremptorily declared himself against it, merely because it has been proposed by Madame Duval; and they have battled the point together with great violence. Mrs. Mirvan says, she will not even *think*, till she hears your opinion. But Lady Howard, to my great surprise, openly avows her appprobation of Madame Duval’s intention; however, she will write her reasons and sentiments upon the subject to you herself.
As to Miss Mirvan, she is my second self, and neither hopes nor fears but as I do.

===Chinese===

我本想把这个话头岔开，可杜瓦尔夫人打定主意要公开。她告诉他们，她一心要把我“*造就成个人物*”，往后他们该改口叫我另一个姓，不叫安维尔了；不过呢，她又并不打算就叫这孩子嫁人。

我实在听不下去，正要出屋；霍华德夫人看出来了，求杜瓦尔夫人把她的高见换个时候再发表；可她急着宣布她的计划，一刻也等不得；于是他们也没拦我，由我去了。说真的，每逢杜瓦尔夫人谈起我的处境或我的事，总是那样直戳、那样不留情面，再没有比听她说更叫我受罪的差事了。

随后米尔文小姐把那场谈话的细节告诉了我；她说，杜瓦尔夫人向他们宣布计划时，一脸的志得意满，还自庆想出了这么个主意，福气不小；可不久她偶然漏了底：撺掇她的是她布兰顿家的亲戚，今天收到的信里头一回提起了这个主张。她声言，什么*绕弯子的路*她一概不走，要公开地、立刻地对簿公堂，好证实我的出身、我的真名，和我对祖先产业的权利。

这些布兰顿多么好事、多么爱管闲人闲事，这样插手我的事情！您简直想象不出，这个计划在这家里掀起了怎样的风波。舰长不问事情的原委，斩钉截铁地反对——只为它是杜瓦尔夫人提出来的；两人为这一点大动干戈。米尔文太太说，不听您的意见，她连*想*都不想。可霍华德夫人，大大出于我的意外，公开赞成杜瓦尔夫人的打算；不过，她的理由和感想，她会亲自写信告诉您。

至于米尔文小姐，她是我的第二个自我，不盼望、也不惧怕我所不盼望、不惧怕的。

===Original===

And as to *me*﻿—I know not what to say, nor even what to wish; I have often thought my fate peculiarly cruel, to have but one parent, and from that one to be banished forever;﻿—while, on the other side, I have but too well known and felt the propriety of the separation. And yet, you may much better imagine, than I can express, the internal anguish which sometimes oppresses my heart, when I reflect upon the strange indifference that must occasion a father never to make the least enquiry after the health, the welfare, or even the life of his child!
O Sir, to *me* the loss is nothing!﻿—greatly, sweetly, and most benevolently have you guarded me from feeling it; but for *him*, I grieve indeed!﻿—I must be divested, not merely of all filial piety, but of all humanity, could I ever think upon this subject, and not be wounded to the soul.
Again I must repeat, I know not what to *wish*; think for me, therefore, my dearest Sir, and suffer my doubting mind, that knows not which way to direct its hopes, to be guided by your wisdom and unerring counsel.
Evelina.

===Chinese===

至于*我*——我不知道说什么，连愿望什么都不知道；我常常想，我的命苦得出奇：只有一个亲人，又被那亲人永远地放逐；——可另一方面，这隔离的合宜，我又知道得太清、感得太切。然而，每当我想到那奇怪的无情——一个父亲，对孩子的安康、福祉、甚至生死，竟从不过问一声——那种咬着内心的痛楚，您想得到，远胜过我说得出。

哦，先生，*于我*，这损失算不得什么！——您伟大地、温存地、至仁至慈地护住了我，不叫我尝到它；可*为他*，我真心悲痛！——我必得剥尽做女儿的孝心，再剥尽为人的天良，才能想这个题目而不痛彻灵魂。

我再说一遍：我不知道该*愿望*什么；那么，替我想吧，最亲爱的先生，容我这颗不知把希望导向何方的疑惑的心，受您智慧和无误的指点引领。

伊芙琳娜。

## Letter / 书信
===Original===

XXVII Lady Howard to the Rev. Mr. Villars
Howard Grove.
Dear Sir,
I cannot give a greater proof of the high opinion I have of your candour, than by the liberty I am now going to take, of presuming to offer you advice, upon a subject concerning which you have so just a claim to act for yourself; but I know you have too unaffected a love of justice, to be partially tenacious of your own judgment.
Madame Duval has been proposing a scheme which has put us all in commotion, and against which, at first, in common with the rest of my family, I exclaimed: but, upon more mature consideration, I own my objections have almost wholly vanished.
This scheme is no other than to commence a lawsuit with Sir John Belmont, to prove the validity of his marriage with Miss Evelyn; the necessary consequence of which proof will be, securing his fortune and estate to his daughter.
And why, my dear Sir, should not this be? I know that, upon first hearing, such a plan conveys ideas that must shock you; but I know, too, that your mind is superior to being governed by prejudices, or to opposing any important cause on account of a few disagreeable attendant circumstances.
Your lovely charge, now first entering into life, has merit which ought not to be buried in obscurity. She seems born for an ornament to the world. Nature has been bountiful to her of whatever she had to bestow; and the peculiar attention you have given to her education, has formed her mind to a degree of excellence, that in one so young I have scarce ever seen equalled. Fortune alone has hitherto been sparing of her gifts; and she, too, now opens the way which leads to all that is left to wish for her.
What your reasons may have been, my good Sir, for so carefully concealing the birth, name, and pretensions of this amiable girl, and forbearing to make any claim upon Sir John Belmont, I am totally a stranger to; but, without knowing, I respect them, from the high opinion that I have of your character and judgment: but I hope they are not insuperable; for I cannot but think, that it was never designed for one who seems meant to grace the world, to have her life devoted to retirement.
Surely Sir John Belmont, wretch as he has shown himself, could never see his accomplished daughter, and not be proud to own her, and eager to secure her the inheritance of his fortune.

===Chinese===

第二十七封 霍华德夫人致维拉尔斯牧师先生
霍华德园林。

亲爱的先生：

我要向您坦诚相告，最雄辩的证明莫过于我此刻要冒昧做的事：就一个您最有权自决的问题，斗胆向您进言；可我知道，您对公道的热爱毫无虚饰，绝不至偏执己见。

杜瓦尔夫人提出了一个计划，闹得我们全家骚然，起初我也同家里人一样连声反对；可再作细想之后，我承认，我的反对几乎烟消云散了。

这个计划不是别的，正是向约翰·贝尔蒙特爵士兴一场讼案，证明他同伊芙琳小姐婚姻的合法有效；这一证明的必然结果，便是把他的财产和地产，归到他的女儿名下。

而且，亲爱的先生，为什么不呢？我知道，初闻这样一个计划，必定震动您；可我也知道，您的头脑高出于偏见之上，绝不会因为几件恼人的附带情形，就阻挡一桩重要的事业。

您照护的可爱姑娘，如今初入人生，她有一份不该埋没于湮没无闻的品德。她仿佛生来就是人间的装饰。造化待她慷慨，凡所有者尽数给了她；而您对她教育那份独有的用心，又把她的心智造就到一个优异的地步——这样年轻，我几乎未见过第二个。唯独命运女神至今对她吝啬；而她呢，如今也亲手开启了通往一切尚可为她企求之物的路。

您的理由何在，我的好先生，为何这样小心地隐瞒这位可爱姑娘的身世、姓名和权利，不去向约翰·贝尔蒙特爵士提出任何主张——我全然不知；可是虽不知，我尊重它们，因为我敬重您的为人和判断；不过，我希望它们并非不可逾越；因为我不能不认为：一个生来似乎要为世间增光的人，绝不该把一生托付给隐居。

约翰·贝尔蒙特爵士固然已自证为无赖，可他见到他那样才艺双全的女儿，断无不骄傲认下、急急为她保住财产继承之理。

===Original===

The admiration she met with in town, though merely the effect of her external attractions, was such, that Mrs. Mirvan assures me, she would have had the most splendid offers, had there not seemed to be some mystery in regard to her birth, which, she was well informed was assiduously, though vainly, endeavoured to be discovered.
Can it be right, my dear Sir, that this promising young creature should be deprived of the fortune and rank of life to which she is lawfully entitled, and which you have prepared her to support and to use so nobly? To despise riches may, indeed, be philosophic; but to dispense them worthily must, surely, be more beneficial to mankind.
Perhaps a few years, or indeed a much shorter time, may make this scheme impracticable: Sir John, though yet young, leads a life too dissipated for long duration; and when too late, we may regret that something was not sooner done: for it will be next to impossible, after he is gone, to settle or prove anything with his heirs and executors.
Pardon the earnestness with which I write my sense of this affair; but your charming ward has made me so warmly her friend, that I cannot be indifferent upon a subject of such importance to her future life.
Adieu, my dear Sir;﻿—send me speedily an answer to this remonstrance, and believe me to be, etc.
M. Howard.

===Chinese===

她在城里所受的仰慕——虽然只是她容貌魅力的结果——已经那般盛大；米尔文夫人向我担保，若非她的身世似乎罩着一层谜，她本可以得到最显赫的求婚。而这层谜，据她所知，有人千方百计想要刺探，只是徒劳。

亲爱的先生，这位前程无量的年轻姑娘，竟被剥夺她合法有权继承的财产与门第——那可是您已为她备好、教她如何崇高地去承担、去运用的东西——这难道是对的吗？鄙弃财富，诚然是哲人风度；可是善用财富，于人类必定更有益处。

也许再过几年，甚至很短一段时间，这个计划就行不通了：约翰爵士虽然还年轻，过的却是过于放荡的生活，长不了；到时悔之晚矣，我们会遗憾没有早些着手：因为他一死，再想同他的继承人和遗嘱执行人商定或证明任何事，几乎就不可能了。

宽恕我在这件事上落笔的恳切；您这位可爱的被监护人已叫我死心塌地做了她的朋友，对这样一件关系她终身的大事，我无法漠然。

再会，亲爱的先生；——请速赐复，回我这番诤言，并请相信我是您忠实的，等等。

M. 霍华德。

## Letter / 书信
===Original===

XXVIII Mr. Villars to Lady Howard
Berry Hill, May 2.
Your letter, Madam, has opened a source of anxiety, to which I look forward with dread, and which, to see closed, I scarcely dare expect. I am unwilling to oppose my opinion to that of your Ladyship; nor, indeed, can I, but by arguments which I believe will rather rank me as a hermit ignorant of the world, and fit only for my cell, than as a proper guardian, in an age such as this, for an accomplished young woman. Yet, thus called upon, it behoves me to explain, and endeavour to vindicate, the reasons by which I have been hitherto guided.
The mother of this dear child﻿—who was led to destruction by her own imprudence, the hardness of heart of Madame Duval, and the villany of Sir John Belmont﻿—was once, what her daughter is now, the best beloved of my heart: and her memory, so long as my own holds, I shall love, mourn and honour! On the fatal day that her gentle soul left its mansion, and not many hours ere she ceased to breathe, I solemnly plighted my faith, *That her child if it lived, should know no father but myself, or her acknowledged husband*.
You cannot, Madam, suppose that I found much difficulty in adhering to this promise, and forbearing to make any *claim* upon Sir John Belmont. Could I feel an affection the most paternal for this poor sufferer, and not abominate her destroyer? Could I wish to deliver to *him*, who had so basely betrayed the mother, the helpless and innocent offspring, who, born in so much sorrow, seemed entitled to all the compassionate tenderness of pity?
For many years, the *name* alone of that man, accidentally spoken in my hearing, almost divested me of my Christianity, and scarce could I forbear to execrate him. Yet I sought not, neither did I desire, to deprive him of his child, had he with any appearance of contrition, or, indeed, of humanity, endeavoured to become less unworthy such a blessing;﻿—but he is a stranger to all parental feelings, and has with a savage insensibility, forborne to enquire even into the existence of this sweet orphan, though the situation of his injured wife was but too well known to him.
You wish to be acquainted with my intentions.

===Chinese===

第二十八封 维拉尔斯先生致霍华德夫人

贝里山，5月2日。

夫人，您的来信开了一道焦虑的泉眼，我怀着恐惧望它奔流，几乎不敢指望见它闭合。我不愿拿我的意见同夫人您相抗；真的，我也抗不了——除了用那样的道理：它们与其说替我说话，不如说要把我归成一个不知世事的隐士，只配守我的修行小屋，不配在如今这样的世代，做一位成熟少女的合格监护人。然而既然承您垂问，我理当解释、并竭力申明，我至今所循的那些理由。

这孩子的母亲——她因自己的失慎、杜瓦尔夫人的心硬、和约翰·贝尔蒙特爵士的恶行而堕入毁灭——曾经就是她女儿如今的模样：是我心头最爱的人。只要我的记忆还在，我就要爱她、悼她、敬她！在她温柔的灵魂离开躯壳的那个致命的日子，在她停止呼吸前不过几个钟头，我郑重立誓：*她的孩子若得活命，除了我、或她正式承认的丈夫，不得认第二个父亲。*

夫人，您一定想得到，信守这个诺言、不向约翰·贝尔蒙特爵士提出任何*要求*，于我并不为难。我能对这个可怜的遭难者怀着最父亲般的慈爱，能不痛恨毁了她的人？我能愿望把那无辜无助的婴孩——她生在那样多的悲苦里，理应得着怜悯的全部温情——*交给他*，交给他这样无耻地辜负了母亲的人？

许多年里，单是那人的*名字*，偶然落进我耳朵，就几乎剥尽我的基督徒心肠，我几乎禁不住要诅咒他。然而我并未设法、也并不想夺走他的孩子——只要他有过一丝悔意、甚至一丝人性的模样，肯使自己稍配这样的福分；——可他对为人父母的一切感情全然陌生，以一种野蛮的麻木，连这可爱孤儿的存在都从不过问，虽然他那受害妻子的情况，他知道得再清楚不过。

您愿闻我的打算。

===Original===

﻿—I must acknowledge they were such as I now perceive would not be honoured with your Ladyship’s approbation; for though I have sometimes thought of presenting Evelina to her father, and demanding the justice which is her due, yet, at other times, I have both disdained and feared the application; disdained lest it should be refused; and feared, lest it should be accepted!
Lady Belmont, who was firmly persuaded of her approaching dissolution, frequently and earnestly besought me, that if her infant was a female, I would not abandon her to the direction of a man so wholly unfit to take the charge of her education: but, should she be importunately demanded, that I would retire with her abroad, and carefully conceal her from Sir John, till some apparent change in his sentiments and conduct should announce him less improper for such a trust. And often would she say, “Should the poor babe have any feelings correspondent with its mother’s, it will have no want while under your protection.” Alas! she had no sooner quitted it herself, than she was plunged into a gulf of misery, that swallowed up her peace, reputation, and life.
During the childhood of Evelina, I suggested a thousand plans for the security of her birthright;﻿—but I as many times rejected them. I was in a perpetual conflict, between the desire that she should have justice done her, and the apprehension that, while I improved her fortune, I should endanger her mind. However, as her character began to be formed, and her disposition to be displayed, my perplexity abated; the road before me seemed less thorny and intricate, and I thought I could perceive the right path from the wrong: for when I observed the artless openness, the ingenuous simplicity of her nature; when I saw that her guileless and innocent soul fancied all the world to be pure and disinterested as herself, and that her heart was open to every impression with which love, pity, or art might assail it;﻿—then did I flatter myself, that to follow my own inclination, and to secure her welfare, was the same thing; since, to expose her to the snares and dangers inevitably encircling a house of which the master is dissipated and unprincipled, without the guidance of a mother, or any prudent and sensible female, seemed to me no less than suffering her to stumble into some dreadful pit, when the sun is in its meridian.

===Chinese===

——我必须承认，它们如今看来，是得不到夫人嘉许的；因为虽说我偶尔也想过，把伊芙琳娜引见给她的父亲，讨还她应得的公道，可在别的时候，我又鄙夷这番申请、又惧怕这番申请：鄙夷，怕它被拒；惧怕，怕它被允！

贝尔蒙特夫人坚信自己死期将至，再三恳切求我：倘若婴儿是个女儿，千万别把她交给一个全然不配管教她的人去摆布；万一他死死相逼，就带她退隐国外，小心瞒着约翰爵士，直到他心性品行上显出显然的改变，表明他稍配这样的信托。她常说：“这可怜的娃娃若有一分随她母亲的心，在您保护之下，就什么也不缺了。”唉！她前脚离开这个世界，后脚就坠进苦难的深渊，吞掉了她的安宁、名声和性命。

伊芙琳娜幼年时，我想过一千条保全她出身权利的计策；——又一千次把它们否了。我永远处在交战里：一边盼她得到公道，一边怕我增进了她的财产，却危及了她的心。可是，等她的品格渐渐成形、天性渐渐显露，我的为难便退了；面前的路好像不那么荆棘、不那么纠结了，我想我认得出正路与歧路了：因为当我看到她天性里坦率的开朗、正直的单纯；当我看到她那不设防的无辜灵魂，把全世界都想成同她自己一样纯洁、一样无私，看到她的心对爱、怜或算计的一切进攻敞开着；——我便自忖：顺从我自己的心愿，同保全她的幸福，原是一回事；因为，叫她暴露在那主人荒唐无行的宅邸必然环绕的陷阱与危险里，又没有一个母亲、或任何一位明慎的妇人指引，在我看来，无异于眼看她在日正中天时，跌进一口可怕的深坑。

===Original===

My plan, therefore, was not merely to educate and to cherish her as my own, but to adopt her the heiress of my small fortune, and to bestow her upon some worthy man, with whom she might spend her days in tranquility, cheerfulness, and good humour, untainted by vice, folly, or ambition.
So much for the time past. Such have been the motives by which I have been governed; and I hope they will be allowed not merely to account for, but also to justify, the conduct which has resulted from them. It now remains to speak of the time to come.
And here, indeed, I am sensible of difficulties which I almost despair of surmounting according to my wishes. I pay the highest deference to your Ladyship’s opinion, which it is extremely painful to me not to concur with;﻿—yet I am so well acquainted with your goodness, that I presume to hope it would not be absolutely impossible for me to offer such arguments as might lead you to think with me, that this young creature’s chance of happiness seems less doubtful in retirement, than it would be in the gay and dissipated world. But why should I perplex your Ladyship with reasoning that can turn to so little account? for, alas! what arguments, what persuasions, can I make use of, with any prospect of success, to such a woman as Madame Duval? Her character and the violence of her disposition, intimidate me from making the attempt: she is too ignorant for instruction, too obstinate for entreaty, and too weak for reason.
I will not, therefore, enter into a contest from which I have nothing to expect but altercation and impertinence. As soon would I discuss the effect of sound with the deaf, or the nature of colours with the blind, as aim at illuminating with conviction a mind so warped by prejudice, so much the slave of unruly and illiberal passions. Unused as she is to control, persuasion would but harden, and opposition incense her. I yield, therefore, to the necessity which compels my reluctant acquiescence; and shall now turn all my thoughts upon considering of such methods for the conducting this enterprise, as may be most conducive to the happiness of my child and least liable to wound her sensibility.
The lawsuit, therefore, I wholly and absolutely disapprove.

===Chinese===

因此我的计划，不只是教养她、疼爱她如己出，还要立她为我微薄家产的继承人，再把她许给一个配得上的人，同他过安宁、开朗、和乐的日子，不受恶行、愚蠢或野心的玷染。

既往，就说到这里。这就是支配着我的种种动机；我希望，它们不单能解释、也能证明由此生出的行为是正当的。如今该说说将来了。

在这一节上，我确实觉出了重重困难，几乎不敢指望照我的愿望克服它们。我对夫人您的意见奉以最高的敬意——不能苟同，实在使我痛苦；——然而我对您的仁厚知之太深，故而敢想：我未必提不出那样的道理，引您同我一样看法——这位年轻生命，她的幸福，在退隐里似乎比在那浮华散荡的世界里，把握更足。可是，何必拿这些注定无用的推理去搅扰夫人您？因为，唉！对杜瓦尔夫人这样的女人，我还能用怎样的道理、怎样的劝诱，指望任何成功？她的为人、她脾性的暴烈，吓得我不敢尝试：教她，她太无知；求她，她太顽固；同她讲理，她太软弱。

因此，我不愿投入一场除了口角和无礼别无所获的争斗。同聋子讨论声音的妙处，同盲人讨论颜色的本性，也强似妄想用信念去照亮那样一颗被偏见拧歪、被放肆刻薄的情欲奴役的心。她不惯受人管束，劝导只会使她更硬，反对只会使她更怒。于是，我屈从于那逼我就范的必然，勉强默许；如今只把全副心思，转向考虑如何经手这件事，才能最有利于我孩子的幸福，最不伤她的敏感。

因此，这场官司，我全然、绝对地不赞成。

===Original===

Will you, my dear Madam, forgive the freedom of an old man, if I own myself greatly surprised, that you could, even for a moment, listen to a plan so violent, so public, so totally repugnant to all female delicacy? I am satisfied your Ladyship has not weighed this project. There was a time, indeed, when to assert the innocence of Lady Belmont, and to blazon to the world the *wrongs*, not *guilt*, by which she suffered, I proposed, nay attempted, a similar plan: but then all assistance and encouragement was denied. How cruel to the remembrance I bear of her woes is this tardy resentment of Madame Duval! She was deaf to the voice of Nature, though she has hearkened to that of Ambition.
Never can I consent to have this dear and timid girl brought forward to the notice of the world by such a method; a method which will subject her to all the impertinence of curiosity, the sneers of conjecture, and the stings of ridicule. And for what?﻿—the attainment of wealth which she does not want, and the gratification of vanity which she does not feel. A child to appear against a father!﻿—no, Madam, old and infirm as I am, I would even yet sooner convey her myself to some remote part of the world, though I were sure of dying in the expedition.
Far different had been the motives which would have stimulated her unhappy mother to such a proceeding; all her felicity in this world was irretrievably lost; her life was become a burden to her; and her fair fame, which she had early been taught to prize above all other things, had received a mortal wound: therefore, to clear her own honour, and to secure from blemish the birth of her child, was all the good which fortune had reserved herself the power of bestowing. But even this last consolation was withheld from her!
Let milder measures be adopted: and﻿—since it must be so﻿—let application be made to Sir John Belmont, but as to a lawsuit, I hope, upon this subject, never more to hear it mentioned.
With Madame Duval, all pleas of delicacy would be ineffectual; her scheme must be opposed by arguments better suited to her understanding. I will not, therefore, talk of its impropriety, but endeavour to prove its inutility.

===Chinese===

亲爱的夫人，请原谅一个老人的直率：您竟有一瞬间听得进这样一个计划——这样暴烈、这样张扬、同女性的全部矜持如此背道而驰——我自己着实吃惊。我确信，夫人您没有掂量过这个计划。诚然，曾有一个时期，为了申明贝尔蒙特夫人的清白，为了向世人张扬她所受的是*冤屈*而非*罪愆*，我提议过、甚至试过一个相似的计划：可那时，一切帮助与鼓励都遭拒绝。杜瓦尔夫人这份迟来的忿恨，对我记忆中她的苦难，是何等残忍！自然的声音她充耳不闻，野心的声音她倒听进去了。

我永远不能同意，叫这位娇怯的可人儿，用这样的法子被推到世人眼前；这法子要她受尽好奇的无礼、猜度的讪笑、讥嘲的芒刺。而为了什么？——为的是她并不缺的财富，和她并无感的虚荣。叫一个女儿出庭对质父亲！——不，夫人，我纵然又老又衰，也宁可亲自带她远走天涯，哪怕死在半路。

她那位不幸的母亲若被迫行此一途，动机何其不同；她在今世的幸福已无可挽回地丧失；生命于她已成重负；而她那自幼被教得贵于一切的美名，已受了致命伤：所以，洗清自己的名誉，保全孩子出身的无瑕，是命运留给她仅能施与的全部好处了。可连这最后的安慰，也没有给她！

让我们采温和些的办法：既然事已至此——就向约翰·贝尔蒙特爵士提出申请；至于官司，我希望，这个题目，永远不再听见有人提起。

对杜瓦尔夫人，一切有关矜持的恳求都是白费；她的计划，得用更合她理解力的道理去反驳。所以我不谈它的不当，只努力证明它的无用。

===Original===

Have the goodness, then, to tell her, that her own intentions would be frustrated by her plan; since, should the lawsuit be commenced, and even should the cause be gained, Sir John Belmont would still have it in his power, and, if irritated, no doubt in his inclination, to cut off her granddaughter with a shilling.
She cannot do better herself than to remain quiet and inactive in the affair: the long and mutual animosity between her and Sir John will make her interference merely productive of debates and ill-will. Neither would I have Evelina appear till summoned. And as to myself, I must wholly decline *acting*; though I will, with unwearied zeal, devote all my thoughts to giving counsel: but, in truth, I have neither inclination nor spirits adequate to engaging personally with this man.
My opinion is, that he would pay more respect to a letter from your Ladyship upon this subject, than from any other person. I, therefore, advise and hope, that you will yourself take the trouble of writing to him, in order to open the affair. When he shall be inclined to see Evelina, I have for him a posthumous letter, which his much injured lady left to be presented to him, if ever such a meeting should take place.
The views of the Branghtons, in suggesting this scheme, are obviously interested. They hope, by securing to Evelina the fortune of her father, to induce Madame Duval to settle her own upon themselves. In this, however, they would probably be mistaken; for little minds have ever a propensity to bestow their wealth upon those who are already in affluence; and, therefore, the less her grandchild requires her assistance, the more gladly she will give it.
I have but one thing more to add, from which, however, I can by no means recede: my word so solemnly given to Lady Belmont, that her child should never be owned but with her self, must be inviolably adhered to. I am, dear Madam, with great respect,
Your Ladyship’s most obedient servant,
Arthur Villars.

===Chinese===

那么，请您告诉她：她自己的打算，恰恰要败在她的计划手里；因为，官司即便开打、即便打赢，约翰·贝尔蒙特爵士依旧有权——一旦被激怒，无疑也有意——只给她的外孙女留一先令，把她一刀两断。

这件事上，她最好安安静静、袖手不动：她同约翰爵士之间那长期的两相仇恨，只会叫她的插手徒生口角与恶感。我也不愿伊芙琳娜在被传之前出头露面。至于我自己，我必须完全谢绝*出面*；不过我愿以不倦的热忱，倾全部心思为您献策：说实在的，同这个人当面周旋，我既无兴致，也无心力。

依我之见，这个题目上，他最敬重的，是夫人您的亲笔信。因此我建议、并切望，您亲自劳神写信给他，把这桩事开场。他愿见伊芙琳娜时，我这里存着一封遗书——他那位深受亏负的夫人留下的，嘱咐在这样一会果真发生时呈给他。

布兰顿一家献这个计，用意昭然是利。他们指望，伊芙琳娜既得着她父亲的财产，杜瓦尔夫人便会把自己的财产落到他们头上。这一点上，他们多半要打错算盘；因为小人物的心性，向来偏爱把钱财送给已经富足的人；所以，她的外孙女越不需要她资助，她给得越痛快。

我只再添一句，却是万万不能退让的：我对贝尔蒙特夫人郑重许下的诺言——她的孩子，除非连同她一起，永远不得被认领——必须一诺不移。亲爱的夫人，谨以最高的敬意，我是

您最恭顺的仆人，
阿瑟·维拉尔斯。

## Letter / 书信
===Original===

XXIX Mr. Villars to Evelina
Berry Hill, May 2.
How sincerely do I sympathise in the uneasiness and concern which my beloved Evelina has so much reason to feel! The cruel scheme in agitation is equally repugnant to my judgment and my inclination;﻿—yet to oppose it seems impracticable. To follow the dictates of my own heart, I should instantly recall you to myself, and never more consent to your being separated from me; but the manners and opinion of the world demand a different conduct. Hope, however, for the best, and be satisfied you shall meet with no indignity; if you are not received into your own family as you ought to be, and with the distinction that is your due, you shall leave it forever; and once again restored to my protection, secure your own tranquillity, and make, as you have hitherto done, all the happiness of my life.
Arthur Villars.

===Chinese===

第二十九封 维拉尔斯先生致伊芙琳娜
贝里山，五月二日。

我挚爱的伊芙琳娜有那么多理由感到不安与忧虑，我对她的同情何其真挚！那个正在密谋中的残忍计划，于我的判断同我的心愿同样扞格；——可要阻挡它，似乎办不到。若依我自己内心的指引，我该立刻把你召回身边，从此再不许你与我分离；可是这个世界的礼俗与舆论，却要求另一种处置。不过，要抱最好的希望，并请你确信：你不会受任何屈辱；倘若你不曾如你应得的那样、带着你应得的敬重被你的家族接纳，你就永远离开它；重新回到我的庇护之下，守住你自己的安宁，一如你至今所做的，继续做我一生的全部幸福。

亚瑟·维拉尔斯。

## Letter / 书信
===Original===

XXX Evelina to the Rev. Mr. Villars
Howard Grove, May 6.
The die is thrown, and I attend the event in trembling! Lady Howard has written to Paris, and sent her letter to town, to be forwarded in the ambassador’s packet; and, in less than a fortnight, therefore, she expects an answer. O, Sir, with what anxious impatience shall I wait its arrival! upon it seems to depend the fate of my future life. My solicitude is so great, and my suspense so painful, that I cannot rest a moment in peace, or turn my thoughts into any other channel.
Deeply interested as I now am in the event, most sincerely do I regret that the plan was ever proposed. Methinks it *cannot* end to my satisfaction: for either I must be torn from the arms of my *more* than father﻿—or I must have the misery of being finally convinced, that I am cruelly rejected by him who has the natural claim to that dear title, which to write, mention, or think of, fills my whole soul with filial tenderness.
The subject is discussed here eternally. Captain Mirvan and Madame Duval, as usual, quarrel whenever it is started: but I am so wholly engrossed by my own reflections, that I cannot even listen to them. My imagination changes the scene perpetually: one moment, I am embraced by a kind and relenting parent, who takes me to that heart from which I have hitherto been banished, and supplicates, through me, peace and forgiveness from the ashes of my mother!﻿—at another, he regards me with detestation, considers me as the living image of an injured saint, and repulses me with horror!﻿—But I will not afflict you with the melancholy phantasms of my brain; I will endeavour to compose my mind to a more tranquil state, and forbear to write again till I have in some measure succeeded.
May Heaven bless you, my dearest Sir! and long, long may it continue you on earth, to bless
Your grateful
Evelina.

===Chinese===

第三十封 伊芙琳娜致维拉尔斯牧师先生
霍华德园林，五月六日。

骰子已经掷出，我在颤抖中等待结局！霍华德夫人已写信去巴黎，信送到城里，由大使的信袋转发；所以不出两个星期，她盼着回音。啊，先生，我将怀着怎样焦灼的不耐等待它的到来啊！我一生的命运，似乎全系在它上面。我的忧悬这样重，我的悬望这样痛，一刻也不得安生，心思也无法转向别处。

如今我同这结局利害攸关至此，我倒最真诚地遗憾这计划当初竟被提出。我想它*断不能*圆满收场：因为，要么我得从我那位胜似父亲的人怀里被夺走——要么我得痛苦地终于确信：对我拥有那份亲爱称谓之天然权利的人，残忍地拒我于门外。那个称谓，无论写下、提起还是想起，都叫我满心孺慕之情。

这个题目在这里被翻来覆去地议论。米尔文上尉同杜瓦尔夫人，一提它就照例吵架：可我全被自己的思绪占满了，连听都听不进。我的想象不住地换着布景：一刹那间，一位慈爱回心的父亲拥抱了我，把我接进那颗至今把我放逐在外的心，并向我母亲的在天之灵，通过我，乞求宽恕与安宁！——又一刹那，他嫌恶地看我，把我看作一个受屈圣徒的活影像，恐怖地把我推开！——可我不要拿我脑子里这些阴郁的幻影折磨您了；我要尽力把心绪安定到更平静的地步，在多少成功之前，先不再执笔。

愿上天保佑您，我最亲爱的先生！愿它久久地把您留在人间，去保佑

您感恩的

伊芙琳娜。

## Letter / 书信
===Original===

XXXI Lady Howard to Sir John Belmont, Bart
Howard Grove, May 5.
Sir,
You will, doubtless, be surprised at receiving a letter from one who had for so short a period the honour of your acquaintance, and that at so great a distance of time; but the motive which has induced me to take this liberty is of so delicate a nature, that were I to commence making apologies for my officiousness, I fear my letter would be too long for your patience.
You have, probably, already conjectured the subject upon which I mean to treat. My regard for Mr. Evelyn, and his amiable daughter, was well known to you: nor can I ever cease to be interested in whatever belongs to their memory or family.
I must own myself somewhat distressed in what manner to introduce the purport of my writing; yet as I think that, in affairs of this kind, frankness is the first requisite to a good understanding between the parties concerned, I will neither torment you nor myself with punctilious ceremonies, but proceed instantly and openly to the business which occasions my giving you this trouble.
I presume, Sir, it would be superfluous to tell you, that your child resides still in Dorsetshire, and is still under the protection of the Reverend Mr. Villars, in whose house she was born: for, though no enquiries concerning her have reached his ears, or mine, I can never suppose it possible you have forborne to make them. It only remains, therefore, to tell you, that your daughter is now grown up; that she has been educated with the utmost care, and the utmost success; and that she is now a most deserving, accomplished, and amiable young woman.
Whatever may be your view for her future destination in life, it seems time to declare it. She is greatly admired, and, I doubt not, will be very much sought after: it is proper, therefore, that her future expectations, and your pleasure concerning her, should be made known.
Believe me, Sir, she merits your utmost attention and regard. You could not see and know her, and remain unmoved by those sensations of affection which belong to so near and tender a relationship.

===Chinese===

第三十一封 霍华德夫人致约翰·贝尔蒙特从男爵
霍华德园林，五月五日。

阁下：

收到一封仅有短日之交、且已隔多年的人的来信，您必定诧异；可促使我冒昧执笔的动机，性质过于微妙，倘若开头为先我的多事告起罪来，只怕这封信会长得超出您的耐性。

我打算谈论的题目，您多半已经猜到了。我对伊芙琳先生和他可爱女儿的敬重，您是熟知的：凡关平他们的遗念与家族的事，我也永远无法漠然。

我必须承认，如何引入此信的正题，颇叫我踌躇；不过我想，这一类的事，坦率是双方达成谅解的头一样要素，所以我不用繁文缛节折磨您，也不折磨自己，径直公开说明劳您阅读此信的正事。

阁下，我想告诉您已属多余：您的孩子如今仍在多塞特郡，仍在维拉尔斯牧师先生的照护之下——她就出生在他家里：因为，虽然探问她的音讯，从未传到他的耳朵或我的耳朵里，我却决不能设想，您竟克制住不曾探问。剩下的只是告诉您：您的女儿如今长大成人了；她受的教养无微不至，成效无微不至；如今她是一位极可敬、极贤能、极可爱的年轻女子。

无论您为她日后的人生作何打算，似乎都到言明的时候了。她广受仰慕，而且我毫不怀疑，追求者将络绎不绝：因此，她的前景、以及您对她的意愿，理当叫人知道。

相信我，阁下，她配得上您最深切的关怀与眷顾。您只要见她、认识她，便不可能不为这份至亲至柔的天伦之情所动。

===Original===

She is the lovely resemblance of her lovely mother;﻿—pardon, Sir, the liberty I take in mentioning that unfortunate lady; but I think it behoves me, upon this occasion, to show the esteem I felt for her: allow me, therefore, to say, and be not offended at my freedom, that the memory of that excellent lady has but too long remained under the aspersions of calumny; surely it is time to vindicate her fame;﻿—and how can that be done in a manner more eligible, more grateful to her friends, or more honourable to yourself, than by openly receiving as your child, *the daughter of the late Lady Belmont*?
The venerable man who has had the care of her education, deserves your warmest acknowledgments, for the unremitting pains he has taken, and the attention he has shown in the discharge of his trust. Indeed she has been peculiarly fortunate in meeting with such a friend and guardian; a more worthy man, or one whose character seems nearer to perfection, does not exist.
Permit me to assure you, Sir, she will amply repay whatever regard and favour you may hereafter show her, by the comfort and happiness you cannot fail to find in her affection and duty. To be owned *properly* by you is the first wish of her heart; and, I am sure, that to merit your approbation will be the first study of her life.
I fear that you will think this address impertinent; but I must rest upon the goodness of my intention to plead my excuse.
I am, Sir,

Your most obedient humble servant,
M. Howard.

===Chinese===

她是她可爱母亲的可爱化身；——宽恕，阁下，我冒昧提起那位不幸的夫人；可我想，在此事上我有责任表一表我对她的敬重：因此请容我说——并请勿见怪我的直率——那位贤淑夫人的名声，蒙受谤语的玷污，已经太久了；如今确是该为她的名誉昭雪的时候；——而昭雪之道，还有哪一条比这更得体、更令她的亲人欣慰、也更有光彩于您自己——公开认下您的孩子，认下*已故贝尔蒙特夫人之女*？

那位承担了她教养之责的可敬老人，值得您最热忱的感谢——为他付出的不懈辛劳、为他履行信托时的那份用心。她遇到这样一位朋友和监护人，实在格外幸运；更值得敬重的人、品格更近乎完美的人，世上再没有第二个。

请容我向您保证，阁下：日后您给她的无论何种眷顾与恩惠，她都将加倍偿还——偿还以您在她孝爱与恭顺中必然寻得的那份安慰与幸福。得到您*名正言顺*的认领，是她心头第一愿望；而且我确信，配得上您的嘉许，将是她毕生的第一门功课。

我怕您会觉得这封信冒昧唐突；可我唯有仰仗我动机的善良，为我自己求恕。

我是，阁下，

您最恭顺的卑微仆人，

M. 霍华德。

## Letter / 书信
===Original===

XXXII Evelina to the Rev. Mr. Villars
Howard Grove, Kent, May 10.
Our house has been enlivened today by the arrival of a London visitor; and the necessity I have been under of concealing the uneasiness of my mind, has made me exert myself so effectually, that I even think it is really diminished; or, at least, my thoughts are not so totally, so very anxiously, occupied by one subject only as they lately were.
I was strolling this morning with Miss Mirvan, down a lane about a mile from the Grove, when we heard the trampling of horses; and, fearing the narrowness of the passage, we were turning hastily back, but stopped upon hearing a voice call out, “Pray, Ladies, don’t be frightened, for I will walk my horse.” We turned again, and then saw Sir Clement Willoughby. He dismounted; and approaching us with the reins in his hand, presently recollected us. “Good Heaven,” cried he, with his usual quickness, “do I see Miss Anville?﻿—and you too, Miss Mirvan?”
He immediately ordered his servant to take charge of his horse; and then, advancing to us, took a hand of each, which he pressed to his lips, and said a thousand fine things concerning his good fortune, our improved looks, and the charms of the country, when inhabited by *such* rural deities. “The town, Ladies, has languished since your absence;﻿—or, at least, I have so much languished myself, as to be absolutely insensible to all it had to offer. One refreshing breeze, such as I now enjoy, awakens me to new vigour, life, and spirit. But I never before had the good luck to see the country in such perfection.”
“Has not almost everybody left town, Sir?” said Miss Mirvan.
“I am ashamed to answer you, Madam﻿—but indeed it is as full as ever, and will continue so till after the birthday. However, you Ladies were so little seen, that there are but few who know what it has lost. For my own part, I felt it too sensibly, to be able to endure the place any longer.”
“Is there anybody remaining there, that we were acquainted with?” cried I.
“O yes, Ma’am.” And then he named two or three persons we have seen when with him; but he did not mention Lord Orville, and I would not ask him, lest he should think me curious. Perhaps, if he stays here some time, he may speak of him by accident.

===Chinese===

第三十二封 伊芙琳娜致尊敬的维拉尔斯牧师先生

肯特郡，霍华德林苑，5月10日。

今天，一位伦敦来客给我们家添了生气；我既必须藏起心上的不安，便那样卖力地打起了精神，甚至觉得那不安真的轻了些；至少，我的念头不再像近来那样，全然、焦灼地，只盘踞着一个题目。

今天早晨我同米尔文小姐在林苑外约一英里的一条小路上散步，忽然听见马蹄声；路窄，我们怕撞上，正要勿勿回身，却听一个声音喊：“二位小姐请别怕，我会奉着马走的。”我们又转回去，看见了克莱门特·威洛比爵士。他下了马，缰绳提在手里朝我们走近，立刻认出了我们。“老天爷，”他照他惯常的机敏喊道，“我没看错吧，安维尔小姐？——还有您，米尔文小姐？”

他随即吩咐仆人牵马；然后走到我们跟前，一手拉住我们一只手，凑到唇边吻了，就他的好运、我们的气色、还有乡村——住着*这样*一批乡野仙姝的乡村——的魅力，说了千句漂亮话。“二位走后，伦敦城都憔悴了；——或者至少，我自己憔悴得厉害，城里供的一切，我全没了知觉。如今这一口提神的风，恰似我此刻享受的，把我又吹醒了，吹出新的精力、生气和精神。可我从前从没有这个福气，见过这样十全十美的乡野。”

“城里的人差不多走空了吧，爵士？”米尔文小姐说。

“我羞于回答您，夫人——城里真的还同先前一样满，而且要一直满到圣寿日以后。不过，二位小姐本来就极少露面，知道城里少了什么的，原也没有几个。拿我自己说，我感得太真，再待下去实在待不住。”

“我们认识的人里，还有谁留在城里吗？”我问。

“哦有的，夫人。”随后他举了两三位我们同他在一起时见过的人；可他没有提奥维尔勋爵，我也不肯问，怕他当我多心。也许他在这儿住些日子，会偶然说起他。

===Original===

He was proceeding in this complimentary style, when we were met by the Captain; who no sooner perceived Sir Clement, than he hastened up to him, gave him a hearty shake of the hand, a cordial slap on the back, and some other equally gentle tokens of satisfaction, assuring him of his great joy at his visit, and declaring he was as glad to see him as if he had been a messenger who brought news that a French ship was sunk. Sir Clement, on the other side, expressed himself with equal warmth; and protested he had been so eager to pay his respects to Captain Mirvan, that he had left London in its full lustre, and a thousand engagements unanswered, merely to give himself that pleasure.
“We shall have rare sport,” said the Captain; “for, do you know, the old French-woman is among us? ’Fore George, I have scarce made any use of her yet, by reason I have had nobody with me that could enjoy a joke: howsomever, it shall go hard but we’ll have some diversion now.”
Sir Clement very much approved of the proposal; and we then went into the house, where he had a very grave reception from Mrs. Mirvan, who is by no means pleased with his visit, and a look of much discontent from Madame Duval, who said to me in a low voice, “I’d as soon have seen Old Nick as that man, for he’s the most impertinentest person in the world, and isn’t never of my side.”
The Captain is now actually occupied in contriving some scheme, which, he says, is *to pay the old Dowager off*; and so eager and delighted is he at the idea, that he can scarcely restrain his raptures sufficiently to conceal his design even from herself. I wish, however, since I do not dare put Madame Duval upon her guard, that he had the delicacy not to acquaint me with his intention.

===Chinese===

他这套恭维话正说到兴头，舰长迎面来了；他一眼看见克莱门特爵士，立刻赶上前去，热热地握手，亲热地一巴掌拍上背，外加几样同样温柔的见礼，向他担保这次来访使自己多么欢喜，声言见了他，就同见到报信“击沉一艘法国船”的使者一样高兴。克莱门特爵士那一边，也表示得同样热烈；声言他急着来向米尔文舰长致敬，连伦敦正当全盛、一千个约都撂着没回，也不管了，专为讨这一桩愉快。

“咱们可有好戏了，”舰长说；“因为，你可知道，那法国老太太就在咱们这儿？老天在上，我一直没大用得着她，因为身边没有一个懂得玩笑的人陪着我：不过么，这回说什么也要找点乐子了。”

克莱门特爵士大大赞成这个提议；随后我们进了屋。米尔文太太待他冷冷淡淡——她一点也不喜欢他来；杜瓦尔夫人则一脸大大的不满，低声对我说：“这人呀，我还宁可看见老尼克，因为他是天下顶顶没规矩的东西，又从来不站我这边。”

舰长如今正埋头盘算一条计策，他说，要*好好收拾收拾那老太君*；他一想到这个就那样起劲、那样乐，连在她本人跟前，都几乎收不住他的得意，藏不住他的设计。只是，我既不敢提醒杜瓦尔夫人，但愿他多少知道点分寸，别把他的打算先告诉我。

===Original===

XXXIII Evelina in Continuation
May 13th.
The Captain’s operations are begun﻿—and, I hope, ended; for, indeed, poor Madame Duval has already but too much reason to regret Sir Clement’s visit to Howard Grove.
Yesterday morning, during breakfast, as the Captain was reading the newspaper, Sir Clement suddenly begged to look at it, saying, he wanted to know if there was any account of a transaction, at which he had been present the evening before his journey hither, concerning a poor Frenchman, who had got into a scrape which might cost him his life.
The Captain demanded particulars; and then Sir Clement told a long story of being with a party of country friends at the Tower, and hearing a man call out for mercy in French; and that, when he enquired into the occasion of his distress, he was informed that he had been taken up upon suspicion of treasonable practices against the government. “The poor fellow,” continued he, “no sooner found that I spoke French, than he besought me to hear him, protesting that he had no evil designs; that he had been but a short time in England, and only waited the return of a lady from the country to quit it forever.”
Madame Duval changed colour, and listened with the utmost attention.
“Now, though I by no means approve of so many foreigners continually flocking into our country,” added he, addressing himself to the Captain, “yet I could not help pitying the poor wretch, because he did not know enough of English to make his defence; however, I found it impossible to assist him; for the mob would not suffer me to interfere. In truth, I am afraid he was but roughly handled.”
“Why, did they duck him?” said the Captain.
“Something of that sort,” answered he.
“So much the better! so much the better!” cried the Captain, “an impudent French puppy! I’ll bet you what you will he was a rascal. I only wish all his countrymen were served the same.”
“I wish you had been in his place, with all my soul!” cried Madame Duval, warmly;﻿—“but pray, Sir, did’n’t nobody know who this poor gentleman was?”
“Why I did hear his name,” answered Sir Clement, “but I cannot recollect it.”
“It wasn’t﻿—it wasn’t﻿—Du Bois?” stammered out Madame Duval.
“The very name!” answered he: “yes, Du Bois, I remember it now.”
Madame Duval’s cup fell from her hand, as she repeated “Du Bois! Monsieur Du Bois, did you say?”
“Du Bois!

5月13日
舰长的行动已经开始——但愿也已经结束；因为，可怜的杜瓦尔夫人实在已经有太多理由，懊悔克莱门特爵士这次霍华德林的来访了。
昨天早晨吃早饭的时候，舰长正读着报纸，克莱门特爵士忽然请他借看一看，说他想知道报上有没有登一桩事——那桩事就发生在他动身来此的前一晚，他当时在场，说的是一个可怜的法国人，惹上了可能送命的祸事。
舰长要求细讲；于是克莱门特爵士编了一大篇话，说他如何同几位乡绅朋友在伦敦塔游玩，听见一个人用法语高声求饶；他去打听那人遭难的缘由，人家告诉他，那人是因涉嫌叛国、图谋不轨被拿下的。“那可怜人一见我说法语，”他接着说，“便求我听他申辩，一口咬定自己绝无恶意；说他到英国还不久，只等一位夫人从乡间回来，便永远离开这个国家。”
杜瓦尔夫人变了脸色，屏息凝神地听着。
“话说回来，我虽说绝不赞成这么多外国人一股脑儿涌进咱们国家，”他又说，这话是对着舰长讲的，“可那可怜虫连用英语替自己分辩都不会，我不由得可怜起他来；只是我想帮也帮不上，因为那群人不许我插手。说实话，恐怕他没少吃苦头。”
“怎么，他们把他浸水了？”舰长问。
“差不多是那么回事。”他答道。
“那才好呢！那才好呢！”舰长嚷道，“一个不要脸的法国小狗！随你赌什么，他准是个流氓。我只盼他的同胞个个都受同样的款待。”
“我倒巴不得你顶了他的位子才好！”杜瓦尔夫人气冲冲地嚷道，“请问爵士，就没有一个人知道这位可怜的先生是谁么？”
“唔，他的名字我倒听说过，”克莱门特爵士答道，“可就是想不起来了。”
“不是——不是——杜布瓦吧？”杜瓦尔夫人结结巴巴地说。
“正是这个名字！”他答道，“对，杜布瓦，我这会儿想起来了。”
杜瓦尔夫人手里的杯子掉了下去，一面直念叨：“杜布瓦！杜布瓦先生，你说的是他？”
“杜布瓦！”

why, that’s *my* friend,” cried the Captain, “that’s *Monseer Slippery*, i’n’t it?﻿—Why, he’s plaguy fond of sousing work; howsomever, I’ll be sworn they gave him his fill of it.”

“It is difficult to say,” answered Sir Clement, very thoughtfully; “but I should suppose, that if he has not good friends to appear for him, he will be in a very unpleasant situation; for these are serious sorts of affairs.”

Sir Clement shook his head, but made no answer.

“我倒可以起誓，”杜瓦尔夫人嚷道，“你是个——可我半个字也不信，你也不必这样得意，因为我说呀，那人才不是杜布瓦先生呢，我不是杜布瓦先生，他也不是。”
“我当时就觉得，”克莱门特爵士一本正经地说，“这位先生似乎在哪里见过；如今想起来了，我记得是在夫人您陪伴之下见的。”
“陪*我*？爵士？”杜瓦尔夫人叫起来。

克莱门特爵士摇了摇头，却不作声。

米尔文太太劝她不要惊慌；她却一阵风似的冲出房间，上楼进了自己的卧房。霍华德夫人怪两位先生太鲁莽，跟着她去了。我本想陪她同去，舰长却拦住了我；他先痛痛快快笑了一场，然后说他要向全体船员宣读委任状。
“你们可听好了，”他说，“至于霍华德夫人，我不打算征她入役，所以她的事就随她自己看着办；可你们这几位，我要的是服从命令、听凭调遣；我眼下正干着一桩冒险的差事，受命护送一条破船开往‘受辱岸’；所以，你们瞧，你们当中有谁有主意，能助这番大业一臂之力——尽管说，欢迎之至；可你们当中，凡是我挑中的船员，若有谁向敌人求和、私订什么条约——我就当他哗变，把他丢下船去，听天由命。”

===Original===

Having finished this harangue, which was interlarded with many expressions, and sea-phrases, that I cannot recollect, he gave Sir Clement a wink of intelligence, and left us to ourselves.
Indeed, notwithstanding the attempts I so frequently make of writing some of the Captain’s conversation, I can only give you a faint idea of his language; for almost every other word he utters is accompanied by an oath, which, I am sure, would be as unpleasant for you to read, as for me to write: and, besides, he makes use of a thousand sea-terms, which are to me quite unintelligible.
Poor Madame Duval sent to enquire at all probable places, whether she could be conveyed to town in any stagecoach: but the Captain’s servant brought her for answer, that no London stage would pass near Howard Grove till today. She then sent to order a chaise; but was soon assured, that no horses could be procured. She was so much inflamed by these disappointments, that she threatened to set out for town on foot; and it was with difficulty that Lady Howard dissuaded her from this mad scheme.
The whole morning was filled up with these enquiries. But when we were all assembled to dinner, she endeavoured to appear perfectly unconcerned, and repeatedly protested that she gave not any credit to the report, as far as it regarded M. Du Bois, being very certain that he was not the person in question.
The Captain used the most provoking efforts to convince her that she deceived herself; while Sir Clement, with more art, though not less malice, affected to be of her opinion; but, at the same time that he pretended to relieve her uneasiness, by saying that he doubted not having mistaken the name, he took care to enlarge upon the danger to which the *unknown gentleman* was exposed, and expressed great concern at his perilous situation.
Dinner was hardly removed, when a letter was delivered to Madame Duval. The moment she had read it, she hastily demanded from whom it came.
“A country boy brought it,” answered the servant, “but he would not wait.”
“Run after him this instant!” cried she, “and be sure you bring him back. *Mon Dieu! quelle aventure! que feraije?*”
“What’s the matter? what’s the matter?” said the Captain.
“Why nothing﻿—nothing’s the matter. *O mon Dieu!*”
And she rose, and walked about the room.
“Why, what﻿—has *Monseer* sent to you?” continued the Captain: “is that there letter from him?”

===Chinese===

这篇训话里还夹杂着好些词句和海上行话，我都记不得了。他讲完之后，朝克莱门特爵士使了个会意的眼色，便丢下我们自便了。
说实话，尽管我一再想把舰长的谈话记下几段来，也只能让您略知个大概；因为他开口几乎每隔一个词就带一句赌咒发誓，我敢说，那类话您读着难受，也不亚于我写着的难受：再者，他还满口海员术语，我听着一概摸不着头脑。
可怜的杜瓦尔夫人打发人四处打听，凡是可能的地方都问了，看能不能搭班车上城里去：可是舰长的仆人回她说，今天以前，没有一班去伦敦的驿车会经过霍华德林附近。她跟着又派人去雇轻便马车；不多时便得了回话，说一匹马也觅不着。接连的失望把她气得火冒三丈，扬言要徒步走进城去；霍华德夫人好说歹说，才劝住她这疯主意。
一个上午便全耗费在这些打探里。可是等大家入座吃饭，她却极力装出满不在乎的样子，再三声言这消息牵涉到杜布瓦先生的那些部分，她一概不信，因为她拿得稳他不是所说的那个人。
舰长使出种种撩人火气的话头，一心要她相信是她自己骗了自己；克莱门特爵士则更用心计——恶意却不见得少——假装与她所见相同；只是他一面假意宽她的心，说自己多半是把名字听岔了，一面又特意细细渲染那位*不知名的先生*身处的险境，对他的危难表示万分的关切。
饭菜才撤下去，一封信便送到了杜瓦尔夫人手里。她一读完，就急急追问信是谁送来的。
“一个乡下孩子送来的，”仆人答道，“可他不肯等。”
“这就去把他追回来！”她嚷道，“务必把他带回来。*天哪！这是什么事！叫我怎么办呀？*”
“怎么了？怎么了？”舰长问。
“没怎么——没怎么。*哦天哪！*”
说着她站起身，在屋里走来走去。
“咦，怎么——是*那位先生*给你写信了？”舰长接着说，“那封信就是他来的？”

===Original===

“No﻿—it i’n’t;﻿—besides, if it is, it’s nothing to you.”
“O then, I’m sure it is! Pray now, Madam, don’t be so close; come tell us all about it﻿—what does he say? how did he relish the horsepond?﻿—which did he find best, sousing *single* or *double*? ’Fore George, ’twas plaguy unlucky you was not with him!”
“It’s no such a thing, Sir,” cried she, very angrily; “and if you’re so very fond of a horsepond, I wish you’d put yourself into one, and not be always a thinking about other people’s being served so.”
The man then came in to acquaint her they could not overtake the boy. She scolded violently, and was in such perturbation, that Lady Howard interfered, and begged to know the cause of her uneasiness, and whether she could assist her.
Madame Duval cast her eyes upon the Captain and Sir Clement, and said she should be glad to speak to her Ladyship without so many witnesses.
“Well, then, Miss Anville,” said the Captain, turning to me, “do you and Molly go into another room, and stay there till Mrs. Duval has opened her mind to us.”
“So you may think, Sir,” cried she, “but who’s fool then? no, no, you needn’t trouble yourself to make a ninny of me neither, for I’m not so easily taken in, I’ll assure you.”
Lady Howard then invited her into the dressing-room, and I was desired to attend her.
As soon as we had shut the door, “O my Lady,” exclaimed Madame Duval, “here’s the most cruelest thing in the world has happened!﻿—but that Captain is such a beast, I can’t say nothing before him﻿—but it’s all true! poor M. Du Bois is tooked up!”
Lady Howard begged her to be comforted, saying that, as M. Du Bois was certainly innocent, there could be no doubt of his ability to clear himself.
“To be sure, my Lady,” answered she, “I know he is innocent; and to be sure they’ll never be so wicked as to hang him for nothing?”
“Certainly not,” replied Lady Howard; “you have no reason to be uneasy. This is not a country where punishment is inflicted without proof.”
“Very true, my Lady: but the worst thing is this; I cannot bear that that fellow the Captain should know about it; for if he does, I shan’t never hear the last of it;﻿—no more won’t poor M. Du Bois.”
“Well, well,” said Lady Howard, “show me the letter, and I will endeavour to advise you.”
The letter was then produced.

===Chinese===

“不是——不是他；——再说，就算是，也与你无关。”
“哦，那准就是了！夫人，求您了，别这样守口如瓶；来，原原本本讲给我们听——他说了什么？那口饮马塘的水味道如何呀？——他尝着哪种最好，*单*人浸还是*双*人浸？老天在上，你没跟他作伴去，可惜真是可惜！”
“根本没有的事，先生，”她气冲冲地嚷道，“你既然这么喜欢饮马塘，干吗不自己跳进去，省得整天惦记着让别人也去受这个。”
这时那仆人进来回话，说没能追上那孩子。她破口大骂，慌乱得不成样子，霍华德夫人便插了进来，求她说说烦恼的缘由，问问有什么可效劳的。
杜瓦尔夫人朝舰长和克莱门特爵士扫了一眼，说有这许多见证人在场，她有话也不好对夫人讲。
“那么，安维尔小姐，”舰长转过身来对我说，“你和莫莉到别的屋里去，待在那儿，等杜瓦尔老太太把心事吐给我们。”
“你想得倒好，先生，”她嚷道，“可谁才是傻子呢？不，不，你也犯不着费心把我当傻子耍，我告诉你，我可没那么容易上当。”
霍华德夫人随即请她进了梳妆室，又叫我随侍在旁。
我们才关上门，“哦夫人，”杜瓦尔夫人就叫起来，“天底下顶惨的事叫我赶上了！——只是那舰长太是个畜生，我当他一句话也说不出口——可都是真的！可怜的杜布瓦先生叫人抓起来了！”
霍华德夫人劝她宽心，说杜布瓦先生既然清白无疑，必能洗刷自己，这还有什么可疑惑的。
“那自然，夫人，”她答道，“我知道他是清白的；他们也断不至于坏到无缘无故绞死他吧？”
“自然不至于，”霍华德夫人答道，“您没有理由这样不安。这个国家决不会没有凭据就加刑于人。”
“很对，夫人：可顶糟的是这个：那个舰长家伙要是知道了，我可受不了；他一旦知道，这事我这辈子就别想听见个完；——可怜的杜布瓦先生也一样逃不了。”
“好啦，好啦，”霍华德夫人说，“把信给我看，我尽力替您出个主意。”
信这才拿了出来。

===Original===

It was signed by the clerk of a country justice; who acquainted her, that a prisoner, then upon trial for suspicion of treasonable practices against the government, was just upon the point of being committed to jail; but having declared that he was known to her, this clerk had been prevailed upon to write, in order to enquire if she really could speak to the character and family of a Frenchman who called himself Pierre Du Bois.
When I heard the letter, I was quite amazed at its success. So improbable did it seem, that a foreigner should be taken before a *country* justice of peace, for a crime of so dangerous a nature, that I cannot imagine how Madame Duval could be alarmed, even for a moment. But, with all her violence of temper, I see that she is easily frightened, and in fact, more cowardly than many who have not half her spirit; and so little does she reflect upon circumstances, or probability, that she is continually the dupe of her own﻿—I ought not to say *ignorance*, but yet I can think of no other word.
I believe that Lady Howard, from the beginning of the transaction, suspected some contrivance of the Captain; and this letter, I am sure, must confirm her suspicion: however, though she is not at all pleased with his frolic, yet she would not hazard the consequence of discovering his designs: her looks, her manner, and her character, made me draw this conclusion from her apparent perplexity; for not a word did she say that implied any doubt of the authenticity of the letter. Indeed there seems to be a sort of tacit agreement between her and the Captain, that she should not appear to be acquainted with his schemes; by which means she at once avoids quarrels, and supports her dignity.
While she was considering what to propose, Madame Duval begged to have the use of her Ladyship’s chariot, that she might go immediately to the assistance of her friend. Lady Howard politely assured her, that it should be extremely at her service; and then Madame Duval besought her not to own to the Captain what had happened, protesting that she could not endure he should know poor M. Du Bois had met with so unfortunate an accident. Lady Howard could not help smiling, though she readily promised not to *inform* the Captain of the affair. As to me, she desired my attendance; which I was by no means rejoiced at, as I was certain that she was going upon a fruitless errand.

===Chinese===

信末署名是一位乡村治安官手下的书记；信上说，有个囚犯正因涉嫌叛国受审，眼看就要押进大牢；只因他声言夫人认识他，这位书记才被说动了提笔写信，打听她是否真能为一位自称皮埃尔·杜布瓦的法国人的人品与家世作保。
我一听这信，真惊讶它竟有这样的效验。一个外国人，犯了这样险恶的罪名，居然会被解到一位*乡间*治安官面前——这事本身就不近情理，我实在想不明白杜瓦尔夫人怎么竟会惊慌，哪怕只慌一小会儿。可是我算是看出来了，她脾气虽凶，胆子却极小，说实在的，比许多气性不及她一半的人还要懦弱；她又全不思量情由与情理，所以老是上自己的当——我不该说*愚昧*，可又想不出别的词来。
我相信，这事从一开始，霍华德夫人便疑心是舰长搞的什么计谋；这封信，我敢说，必定了她的疑心：不过，她虽全不赞成他这场恶作剧，却也不肯点破他的设计而自惹后果：她的神色、她的举止、她的为人，都叫我从她表面的为难中得出这个结论；因为信的真伪，她连一句疑心的话也没有露。说起来，她同舰长之间仿佛有种默契：她只作不知道他的计策；这样一来，她既免了口角，又保住了自己的体面。
她正盘算着提什么建议，杜瓦尔夫人便求借夫人的马车，好立刻赶去搭救她的朋友。霍华德夫人客气地满口应承，说马车尽管听她使用；杜瓦尔夫人跟着又央告她，千万别把这事对舰长说起，声言她实在受不了让他知道可怜的杜布瓦先生遭了这样的意外。霍华德夫人忍不住笑了，却爽爽快快答应不向舰长*告知*此事。至于我，她要我随行；我实在高兴不起来，因为我拿得准她这一趟是白跑。

===Original===

I was then commissioned to order the chariot.
At the foot of the stairs I met the Captain, who was most impatiently waiting the result of the conference. In an instant we were joined by Sir Clement. A thousand enquiries were then made concerning Madame Duval’s opinion of the letter, and her intentions upon it: and when I would have left them, Sir Clement, pretending equal eagerness with the Captain, caught my hand, and repeatedly detained me, to ask some frivolous question, to the answer of which he must be totally indifferent. At length, however, I broke from them; they retired into the parlour, and I executed my commission.
The carriage was soon ready; and Madame Duval, having begged Lady Howard to say she was not well, stole softly downstairs, desiring me to follow her. The chariot was ordered at the garden-door; and, when we were seated, she told the man, according to the clerk’s directions, to drive to Mr. Justice Tyrell’s, asking at the same time, how many miles off he lived?
I expected he would have answered, that he knew of no such person; but, to my great surprise, he said, “Why, ’Squire Tyrell lives about nine miles beyond the park.”
“Drive fast, then,” cried she, “and you shan’t be no worse for it.”
During our ride, which was extremely tedious, she tormented herself with a thousand fears for M. Du Bois’s safety; and piqued herself very much upon having escaped unseen by the Captain, not only that she avoided his triumph, but because she knew him to be so much M. Du Bois’s enemy, that she was sure he would prejudice the justice against him, and endeavour to take away his life. For my part, I was quite ashamed of being engaged in so ridiculous an affair, and could only think of the absurd appearance we should make upon our arrival at Mr. Tyrell’s.
When we had been out near two hours, and expected every moment to stop at the place of our destination, I observed that Lady Howard’s servant, who attended us on horseback, rode on forward till he was out of sight: and soon after returning, came up to the chariot window, and delivering a note to Madame Duval, said he had met a boy who was just coming with it to Howard Grove from the clerk of Mr. Tyrell.

===Chinese===

接着她们便差我去吩咐备车。
在楼梯脚下我撞见了舰长，他正等得心焦，盼着那场密谈的结果。一转眼克莱门特爵士也凑了过来。两人于是千遍百遍地打听：杜瓦尔夫人对那封信怎么想，打算怎么办：我正要走开，克莱门特爵士装出同舰长一样着急的样子，一把抓住我的手，再三把我缠住，问些鸡毛蒜皮的问题——那些答案他其实半点也不放在心上。不过我终于还是脱了身；他们退进客厅去了，我也把差事办妥了。
车很快备好；杜瓦尔夫人求霍华德夫人只推说她身上不爽，便蹑手蹑脚溜下楼来，叫我跟着她。马车停在园门前；我们坐定之后，她便照书记信上的嘱咐，吩咐车夫赶去泰瑞尔治安官府上，一面又问那官人家住在多少里外？
我只当车夫会答一句“不认得这么个人”；谁知他竟说：“咦，泰瑞尔老爷就住在大园子那头，约莫九英里。”
“那快些赶，”她嚷道，“少不了你的好处。”
一路之上，车子走得磨蹭极了，她拿杜布瓦先生的安危千百样地吓唬自己；同时又一味得意，自庆躲过了舰长的眼睛——这不单是为了免得他称心夸胜，也是因为她深知他同杜布瓦先生仇怨太深，她拿得准他会在治安官跟前说坏话害他，还要想法取他的性命。至于我，卷进这样一桩荒唐事里，真是臊得慌，满心只想着我们到了泰瑞尔先生府上时那副可笑的嘴脸。
出门将近两个钟头，眼看每一刻都要到地头了，我却看见霍华德夫人那名骑马跟班的仆人，催马跑到前头，直到望不见影儿：不多时他折回来，赶到车窗旁，递给杜瓦尔夫人一张字条，说路上撞见一个孩子，正要把这字条从泰瑞尔先生的书记那里捎到霍华德林去。

===Original===

While she was reading it, he rode round to the other window, and making a sign for secrecy, put into my hand a slip of paper, on which was written, “Whatever happens, be not alarmed﻿—for *you* are safe﻿—though you endanger all mankind!”
I readily imagined that Sir Clement must be the author of this note, which prepared me to expect some disagreeable adventure: but I had no time to ponder upon it; for Madame Duval had no sooner read her own letter, than, in an angry tone of voice, she exclaimed, “Why, now, what a thing is this! here we’re come all this way for nothing!”
She gave me the note; which informed her, that she need not trouble herself to go to Mr. Tyrell’s, as the prisoner had had the address to escape. I congratulated her upon this fortunate incident; but she was so much concerned at having rode so far in vain, that she seemed to be less pleased than provoked. However, she ordered the man to make what haste he could home, as she hoped, at least, to return before the Captain should suspect what had passed.
The carriage turned about; and we journeyed so quietly for near an hour, that I began to flatter myself we should be suffered to proceed to Howard Grove without any molestation, when suddenly, the footman called out, “John, are we going right?”
“Why, I a’n’t sure,” said the coachman, “But I’m afraid we turned wrong.”
“What do you mean by that, sirrah?” said Madame Duval; “why, if you lose your way, we shall all be in the dark.”
“I think we should turn to the left,” said the footman.
“To the left!” answered the other; “No, no, I’m partly sure we should turn to the right.”
“You had better make some enquiry,” said I.
“*Ma foi!*” cried Madame Duval, “we’re in a fine hole here!﻿—they neither of them know no more than the post. However, I’ll tell my Lady as sure as you’re born, you’d better find the way.”
“Let’s try this lane,” said the footman.
“No,” said the coachman, “that’s the road to Canterbury; we had best go straight on.”
“Why, that’s the direct London road,” returned the footman, “and will lead us twenty miles about.”
“*Pardi*,” cried Madame Duval, “why, they won’t go one way nor t’other! and now we’re come all this jaunt for nothing, I suppose we shan’t get home tonight!”
“Let’s go back to the public-house,” said the footman, “and ask for a guide.”

===Chinese===

她读信的当儿，他绕到另一扇车窗前，做了个噤声的手势，塞进我手里一张纸条，上面写着：“无论出什么事，切莫惊慌——*你*是安全的——哪怕你坑害了全人类！”
我一猜便中，这字条准是克莱门特爵士的手笔，心里也就有了预备，知道要有一场不痛快的风波：只是不容我细想；杜瓦尔夫人那边才看完信，就气冲冲地嚷起来：“哎呀，你瞧这是什么事！我们大老远赶来，竟是白跑一趟！”
她把信递给我；信上说，她不必劳神再去泰瑞尔先生府上，因为那囚犯有本事，越狱逃掉了。我道贺说这事再侥幸不过；可是她痛惜这一趟跑得冤枉，与其说是欢喜，不如说是恼火。不过她还是吩咐下人拼命往家赶，指望至少赶在舰长起疑之前回到家里。
马车掉转头；我们安安静静走了将近一个钟头，我开始存侥幸之心，以为这一路可以不受搅扰、径直到得霍华德林，不想那跟班忽然喊道：“约翰，咱这条路走得对么？”
“唉，说不准，”车夫道，“只怕咱们拐错了。”
“你这话什么意思，小子？”杜瓦尔夫人说，“哎呀，你们要是迷了路，咱们可就两眼一抹黑了。”
“我看咱们该靠左拐。”跟班说。
“靠左！”另一个答道，“不，不，我八成拿得准该靠右。”
“你们顶好打听打听。”我说。
“*我的妈呀！*”杜瓦尔夫人嚷道，“咱们这可掉进好坑里了！——他们俩懂得的路，不比一根木桩子多。反正，我对夫人说定了，你们赶紧把路找出来。”
“试试这条小道吧。”跟班说。
“不行，”车夫说，“那是去坎特伯雷的路；咱们顶好照直走。”
“咦，那正是直通伦敦的大道，”跟班回嘴道，“要绕咱们二十英里的冤枉路。”
“*天晓得！*”杜瓦尔夫人嚷道，“哎呀，他们横竖哪条路都不肯走！这趟白跑也跑了，我看今晚咱们是到家不成了！”
“回到那家酒店去，”跟班说，“找个向导。”

===Original===

“No, no,” said the other, “if we stay here a few minutes, somebody or other will pass by; and the horses are almost knocked up already.”
“Well, I protest,” cried Madame Duval, “I’d give a guinea to see them sots both horsewhipped! As sure as I’m alive they’re drunk! Ten to one but they’ll overturn us next.”
After much debating, they at length agreed to go on till we came to some inn, or met with a passenger who could direct us. We soon arrived at a farmhouse, and the footman alighted, and went into it.
In a few minutes he returned, and told us we might proceed, for that he had procured a direction: “But,” added he, “it seems there are some thieves hereabouts; and so the best way will be for you to leave your watches and your purses with the farmer, whom I know very well, and who is an honest man, and a tenant of my Lady’s.”
“Thieves!” cried Madame Duval, looking aghast; “the Lord help us!﻿—I’ve no doubt but we shall be all murdered!”
The farmer came up to us, and we gave him all we were worth, and the servants followed our example. We then proceeded; and Madame Duval’s anger so entirely subsided, that, in the mildest manner imaginable, she entreated them to make haste, and promised to tell their Lady how diligent and obliging they had been. She perpetually stopped them, to ask if they apprehended any danger; and was at length so much overpowered by her fears, that she made the footman fasten his horse to the back of the carriage, and then come and seat himself within it. My endeavours to encourage her were fruitless: she sat in the middle, held the man by the arm, and protested that if he did but save her life, she would make his fortune. Her uneasiness gave me much concern, and it was with the utmost difficulty I forbore to acquaint her that she was imposed upon; but the mutual fear of the Captain’s resentment to me, and of her own to him, neither of which would have any moderation, deterred me. As to the footman, he was evidently in torture from restraining his laughter; and I observed that he was frequently obliged to make most horrid grimaces, from pretended fear, in order to conceal his risibility.
Very soon after, “The robbers are coming!” cried the coachman.
The footman opened the door, and jumped out of the chariot.
Madame Duval gave a loud scream.
I could no longer preserve my silence.

===Chinese===

“不，不，”另一个说，“咱们在这儿待上几分钟，总会有人打这儿过；再说这几匹马也快累趴下了。”
“咳，我说，”杜瓦尔夫人嚷道，“我情愿出一个几尼，看人拿马鞭抽那两个醉鬼！千真万确他们是喝醉了！十有八九，下一刻就要把咱们翻到沟里去。”
两人争执了半天，最后说定接着往前走，碰到一家客店，或是遇上一个能指路的人再说。不多时我们到了一处农舍，跟班下了车，进去了。
几分钟后他回来，说可以走了，他已经问明白了路径：“不过，”他添了一句，“这一带听说有几个贼；所以顶好的法子，是你们把表和钱袋都寄放在那庄稼人家里——我跟他熟得很，他是个老实人，是咱们夫人的佃户。”
“贼！”杜瓦尔夫人叫起来，脸都吓白了；“老天爷保佑！——我说不定咱们全要遭杀害了！”
那庄稼人走到车前来，我们把随身值钱的东西尽数交给了他，仆人们也学我们的样。随后我们接着赶路；杜瓦尔夫人的火气竟消得干干净净，她拿出想象得出的顶温和的口气，央告他们快些赶车，还许愿要在夫人跟前夸他们勤快、殷勤。她时不时叫停车，问他们可觉得有什么危险；末了竟被自己的恐惧压倒，叫跟班把马拴在车后，进车里来坐在她身旁。我百般给她壮胆，全然无用：她坐在当中，一把攥住那人的胳膊，声言只要他能救她这条命，她保管叫他发一笔财。她的惶恐叫我心里老大不安，我拼命忍着才没向她点破她是叫人捉弄了；可我一怕舰长报复我，二怕她报复舰长——这两样火气都不会有分寸——便只好作罢。至于那跟班，他憋笑憋得显然苦不堪言；我屡屡看见他不得不装出害怕的样子，做出种种狰狞的鬼脸，好遮掩他那快要绷不住的笑。
没过多久，“强盗来啦！”车夫喊道。
跟班打开车门，跳下马车。
杜瓦尔夫人尖叫一声。
我再也不能不作声了。

===Original===

“For Heaven’s sake, my dear Madame,” said I, “don’t be alarmed﻿—you are in no danger﻿—you are quite safe﻿—there is nothing but﻿—”
Here the chariot was stopped by two men in masks; who at each side put in their hands as if for our purses. Madame Duval sunk to the bottom of the chariot, and implored their mercy. I shrieked involuntarily, although prepared for the attack: one of them held me fast, while the other tore poor Madame Duval out of the carriage, in spite of her cries, threats, and resistance.
I was really frightened, and trembled exceedingly. “My angel!” cried the man who held me, “you cannot surely be alarmed﻿—do you not know me?﻿—I shall hold myself in eternal abhorrence, if I have really terrified you.”
“Indeed, Sir Clement, you have,” cried I:﻿—“but, for Heaven’s sake, where is Madame Duval?﻿—why is she forced away?”
“She is perfectly safe; the Captain has her in charge: but suffer me now, my adored Miss Anville, to take the only opportunity that is allowed me, to speak upon another, a much dearer, much sweeter subject.”
And then he hastily came into the chariot, and seated himself next to me. I would fain have disengaged myself from him, but he would not let me: “Deny me not, most charming of women,” cried he, “deny me not this only moment that is lent me, to pour forth my soul into your gentle ears﻿—to tell you how much I suffer from your absence﻿—how much I dread your displeasure﻿—and how cruelly I am affected by your coldness!”
“O, Sir, this is no time for such language;﻿—pray leave me, pray go to the relief of Madame Duval﻿—I cannot bear that she should be treated with such indignity.”
“And will you﻿—can you command my absence?﻿—When may I speak to you, if not now?﻿—Does the Captain suffer me to breathe a moment out of his sight?﻿—and are not a thousand impertinent people forever at your elbow?”
“Indeed, Sir Clement, you must change your style, or I will not hear you. The *impertinent people* you mean are among my best friends; and you would not, if you really wished me well, speak of them so disrespectfully.”
“Wish you well!﻿—O, Miss Anville, point but out to me how, in what manner, I may convince you of the fervour of my passion;﻿—tell me but what services you will accept from me﻿—and you shall find my life, my fortune, my whole soul at your devotion.”

===Chinese===

“看在老天爷份上，亲爱的夫人，”我说，“别惊慌——您没有危险——您安全得很——不过是——”
话音未落，马车便被两个戴面具的人截住了；他们从两边把伸进手来，仿佛是来抢钱袋的。杜瓦尔夫人瘫倒在车厢底，苦苦哀求饶命。我虽早有防备，还是不由自主尖叫了一声：一个紧紧捉住我，另一个不顾可怜的杜瓦尔夫人的哭喊、威吓和挣扎，硬把她从车里拖了出去。
我真吓着了，抖得厉害。“我的天使！”捉住我的那人喊道，“你可千万不必惊慌——你难道不认得我么？——倘若我真吓着了你，我要一辈子恨死我自己。”
“克莱门特爵士，您确实吓着我了，”我叫道，“——可是看老天爷份上，杜瓦尔夫人在哪儿？——为什么把她硬拖走？”
“她安全得很；有舰长照管她呢：只是此刻，我倾心爱慕的安维尔小姐，容我趁着这仅有的机会，谈一谈另一件事，一件亲爱得多、甜蜜得多的事。”
说着他急忙钻进马车，在我身旁坐定。我想挣脱他，他却死活不放：“别拒绝我，最迷人的小姐，”他嚷道，“别拒绝我借来的这唯一的时刻，让我把满腔心事倾吐给你温柔的耳朵——告诉你，别后我多么苦楚——我多么怕你不悦——你的冷淡叫我多么伤心！”
“哦，爵士，眼下不是说这些话的时候；——求您走开，快去照看杜瓦尔夫人吧——她受这样的作践，我实在看不下去。”
“你当真要——你竟能下令叫我走么？——不然我何时才能同你说话？——舰长可容我在他眼皮底下喘一口气？——何况还有一千个讨嫌的人，不总在你胳膊肘边围着？”
“克莱门特爵士，您非换个腔调不可，不然我就不听了。您说的那些*讨嫌的人*，是我顶好的朋友；您若真盼着我好，就决不会这样不客气地议论他们。”
“盼着你好！——哦，安维尔小姐，只要你指给我看，教我怎样、用什么法子，才能叫你相信我这片痴情；——只要你说出你肯受我什么效劳——你就会看到，我的性命、我的家财、我整个的灵魂，全都听凭你驱遣。”

===Original===

“I want *nothing*, Sir, that you can offer;﻿—I beg you not to talk to me so﻿—so strangely. Pray leave me; and pray assure yourself you cannot take any method so successless to show any regard for me, as entering into schemes so frightful to Madame Duval, and so disagreeable to myself.”
“The scheme was the Captain’s: I even opposed it: though, I own, I could not refuse myself the so-long-wished-for happiness of speaking to you once more, without so many of﻿—your *friends* to watch me. And I had flattered myself, that the note I charged the footman to give you, would have prevented the alarm you have received.”
“Well Sir, you have now, I hope, said enough; and, if you will not go yourself to see for Madame Duval, at least suffer *me* to enquire what is become of her.”
“And when may I speak to you again?”
“No matter when﻿—I don’t know﻿—perhaps﻿—”
“Perhaps what, my angel?”
“Perhaps *never*, Sir﻿—if you torment me thus.”
“Never! O, Miss Anville, how cruel, how piercing to my soul is that icy word!﻿—Indeed I cannot endure such displeasure.”
“Then, Sir, you must not provoke it. Pray leave me directly.”
“I will Madam: but let me, at least, make a merit of my obedience﻿—allow me to hope that you will, in future, be less averse to trusting yourself for a few moments alone with me.”
I was surprised at the freedom of this request: but, while I hesitated how to answer it, the other mask came up to the chariot-door, and, in a voice almost stifled with laughter said, “I’ve done for her!﻿—the old buck is safe;﻿—but we must sheer off directly, or we shall be all ground.”
Sir Clement instantly left me, mounted his horse, and rode off. The Captain having given some directions to the servants, followed him.
I was both uneasy and impatient to know the fate of Madame Duval, and immediately got out of the chariot to seek her. I desired the footman to show me which way she was gone; he pointed with his finger by way of answer, and I saw that he dared not trust his voice to make any other. I walked on at a very quick pace, and soon, to my great consternation, perceived the poor lady seated upright in a ditch. I flew to her with unfeigned concern at her situation. She was sobbing, nay, almost roaring, and in the utmost agony of rage and terror. As soon as she saw me, she redoubled her cries; but her voice was so broken, I could not understand a word she said.

===Chinese===

“我能要的东西，先生，您一样也给不了；——求您别再用这样——这样古怪的话同我说话。求您走开；也请您相信，您要想对我表示什么情意，再没有比搅进这种计策里更没用的法子了——这计策吓坏了杜瓦尔夫人，也叫我自己说不出的厌烦。”
“这计策是舰长出的：我还反对来着：不过，老实说，能不受你那许多——你那些*朋友*——的监视，再同你说一回话，这份盼望已久的福气，我实在舍不得推掉。我原本还指望，我让跟班递你的那张字条，总可以免了你这一场惊吓。”
“好了，爵士，我希望，您如今话说得够多了；您既不肯亲自去看看杜瓦尔夫人，至少容*我*去问问她怎么样了。”
“那我什么时候还能同你说话？”
“管他什么时候——我不知道——也许——”
“也许什么，我的天使？”
“也许*永远*不——您要是这样纠缠我的话。”
“永远不！哦，安维尔小姐，这个冷冰冰的字眼多么狠心，多么刺痛我的灵魂！——真的，这样动怒我可受不了。”
“那么，爵士，您就不要招它。求您这就走开。”
“我走，小姐：可至少容我把这番服从记上一功——容我存一点指望：往后你再同我单独待上一小会儿时，不至于那样避之不及。”
这样放肆的要求真叫我吃惊：可我正迟疑着怎么回答，另一个戴面具的走到车门前来，声音叫笑意憋得几乎透不出来，说道：“我把她办妥了！——那老家伙稳稳当当；——不过咱们得马上开溜，不然全都要搁浅。”
克莱门特爵士立刻丢下我，翻身上马，疾驰而去。舰长对仆人们吩咐了几句，也跟着他去了。
我又不安又心急，急着要知道杜瓦尔夫人的下落，立刻下车去寻她。我请跟班指给我她被拖去的方向；他只拿手指一指，算作回答，我看得出他不敢开口，一开口声音就得露馅。我快步赶去，不多时便看见了——真叫我大骇——那可怜的夫人端端正正坐在一条沟里。我满心真切地挂念她的处境，飞奔到她跟前。她正在抽噎，不，简直是嚎啕，又怒又怕，苦到极处。她一见我，哭喊得更凶了；只是她的嗓子哭破了，说的一个字我也听不清。

===Original===

I was so much shocked, that it was with difficulty I forebore exclaiming against the cruelty of the Captain for thus wantonly ill-treating her; and I could not forgive myself for having passively suffered the deception. I used my utmost endeavours to comfort her, assuring her of our present safety, and begging her to rise and return to the chariot.
Almost bursting with passion, she pointed to her feet, and with frightful violence she actually tore the ground with her hands.
I then saw that her feet were tied together with a strong rope, which was fastened to the upper branch of a tree, even with a hedge which ran along the ditch where she sat. I endeavoured to untie the knot; but soon found it was infinitely beyond my strength. I was, therefore, obliged to apply to the footman; but, being very unwilling to add to his mirth by the sight of Madame Duval’s situation, I desired him to lend me a knife: I returned with it, and cut the rope. Her feet were soon disentangled; and then, though with great difficulty, I assisted her to rise. But what was my astonishment, when, the moment she was up, she hit me a violent slap on the face! I retreated from her with precipitation and dread: and she then loaded me with reproaches, which, though almost unintelligible, convinced me that she imagined I had voluntarily deserted her; but she seemed not to have the slightest suspicion that she had not been attacked by real robbers.
I was so much surprised and confounded at the blow, that, for some time, I suffered her to rave without making any answer; but her extreme agitation, and real suffering, soon dispelled my anger, which all turned into compassion. I then told her, that I had been forcibly detained from following her, and assured her of my real sorrow of her ill-usage.
She began to be somewhat appeased; and I again entreated her to return to the carriage, or give me leave to order that it should draw up to the place where we stood. She made no answer, till I told her, that the longer we remained still, the greater would be the danger of our ride home. Struck with this hint, she suddenly, and with hasty steps, moved forward.
Her dress was in such disorder, that I was quite sorry to have her figure exposed to the servants, who all of them, in imitation of their master, hold her in derision: however the disgrace was unavoidable.

===Chinese===

我又惊又痛，好不容易才忍住，没当场骂出舰长的狠毒——他竟这样没来由地作践她；我自己听凭这场骗局糊弄过去，也自恨不能饶恕。我使出浑身解数安慰她，一面担保我们如今平安无事，一面求她起身回到马车上去。
她怒气几乎要把胸膛胀破，指着自己的双脚，竟伸出手去，狠狠地刨地，那样子怕人极了。
我这才发现，她的双脚被一条粗绳捆在一起，绳头拴在高处一根树杈上，那树同沿沟的篱笆一般高，她正是坐在沟里。我动手去解那绳结；可很快便看出，那远非我的力气所及。我只得去求跟班帮忙；又不忍让他瞧见杜瓦尔夫人的样子、再添他的笑料，便只问他借了一把小刀：我拿着刀回来，割断了绳子。她的双脚很快解开了；随后我费了好大的劲，才扶她起身。谁知她才站起身，劈面就重重给了我一个耳光，你道我多么吃惊！我慌忙又怕又急地躲开她：她跟着就百般数落我，那些话虽然几乎听不懂，却叫我明白，她只当我是有意丢下她不管了；可她竟丝毫没有疑心，抢劫她的并非真的强盗。
这一个耳光打得我又惊又懵，有一阵子，只由她叫骂，一声也不答；可她那过度的激动和真实的苦楚，不久便消了我的气，气全化成了怜惜。我便告诉她，我是被人硬拦住，才没能跟她去，又真心实意为她受的作践表示难过。
她的火气这才平了些；我又求她回车上去，要不就容我吩咐把车赶到我们站的地方来。她一声不吭，直到我说，我们在这儿待得越久，回家的路上危险就越大。这句话点醒了她，她忽然拔脚，急急往前就走。
她的衣衫乱成那样，真叫我不忍让仆人们看见她的模样——他们学他们主人的样，个个拿她取笑：不过这一场出丑，终究躲不过去。

===Original===

The ditch, happily, was almost quite dry, or she must have suffered still more seriously; yet so forlorn, so miserable a figure, I never before saw her. Her headdress had fallen off, her linen was torn, her negligee had not a pin left in it, her petticoats she was obliged to hold on, and her shoes were perpetually slipping off. She was covered with dirt, weeds, and filth, and her face was really horrible; for the pomatum and powder from her head, and the dust from the road, were quite *pasted* on her skin by her tears, which, with her rouge, made so frightful a mixture, that she hardly looked human.
The servants were ready to die with laughter the moment they saw her; but not all my remonstrances could prevail upon her to get into the carriage, till she had most vehemently reproached them both for not rescuing her. The footman, fixing his eyes on the ground, as if fearful of again trusting himself to look at her, protested that the robbers had vowed they would shoot him if he moved an inch, and that one of them had stayed to watch the chariot, while the other carried her off, adding, that the reason of their behaving so barbarously, was to revenge our having secured our purses. Notwithstanding her anger, she gave immediate credit to what he said; and really imagined that her want of money had irritated the pretended robbers to treat her with such cruelty. I determined, therefore, to be carefully upon my guard not to betray the imposition, which could now answer no other purpose, then occasioning an irreparable breach between her and the Captain.
Just as we were seated in the chariot, she discovered the loss which her head had sustained, and called out, “My God! what is become of my hair?﻿—why, the villain has stole all my curls!”
She then ordered the man to run and see if he could find any of them in the ditch. He went, and presently returning, produced a great quantity of hair, in such nasty condition, that I was amazed she would take it; and the man, as he delivered it to her, found it impossible to keep his countenance; which she no sooner observed, than all her stormy passions were again raised. She flung the battered curls in his face, saying, “Sirrah, what do you grin for?

===Chinese===

所幸那沟几乎全干了，不然她还得多受一番罪；可是这样凄惶、这样狼狈的样子，我从没见过她。头上的假发包掉了，里衣撕破了，家常长袍上连一根别针也不剩，衬裙只得用手按住，鞋子一双不停地往下掉。她满身是泥、是草屑、是秽物，那张脸真是怕人：头上润发的香油和香粉，加上路上的尘土，全叫眼泪*糊*在了皮肤上，再和着胭脂，调成那样可怕的一团，简直不像个人样了。
仆人们一见了她，都险些笑死；可任凭我怎样劝，她死也不肯上车，先把两人狠狠数落了一顿，怪他们不去救她。那跟班眼睛死死盯着地上，仿佛怕再看她一眼又要失态，一口咬定说，两个强盗赌过咒，他只要动一动就开枪打他，还说一个留下看着马车，另一个才把她掳走的，又说他们行事这样狠毒，就是为了报我们藏起钱袋的仇。她虽然气急，对他这话却信了个十足；还当真以为，就因为她身上没钱，才惹得那假强盗们这样毒害她。于是我打定主意，千万小心，不点破这场骗局——事到如今，点破了别无好处，只会在她同舰长之间造成一道再难弥补的裂痕。
我们才在车里坐定，她发觉了头上遭的损失，叫起来：“我的天！我的头发哪儿去了？——哎呀，那恶棍把我的鬈发全偷走啦！”
她跟着就吩咐那仆人跑去沟里找找，看还能寻回几绺来。他去了，不多时回来，捧上一大把头发，那样子脏得叫我吃惊，她竟肯收下；那仆人交头发给她时，再也绷不住脸上的肌肉；她一见，满腔的怒火又轰地烧起来。她把那几绺打瘪了的鬈发摔在他脸上，骂道：“小子，你咧什么嘴？”

===Original===

I wish you’d been served so yourself, and you wouldn’t have found it no such joke; you are the impudentest fellow ever I see; and if I find you dare grin at me any more, I shall make no ceremony of boxing your ears.”
Satisfied with the threat, the man hastily retired, and we drove on.
Her anger now subsiding into grief, she began most sorrowfully to lament her case. “I believe,” she cried, “never nobody was so unlucky as I am! and so here, because I ha’n’t had misfortunes enough already, that puppy has made me lose my curls!﻿—Why, I can’t see nobody without them:﻿—only look at me﻿—I was never so bad off in my life before. *Pardi*, if I’d know’d as much, I’d have brought two or three sets with me: but I’d never a thought of such a thing as this.”
Finding her now somewhat pacified, I ventured to ask an account of her adventure, which I will endeavour to write in her own words.
“Why, child, all this misfortune comes of that puppy’s making us leave our money behind us; for, as soon as the robber see I did put nothing in his hands, he lugged me out of the chariot by main force, and I verily thought he’d have murdered me. He was as strong as a lion; I was no more in his hands than a child. But I believe never nobody was so abused before; for he dragged me down the road, pulling and hauling me all the way, as if’d no more feeling than a horse. I’m sure I wish I could see that man cut up and quartered alive! however, he’ll come to the gallows, that’s one good thing. So soon as we’d got out of sight of the chariot, though he needn’t have been afraid, for if he’d beat me to a mummy, those cowardly fellows wouldn’t have said nothing to it﻿—so, when I was got there, what does he do, but all of a sudden he takes me by both the shoulders, and he gives me such a shake!﻿—*Mon Dieu* I shall never forget it, if I live to be an hundred. I’m sure I dare say I’m out of joint all over. And though I made as much noise as I ever could, he took no more notice of it than nothing at all; there he stood, shaking me in that manner, as if he was doing it for a wager. I’m determined, if it costs me all my fortune, I’ll see that villain hanged. He shall be found out, if there’s e’er a justice in England. So when he had shook me till he was tired, and I felt all over like a jelly, without saying never a word, he takes and pops me into the ditch!

===Chinese===

“巴望你自个儿也这样受一回，你就知道这可不是闹着玩的；你是我这辈子见过的顶顶不要脸的家伙；往后我再瞧见你敢冲我咧嘴，我可不客气，非扇你耳刮子不可。”
这一通威吓发得心满意足，那仆人慌忙退了下去，我们便又上路。
她的怒气如今化作悲伤，开始凄凄惨惨地哭诉自己的命。“我相信，”她嚷道，“天底下再没有比我更倒霉的人了！这不，我吃的苦头还不够多似的，那小混蛋又害我丢了鬈发！——唉，没了鬈发我简直见不得人：——你瞧瞧我这副样子——我活了这辈子，从来没这样狼狈过。*真的*，我早知道有这一出，就带两三副来了：可我想破了脑袋也想不到会出这种事呀。”
见她火气平了些，我大着胆子请她讲讲这一场遭遇，她怎么说的，我尽力照原话记下来。
“唉，孩子，这场大祸，全怪那小混蛋逼咱们把钱留在家里；因为那强盗一见我手里没把钱交给他，就凭蛮力把我从车里硬拽出去，我真当他要杀了我呢。他壮得像头狮子；我在他手里就跟个孩子似的。可我相信，天底下谁也没受过这样的作践；他拽着我顺大路走，一路连拖带拉，只当我连牲口都不如。我真巴不得亲眼看那男人活活剁成八块！不过他早晚要上绞架的，这还算件好事。等我们走到马车瞧不见的地方——其实他大可不必害怕，就算他把我打成一团肉泥，那两个胆小鬼也决不敢哼一声——到了那儿，你猜他干什么？他冷不丁抓住我两边肩膀，狠狠摇了我一顿！——*老天爷*，我活到一百岁也忘不了。我敢说，我浑身骨头都摇散了。任凭我放开嗓子拼命地叫，他只当没听见；他就站在那儿，那样摇着我，仿佛在跟人打赌似的。我打定了主意，哪怕花光全部家当，我也要看着那恶棍上绞架。只要英格兰还有一个治安官，他就跑不了。后来他摇我摇累了，摇得我浑身像一摊肉冻，他一声不吭，拎起我就把我塞进了沟里！”

===Original===

I’m sure, I thought he’d have murdered me, as much as ever I thought anything in my life; for he kept bumping me about, as if he thought nothing too bad for me. However, I’m resolved I’ll never leave my purse behind me again, the longest day I have to live. So when he couldn’t stand over me no longer, he holds out his hands again for my money; but he was as cunning as could be, for he wouldn’t speak a word, because I shouldn’t swear to his voice; however, that shan’t save him, for I’ll swear to him any day in the year, if I can but catch him. So, when I told him I had no money, he fell to jerking me again, just as if he had but that moment begun! And, after that, he got me close by a tree, and out of his pocket he pulls a great cord!﻿—It’s a wonder I did not swoon away: for as sure as you’re alive, he was going to hang to me that tree. I screamed like anything mad, and told him if he would but spare my life, I’d never prosecute him, nor tell anybody what he’d done to me: so he stood some time quite in a brown study, a-thinking what he should do. And so, after that, he forced me to sit down in the ditch, and he tied my feet together, just as you see them: and then, as if he had not done enough, he twitched off my cap, and without saying nothing, got on his horse and left me in that condition; thinking, I suppose, that I might lie there and perish.”
Though this narrative almost compelled me to laugh, yet I was really irritated with the Captain, for carrying his love of tormenting﻿—*sport*, he calls it﻿—to such barbarous and unjustifiable extremes. I consoled and soothed her, as well as I was able: and told her, that since M. Du Bois had escaped, I hoped, when she recovered from her fright, all would end well.
“Fright, child!” repeated she﻿—“why that’s not half;﻿—I promise you, I wish it was; but here I’m bruised from top to toe and it’s well if ever I have the right use of my limbs again. However, I’m glad the villain got nothing but his trouble for his pains. But here the worst is to come, for I can’t go out, because I’ve got no curls, and so he’ll be escaped before I can get to the justice to stop him. I’m resolved I’ll tell Lady Howard how her man served me; for if he hadn’t made me fling ’em away, I dare say I would have pinned them up well enough for the country.”
