“Perhaps Lady Howard may be able to lend you a cap that will wear without them.”

===Chinese===

“说真的，我这辈子就没这么死心塌地地信过一件事：我以为他真要杀了我；因为他把我颠来撞去，仿佛怎么糟践我都不嫌够。不过我拿定主意了，只要我还活一天，往后再也不把钱包留在家里了。后来他不能再守着我了，又伸出手来跟我要钱；可他狡猾到家了，一个字也不肯说，为的是叫我认不出他的嗓音；可这救不了他，只要我逮得住他，一年里随便哪天，我都能一口咬定是他。等我告诉他我没钱，他又揪着我摇晃起来，倒像方才那顿才开了个头！再后来，他把我逼到一棵树跟前，从口袋里掏出一根粗绳！——我没当场晕过去真是奇迹：千真万确，他要把我吊上那棵树。我疯了一样地尖叫，跟他说只要饶我这条命，我决不告他，也决不把他干的事告诉任何人：他于是呆呆站了半天，出神地琢磨该怎么办。再后来，他就逼我坐进沟里，把我的两只脚捆在一起，就是你瞧见的这样：然后呢，好像他还没作践够，又一把扯掉我的帽子，一声不吭，跨上马，就把我撂在那个模样儿里；我琢磨着，他是打算让我躺在那儿烂掉。”
这一篇话险些逗得我笑出来，可我心里实在怨舰长，他把那点捉弄人的嗜好——他管这叫*玩意儿*——使到这样野蛮、这样没道理的地步。我尽力宽慰她、劝解她：并对她说，杜布瓦先生既然脱身了，但愿等她缓过这场惊吓，一切都会有个好结果。
“惊吓，孩子！”她接口道——“这连一半都不算；——我巴不得只是受场惊吓呢；可我瞧我是从头顶青一块紫一块到脚底，往后这两条腿还能不能听使唤，难说得很。不过呢，那恶棍白忙一场什么也没捞着，我倒高兴。可顶糟的还在后头：我出不了门了，因为我没了鬈发，等我赶到治安官那儿去拦他，他早逃啦。我拿定主意要把她家仆人怎么整治我的事，一五一十告诉霍华德夫人；要不是他惹得我把鬈发摔了，我说不定早用别针把它们别得好好的，乡下见见人也尽够了。”
“兴许霍华德夫人能借您一顶不戴鬈发也能出门的帽子。”

===Original===

“Lady Howard, indeed! why, do you think I’d wear one of her dowdies? No, I’ll promise you, I shan’t put on no such disguisement. It’s the unluckiest thing in the world that I did not make the man pick up the curls again; but he put me in such a passion, I could not think of nothing. I know I can’t get none at Howard Grove for love nor money: for of all the stupid places ever I see, that Howard Grove is the worst; there’s never no getting nothing one wants.”
This sort of conversation lasted till we arrived at our journey’s end; and then a new distress occurred: Madame Duval was eager to speak to Lady Howard and Mrs. Mirvan, and to relate her misfortunes; but she could not endure that Sir Clement or the Captain should see her in such disorder; so she said they were so ill-natured, that instead of pitying her, they would only make a jest of her disasters. She therefore sent me first into the house, to wait for an opportunity of their being out of the way, that she might steal upstairs unobserved. In this I succeeded, as the gentlemen thought it most prudent not to seem watching for her; though they both contrived to divert themselves with peeping at her as she passed.
She went immediately to bed, where she had her supper. Lady Howard and Mrs. Mirvan both of them very kindly sat with her, and listened to her tale with compassionate attention; while Miss Mirvan and I retired to our own room, where I was very glad to end the troubles of the day in a comfortable conversation.
The Captain’s raptures, during supper, at the success of his plan, were boundless. I spoke afterwards to Mrs. Mirvan with the openness which her kindness encourages, and begged her to remonstrate with him upon the cruelty of tormenting Madame Duval so causelessly. She promised to take the first opportunity of starting up the subject; but said he was at present so much elated, that he would not listen to her with any patience. However, should he make any new efforts to molest her, I can by no means consent to be passive. Had I imagined he would have been so violent, I would have risked his anger in her defence much sooner.
She has kept her bed all day, and declares she is almost bruised to death.
Adieu, my dear Sir. What a long letter have I written! I could almost fancy I sent it to you from London!

===Chinese===

“霍华德夫人，亏你说得出口！怎么，你以为我肯戴她那种老古董么？不，我告诉你吧，我才不穿这身吓人的行头呢。天下顶倒霉的就是，我没叫那仆人把鬈发捡回来；可他把我气得那样，我脑子里一片空白。我知道，在霍华德林，随你出多大价钱、说多少好话，也弄不到一副：我平生见过的顶顶死气沉沉的地方，就数霍华德林；人想要的东西，那儿从来一样也弄不着。”
这样的谈话一直持续到我们抵达旅程的尽头；跟着又出了一桩新的愁事：杜瓦尔夫人急着要见霍华德夫人和米尔文太太，好诉说她的不幸；可她又万万受不了让克莱门特爵士或舰长看见自己这副狼狈相；她说他们心眼儿顶坏，非但不可怜她，反倒只拿她的灾祸当笑柄。于是她先打发我进屋去，瞅个两位先生不在跟前的机会，好让她悄悄上楼不叫人瞧见。这事我办成了——两位先生也觉得只作没有守着她等最为妥当；不过她经过的时候，两人还是各自设法偷看了一眼，取了个乐。
她立刻上了床，晚饭也是在床上用的。霍华德夫人和米尔文太太都好性地陪坐在她床边，满怀怜惜地听她讲述；米尔文小姐同我则回了自己房间，我很乐意在一场舒心的闲谈里，把这一天的烦恼收了尾。
晚饭席上，舰长为自己的计策这样成功而欢喜得没边儿。事后我趁着米尔文太太待我的好意所鼓起的坦率，同她开了心，求她劝劝舰长，这样无缘无故地捉弄杜瓦尔夫人，未免太狠心了。她答应一有便就提这个话头；只是说舰长眼下正得意忘形，怎么也听不进她的话。不过，他若再想法糟践她，我断不能再袖手旁观。早知道他会闹到这样地步，我早就豁出他动怒，出头护着她了。
她卧了一整天的床，直说自己差点儿给打得体无完肤。
再会了，亲爱的先生。瞧我写了多长的一封信！我几乎要当自己是又回到伦敦，在那儿寄信给您了！

## Letter / 书信
===Original===

XXXIV Evelina in Continuation
Howard Grove, May 15.
This insatiable Captain, if left to himself, would not, I believe, rest, till he had tormented Madame Duval into a fever. He seems to have no delight but in terrifying or provoking her; and all his thoughts apparently turn upon inventing such methods as may do it most effectually.
She had her breakfast again in bed yesterday morning: but during ours, the Captain, with a very significant look at Sir Clement, gave us to understand, that he thought she had now rested long enough to bear the hardships of a fresh campaign.
His meaning was obvious; and, therefore, I resolved to endeavour immediately to put a stop to his intended exploits. When breakfast was over, I followed Mrs. Mirvan out of the parlour, and begged her to lose no time in pleading the cause of Madame Duval with the Captain. “My love,” answered she, “I have already expostulated with him; but all I can say is fruitless, while his favourite, Sir Clement, contrives to urge him on.”
“Then I will go and speak to Sir Clement,” said I, “for I know he will desist if I request him.”
“Have a care, my dear!” said she, smiling; “it is sometimes dangerous to make requests to men who are too desirous of receiving them.”
“Well, then, my dear Madam, will you give me leave to speak myself to the Captain?”
“Willingly; nay, I will accompany you to him.”
I thanked her, and we went to seek him. He was walking in the garden with Sir Clement. Mrs. Mirvan most obligingly made an opening for my purpose, by saying, “Mr. Mirvan, I have brought a petitioner with me.”
“Why, what’s the matter now?” cried he.
I was fearful of making him angry, and stammered very much, when I told him, I hoped he had no new plan for alarming Madame Duval.
“*New* plan!” cried he; “why, you don’t suppose the *old* one would do again, do you? Not but what it was a very good one, only I doubt she wouldn’t bite.”
“Indeed, Sir,” said I, “she has already suffered too much; and I hope you will pardon me, if I take the liberty of telling you, that I think it my duty to do all in my power to prevent her being again so much terrified.”
A sullen gloominess instantly clouded his face, and, turning short from me, he said, I might do as I pleased, but that I should much sooner repent than repair my officiousness.

===Chinese===

第三十四封 伊芙琳娜续记
霍华德林，5月15日
这位欲壑难填的舰长，倘若任着他性子，我相信不把杜瓦尔夫人折磨出一场热病来，他就不肯罢休。他仿佛除了吓唬她、撩拨她，再没有别的乐趣；他满脑子转的，显然净是些怎样下手最见效的新花招。
昨天早晨，她又是躺在床上用的早饭：可我们用早饭的当儿，舰长意味深长地朝克莱门特爵士递了个眼色，让我们明白：他看老太太如今歇得也够久了，禁得起一场新战役的劳顿了。
他的用意再明白不过；于是我打定主意，立刻设法拦下他蓄谋的新战绩。早饭一撤，我便跟着米尔文太太出了客厅，求她赶紧为杜瓦尔夫人向舰长求个情。“亲爱的，”她答道，“我已经劝过他了；可只要他那宝贝克莱门特爵士还在一旁撺掇，我说什么都白费。”
“那我去同克莱门特爵士说，”我说，“我知道只要我开口求他，他就会住手的。”
“留神哪，亲爱的！”她含笑说道，“对那些巴不得你去求的男人开口求情，有时是危险的。”
“那么，亲爱的夫人，您容我自己去同舰长说说，行么？”
“乐意之至；这样吧，我陪你同去。”
我谢过了她，我们便去寻他。他正同克莱门特爵士在园子里散步。米尔文太太殷勤地替我起了个话头，说道：“米尔文先生，我带来一位请愿的。”
“咦，这又怎么了？”他嚷道。
我怕惹恼他，结结巴巴地同他说，我希望他没有再定什么吓唬杜瓦尔夫人的新计策。
“*新*计策！”他嚷道，“怎么，你以为那条*老*计策还能再用一回么？倒不是它不好——它好得很——只怕她不肯再上钩了。”
“说真的，先生，”我说，“她已经受够苦了；恕我冒昧说一句，我认为自己有责任尽力不让她再受这样的惊吓，还望您原谅。”
一层阴沉的怒色立刻罩上他的脸，他猛地转过身去，说我爱怎么办就怎么办，只是我这番多管闲事，将来懊悔也来不及补救。

===Original===

I was too much disconcerted at this rebuff to attempt making any answer; and finding that Sir Clement warmly espoused my cause, I walked away, and left them to discuss the point together.
Mrs. Mirvan, who never speaks to the Captain when he is out of humour, was glad to follow me, and with her usual sweetness made a thousand apologies for her husband’s ill-manners.
When I left her, I went to Madame Duval, who was just risen, and employed in examining the clothes she had on the day of her ill usage.
“Here’s a sight!” she cried. “Come, here child﻿—only look﻿—*Pardi*, so long as I’ve lived, I never see so much before! Why, all my things are spoilt; and what’s worse, my sacque was as good as new. Here’s the second negligee I’ve used in this manner!﻿—I’m sure I was a fool to put it on in such a lonesome place as this; however if I stay here these ten years, I’ll never put on another good gown, that I’m resolved.”
“Will you let the maid try if she can iron it out, or clean it, Ma’am?”
“No, she’ll only make bad worse.﻿—But look here, now, here’s a cloak! *Mon Dieu!* why it looks like a dish-clout! Of all the unluckiness that ever I met, this is the worst! for, do you know, I bought it but the day before I left Paris!﻿—Besides, into the bargain, my cap’s quite gone: where the villain twitched it, I don’t know; but I never see no more of it from that time to this. Now you must know that this was the becomingest cap I had in the world, for I’ve never another with pink ribbon in it; and, to tell you the truth, if I hadn’t thought to have seen M. Du Bois, I’d no more have put it on than I’d have flown; for as to what one wears in such a stupid place as this, it signifies no more than nothing at all.”
She then told me, that she had been thinking all night of a contrivance to hinder the Captain from finding out her loss of curls; which was having a large gauge handkerchief pinned over her head as a hood, and saying she had the toothache.
“To tell you the truth,” added she, “I believe that Captain is one of the worst men in the world; he’s always making a joke of me; and as to his being a gentleman, he has no more manners than a bear, for he’s always upon the grin when one’s in distress; and, I declare I’d rather be done anything to than laughed at, for, to my mind, it’s one or other the disagreeablest thing in the world.”
Mrs.

===Chinese===

碰了这个钉子，我狼狈得很，一句答话也搭不上来；见克莱门特爵士热心地站在我这边，我便走开了，由他们两人争论去。
米尔文太太——舰长不痛快时她从不理他——乐得跟着我走，又照她往常的温柔，为她丈夫的失礼说了千百个不是。
辞了她，我便去看杜瓦尔夫人；她才起身，正忙着检视遭难那天穿的那身衣裳。
“你瞧瞧这光景！”她嚷道，“来，孩子，过来——你只管瞧——*真的*，我活了这大年纪，还没见过这样的！唉，我的衣裳全毁了；更糟的是，我那件晨衣还跟新的一样。这已经是我这样糟蹋掉的第二件家常袍了！——我真是个傻子，跑到这样个荒凉地方来，还穿它出来；不过，我在这里哪怕住上十年，也再不穿一件好衣裳了，这主意我拿定了。”
“夫人，要不要叫女仆试试，看能不能熨平，或是洗干净？”
“不用，她只会越弄越糟。——可你瞧这儿，瞧这斗篷！*老天爷！*瞧它成了块抹布了！我一辈子倒霉，数这一回顶顶倒霉！你知道么，我离开巴黎的前一天才买它的！——还不算完，搭上我那顶帽子也整个没了：那恶棍把它扯到哪儿去了，我不知道；反正从那时到这会儿，我再没见过它的影子。还有你得知道，那是我天底下戴了顶好看的一顶帽子，我另外再没有一顶带粉红缎带的；老实告诉你，要不是想着能见着杜布瓦先生，我才不肯戴它呢，戴上它还不如叫我长翅膀飞；至于在这样个死地方穿什么，那顶不顶用，半点也不打紧。”
她接着告诉我，她想了一整夜，琢磨出一条计策，好叫舰长发现不了她丢了鬈发：就是拿一方大格子绸巾用别针别在头上兜起来，只说自己牙疼。
“老实说，”她又道，“我看那舰长是天底下顶坏的男人之一；他老是拿我开玩笑；说到他是个上等人，他那点规矩还不及一头熊，人家遭了难，他老咧着嘴笑；我说呀，什么罪我都能受，就是受不了叫人笑话，因为依我看，这算得上天底下顶顶难受的事了。”
米尔文

===Original===

Mirvan, I found, had been endeavouring to dissuade her from the design she had formed of having recourse to the law, in order to find out the supposed robbers; for she dreads a discovery of the Captain, during Madame Duval’s stay at Howard Grove, as it could not fail being productive of infinite commotion. She has, therefore, taken great pains to show the inutility of applying to justice, unless she were more able to describe the offenders against whom she would appear; and has assured her, that as she neither heard their voices, nor saw their faces, she cannot possibly swear to their persons, or obtain any redress.
Madame Duval, in telling me this, extremely lamented her hard fate, that she was thus prevented from revenging her injuries; which, however, she vowed she would not be persuaded to *pocket tamely*: “because,” added she, “if such villains as these are let to have their own way, and nobody takes no notice of their impudence, they’ll make no more ado than nothing at all of tying people in ditches, and such things as that: however, I shall consult with M. Du Bois, as soon as I can ferret out where he’s hid himself. I’m sure I’ve a right to his advice, for it’s all along of his gaping about at the Tower that I’ve met with these misfortunes.”
“M. Du Bois,” said I, “will, I am sure, be very sorry when he hears what has happened.”
“And what good will that do now?﻿—that won’t unspoil all my clothes; I can tell him, I a’n’t much obliged to him, though it’s no fault of his;﻿—yet it i’n’t the less provokinger for that. I’m sure, if he had been there, to have seen me served in that manner, and put neck and heels into a ditch, he’d no more have thought it was me than the Pope of Rome. I’ll promise you, whatever you may think of it, I shan’t have no rest, night nor day, till I find out that rogue.”
“I have no doubt, Madam, but you will soon discover him.”
“*Pardi*, if I do, I’ll hang him, as sure as fate!﻿—but what’s the oddest, is, that he should take such a special spite against *me* above all the rest! it was as much for nothing as could be; for I don’t know what I had done, so particular bad, to be used in that manner: I’m sure, I hadn’t given no offence, as I know of, for I never see his face all the time; and as to screaming a little, I think it’s very hard if one mustn’t do such a thing as that, when one’s put in fear of one’s life.”

===Chinese===

太太，我后来得知，一直在劝她打消那个念头——她想求告官府，把那两个假强盗查出来；因为杜瓦尔夫人住在霍华德林期间，她生怕舰长的事被拆穿，那必定惹起无穷的风波。于是她费尽唇舌，叫她明白报官也是白报：她要想告人，总得先把那两人的模样说得出才行；又拿话叫她信服：她既没听见过他们的嗓音，也没看清他们的脸，便绝无凭据指认其人，更别想讨回什么公道。
杜瓦尔夫人对我说起这些时，痛惜自己命苦，说这样一来，她的仇就报不成了；可是她赌咒说，谁也别想劝她*忍气吞声*：“因为，”她又说，“要是任凭这样的恶棍横行，没一个人理会他们的胆大妄为，往后他们把人捆到沟里去，还有这类的事，干起来就更不当一回事了：不过，等我打听到杜布瓦先生躲在哪儿，我马上就同他商量。我说呀，他的主意我尽可以讨，我遭的这些难，还不都怪他在伦敦塔东张西望。”
“杜布瓦先生听说了这些事，”我说，“准会很难过的。”
“难过顶什么用？——难过也救不回我的衣裳；我可以告诉他，我领不了他多少情，虽说不是他的错；——可错虽不是他的，火气并不因此就小些。说真的，他要在场，瞧见人家那样整治我，把我手脚一捆塞进沟里，他准以为那不是我，是罗马教皇呢。随你怎么想，我告诉你，找不出那流氓，我日夜都不得安生。”
“夫人，您不久定能寻到他，这我毫不怀疑。”
“*真的*，寻着了我就绞死他，一定的！——只是顶古怪的是，旁人他都不挑，偏单单跟我过不去！这真是无妄之灾；我不知道我做了什么顶特别的坏事，要受那样的摆布：我敢说，我没有得罪他，据我知道没有；从头到尾我就没瞧见过他的脸；至于叫唤了几声，我想，一个人的性命都吓得悬了，连这一点都不许，那也未免太苛刻了。”

===Original===

During this conversation, she endeavoured to adjust her headdress, but could not at all please herself. Indeed, had I not been present, I should have thought it impossible for a woman, at her time of life, to be so very difficult in regard to dress. What she may have in view, I cannot imagine, but the labour of the toilette seems the chief business of her life.
When I left her, in my way downstairs, I met Sir Clement; who with great earnestness, said he must not be denied the honour of a moment’s conversation with me; and then, without waiting for an answer, he led me to the garden; at the door of which, however, I absolutely insisted upon stopping.
He seemed very serious, and said, in a grave tone of voice, “At length, Miss Anville, I flatter myself I have hit upon an expedient that will oblige you; and therefore, though it is death to myself, I will put in practice.”
I begged him to explain himself.
“I saw your desire of saving Madame Duval, and scarce could I refrain giving the brutal Captain my real opinion of his savage conduct; but I am unwilling to quarrel with him, lest I should be denied entrance into a house which you inhabit; I have been endeavouring to prevail with him to give up his absurd new scheme, but I find him impenetrable:﻿—I have therefore determined to make a pretense for suddenly leaving this place, dear as it is to me, and containing all I most admire and adore;﻿—and I will stay in town till the violence of this boobyish humour is abated.”
He stopped; but I was silent, for I knew not what I ought to say. He took my hand, which he pressed to his lips, saying, “And must I then, Miss Anville, must I quit you﻿—sacrifice voluntarily my greatest felicity;﻿—and yet not be honoured with one word, one look of approbation?”
I withdrew my hand, and said with half a laugh, “You know so well, Sir Clement, the value of the favours you confer, that it would be superfluous for me to point it out.”
“Charming, charming girl! how does your wit, your understanding, rise upon me daily; and must I, can I part with you?﻿—will no other method﻿—”
“O, Sir, do you so soon repent the good office you had planned for Madame Duval?”
“For Madame Duval!﻿—cruel creature, and will you not even suffer me to place to your account the sacrifice I am about to make?”

===Chinese===

这一番说话的当儿，她一直在拾掇头上的装裹，可怎么也拾掇不称心。说真的，倘若不是我亲眼在场，我断想不到一个女人到了她这把年纪，在穿着上还能这样地讲究。她究竟图个什么，我实在想不出，只是梳妆打扮这门功课，仿佛是她平生头一件大事。
辞别了她，我下楼时又撞见克莱门特爵士；他一片恳切，说务必赏脸同他谈一小会儿；不等我答话，便引着我往园子里去；不过走到园门口，我说什么也站住不肯再走了。
他神色郑重，语气沉沉地说：“安维尔小姐，这一回，我自信总算想出了一条两全之计，保管合你的心意；所以，哪怕它要了我的命，我也要照着办。”
我求他把话说个明白。
“我瞧出了你要搭救杜瓦尔夫人的心，差点忍不住把那野蛮舰长的行径，当面给他下个考语；只是我不愿同他闹翻，怕的是往后连你这门宅子也进不来了；我一直劝他放弃那条荒唐的新计策，可这人油盐不进：——于是我只得拿个由头，突然离开此地——这地方于我何等亲爱，藏着我顶敬慕、顶倾心的一切；——我要在城里住下，等这股蠢牛似的疯劲儿过去了再说。”
他停住了；我却不作声，因为不知道该说什么才好。他握住我的手，凑到唇边吻着，说：“那么，安维尔小姐，难道我就得离开你——亲手舍掉我最大的幸福；——却连一句嘉许的话、一道嘉许的眼色也博不到么？”
我抽回手，带笑说道：“克莱门特爵士，您施与人的恩惠值多少钱，您自己再清楚不过，还要我来说破，岂不多余。”
“迷人的姑娘，太迷人了！你的机锋，你的心智，一天赛过一天地叫我倾倒；难道我竟能、竟舍得同你分手？——再没有别的法子——”
“哦，爵士，您为杜瓦尔夫人筹划的那桩好事，这么快就反悔了么？”
“好一个杜瓦尔夫人！——狠心的姑娘，我行将作出的牺牲，你连让我记在你的账上都不肯么？”

===Original===

“You must place it, Sir, to what account you please; but I am too much in haste now to stay here any longer.”
And then I would have left him; but he held me, and rather impatiently said, “If, then, I cannot be so happy as to oblige *you*, Miss Anville, you must not be surprised should I seek to oblige myself. If my scheme is not honoured with your approbation, for which alone it was formed, why should I, to my own infinite dissatisfaction, pursue it?”
We were then, for a few minutes, both silent; I was really unwilling he should give up a plan which would so effectually break into the Captain’s designs, and, at the same time, save me the pain of disobliging him; and I should instantly and thankfully have accepted his offered civility, had not Mrs. Mirvan’s caution made me fearful. However, when he pressed me to speak, I said, in an ironical voice, “I had thought, Sir, that the very strong sense you have yourself of the favour you propose to me, would sufficiently have repaid you; but, as I was mistaken, I must thank you myself. And now,” making a low courtesy, “I hope, Sir, you are satisfied.”
“Loveliest of thy sex﻿—” he began; but I forced myself from him and ran upstairs.
Soon after Miss Mirvan told me that Sir Clement had just received a letter, which obliged him instantly to leave the Grove, and that he had actually ordered a chaise. I then acquainted her with the real state of the affair. Indeed, I conceal nothing from her; she is so gentle and sweet-tempered, that it gives me great pleasure to place an entire confidence in her.
At dinner, I must own, we all missed him; for though the flightiness of his behaviour to me, when we are by ourselves is very distressing; yet, in large companies, and general conversation, he is extremely entertaining and agreeable. As to the Captain, he has been so much chagrined at his departure, that he has scarce spoken a word since he went: but Madame Duval, who made her first public appearance since her accident, was quite in raptures that she escaped seeing him.
The money which we left at the farmhouse has been returned to us. What pains the Captain must have taken to arrange and manage the adventures which he chose we should meet with! Yet he must certainly be discovered; for Madame Duval is already very much perplexed, at having received a letter this morning from M.

===Chinese===

“这笔账记在哪儿，先生，随您的便；只是我此刻急着呢，不能再站在这儿了。”
说着我便要走；他却拉住我，颇不耐烦地说：“那么，安维尔小姐，我既无福讨*你*的欢心，往后我图自己的快活，你可别见怪。我这计策原是单单为你才定的，既然蒙你不屑一顾，我何必又苦苦奉行，自寻没趣？”
一时间，两人都默然；说心里话，我不愿他放弃这条计策——它既能一举搅了舰长的布置，又省得我得罪他；若不是记着米尔文太太的告诫叫我提防，我本要当场领他这份情、道一声谢的。可他催我开口时，我便拿话讽刺道：“先生，我原以为，您向我施惠，您自己心里那份受用，已经尽够酬谢您了；既然我想错了，那就由我自己来谢您。这下，”我深深行了个屈膝礼，“先生，您该心满意足了吧。”
“女人里头顶顶可爱的——”他才起了个头；我奋力挣脱他，跑上楼去了。
不多时，米尔文小姐告诉我，克莱门特爵士刚接到一封信，不得不立刻离开林子，他已经当真吩咐备车了。我便把这件事的实情讲给她听了。的确，我什么事都不瞒她；她性子那样温柔和顺，我对她推心置腹，只觉得欢喜。
吃饭的时候，说来不瞒您，我们都想他；因为虽说两人独处时，他待我那样轻狂，很叫我窘；可一到人多的场合、大伙闲谈的时候，他实在是个顶有趣、顶随和的人。至于舰长，他一走，舰长懊丧得很，从那时起几乎没开过口：倒是杜瓦尔夫人——那是她遭难后头一回当众露面——想到躲开了同他见面，欢喜得不得了。
寄存在农家的那笔钱已经归还我们了。舰长为我们安排、经营这许多奇遇，想必费了不少心血！不过他早晚必定露馅；因为杜瓦尔夫人今早接到杜

===Original===

Du Bois, in which he makes no mention of his imprisonment. However, she has so little suspicion, that she imputes his silence upon the subject to his fears that the letter might be intercepted.
Not one opportunity could I meet with, while Sir Clement was here, to enquire after his friend Lord Orville: but I think it was strange he should never mention him unasked. Indeed, I rather wonder that Mrs. Mirvan herself did not introduce the subject, for she always seemed particularly attentive to him.
And now, once more, all my thoughts involuntarily turn upon the letter I so soon expect from Paris. This visit of Sir Clement has, however, somewhat diverted my fears; and, therefore, I am very glad he made it at this time. Adieu, my dear Sir.

===Chinese===

布瓦先生的信，信上却只字不提他被捕下狱的事，她正为此纳闷呢。不过她疑心极少，只当他缄口不提，是怕信半路叫人截了去。
克莱门特爵士在这里的时候，我连一个向他打听他朋友奥维尔勋爵的机会也没碰上：可他不等人问就从不提起勋爵，我想来也觉古怪。说真的，连米尔文太太自己也始终没提这个话头，我倒更觉诧异，因为她平日待勋爵仿佛格外关切。
而今，我的心事又一次不由自主地转到那封巴黎来信上——我盼它快些到。不过克莱门特爵士这次来访，多少岔开了我的忧惧；因此，他赶在这个当口来，我倒很高兴。再会了，亲爱的先生。

## Letter / 书信
===Original===

XXXV Sir John Belmont to Lady Howard
Paris, May 11.
Madam,
I have this moment the honour of your Ladyship’s Letter, and I will not wait another, before I return an answer.
It seldom happens that a man, though extolled as a saint, is really without blemish; or that another, though reviled as a devil, is really without humanity. Perhaps the time is not very distant, when I may have the honour to convince your Ladyship of this truth, in regard to Mr. Villars and myself.
As to the young lady, whom Mr. Villars so obligingly proposes presenting to me, I wish her all the happiness to which, by your ladyship’s account, she seems entitled; and, if she has a third part of the merit of *her* to whom you compare her, I doubt not but Mr. Villars will be more successful in every other application he may make for her advantage, than he can ever be in any with which he may be pleased to favour me.
I have the honour to be Madam,

Your Ladyship’s most humble,

and most obedient servant,
John Belmont.

===Chinese===

第三十五封 约翰·贝尔蒙特爵士致霍华德夫人
5月11日，于巴黎。
夫人：
尊函刚刚这一刻到我手上，我便不待下一刻，即刻作复。
一个人纵被捧作圣人，也难得真无瑕玷；另一个人纵被骂作魔鬼，也难得真无人心。或许这日子不远了：那时我有幸使夫人信服这条真理，就维拉尔斯先生同我这两人而言。
至于维拉尔斯先生如此殷勤地打算引见给我的那位小姐，我愿她事事如意——照夫人的叙述，她似乎也配得这份福；倘若她有夫人拿来同她相比的*那一位*三分之一的贤德，我便毫不怀疑：维拉尔斯先生日后为她谋求好处的一切请托，样样都会比他惠然赐予我的这一桩更加顺遂。
夫人，我殊荣在身，得为您效犬马之劳——

您最谦卑、最恭顺的仆人，
约翰·贝尔蒙特。

## Letter / 书信
===Original===

XXXVI Evelina to the Rev. Mr. Villars
Howard Grove, May 18.
Well, my dear Sir, all is now over! the letter so anxiously expected is at length arrived, and my doom is fixed. The various feelings which oppress me, I have not language to describe; nor need I﻿—you know my heart, you have yourself formed it﻿—and its sensations upon this occasion you may but too readily imagine.
Outcast as I am, and rejected forever by him to whom I of right belong﻿—shall I now implore *your* continued protection?﻿—No, no;﻿—I will not offend your generous heart, which, open to distress, has no wish but to relieve it, with an application that would seem to imply a doubt. I am more secure than ever of your kindness, since you now know upon that is my sole dependence.
I endeavour to bear this stroke with composure, and in such a manner as if I had already received your counsel and consolation. Yet, at times, my emotions are almost too much for me. O, Sir, what a letter for a parent to write! Must I not myself be deaf to the voice of nature, if I could endure to be thus absolutely abandoned without regret? I dare not even to you, nor would I, could I help it, to myself, acknowledge all that I might think; for, indeed, I have sometimes sentiments upon this rejection, which my strongest sense of duty can scarcely correct. Yet, suffer me to ask﻿—might not this answer have been softened?﻿—was it not enough to disclaim me forever, without treating me with contempt, and wounding me with derision?
But while I am thus thinking of myself, I forget how much more he is the object of sorrow than I am! Alas! what amends can he make himself for the anguish he is hoarding up for time to come! My heart bleeds for him, whenever this reflection occurs to me.
What is said of *you*, my protector, my friend, my benefactor! I dare not trust myself to comment upon. Gracious Heaven! what a return for goodness so unparalleled!
I would fain endeavour to divert my thoughts from this subject; but even that is not in my power; for, afflicting as this letter is to me, I find that it will not be allowed to conclude the affair, though it does all my expectations; for Madame Duval has determined not to let it rest here.

===Chinese===

第三十六封 伊芙琳娜致可敬的维拉尔斯先生
5月18日，于霍华德庄园。
唉，亲爱的先生，一切都完了！那封望眼欲穿的信终于到了，我的命运定了。压在我心头的种种滋味，我找不出言语形容；也不必形容——您知道我的心，那心本是您亲手琢成——此刻它在怎样翻腾，您太容易想象了。
我是个奔女，被那本该属于我的人永远丢弃了——如今我还能不能恳求*您*的持续庇护？——不，不；我不愿冒犯您那颗慷慨的心，它见人有难便敞开，一心只想解救；我这般恳求，倒像是对它存了疑。如今您既知道我只单单依仗您一人，我对您的好意，比从前更放心了。
我竭力想沉住气捱过这一击，仿佛已经先领了您的劝慰。可是有些时候，我的激动几乎要漫过堤去。啊，先生，做父亲的写出这样一封信来！倘若我被人这样一笔勾销地抛下，居然能毫无哀伤，那我不也成了听不见天性之声的人么？连对您，我都不敢把心里想的全说出来；若能克制，对自己我也不愿承认。因为，说真话，对待这件回绝，我有时心里冒出的那些念头，连我最强的责任感都几乎压不住。可是，容我问一句——这封回信就不能写得缓和些么？——永远不认我，难道还不够么，何必再加以轻蔑、再用讥诣来伤我？
可我只顾想自己，倒忘了他比我更堪悲悯！唉！他为自己日后囤下的那份痛悔，将来拿什么去补救！一念及此，我便替他心碎。
至于信里说到*您*——我的保护人、我的朋友、我的恩人——的话，我不敢让自己去评论。仁慈的上天！这般无与伦比的好意，得到的竟是这般回报！
我很想把这个念头岔开；可连这也由不得我；因为，这封信虽然叫我伤心，事情却不肯就此了结——我的指望是了结了，杜瓦尔夫人却打定了主意，不肯罢休。

===Original===

She heard the letter in great wrath, and protested she would not be so easily answered; she regretted her facility in having been prevailed upon to yield the direction of this affair to those who knew not how to manage it, and vowed she would herself undertake and conduct it in future.
It is in vain that I have pleaded against her resolution, and besought her to forbear an attack where she has nothing to expect but resentment: especially as there seems to be a hint, that Lady Howard will one day be more openly dealt with. She will not hear me: she is furiously bent upon a project which is terrible to think of;﻿—for she means to go herself to Paris, take me with her, and there, *face to face*, demand justice!
How to appease or to persuade her, I know not; but for the universe would I not be dragged, in such a manner, to an interview so awful, with a parent I have never yet beheld!
Lady Howard and Mrs. Mirvan are both of them infinitely shocked at the present state of affairs, and they seem to be even more kind to me than ever; and my dear Maria, who is the friend of my heart, uses her utmost efforts to console me; and, when she fails in her design, with still greater kindness she sympathises in my sorrow.
I very much rejoice, however, that Sir Clement Willoughby had left us before this letter arrived. I am sure the general confusion of the house would otherwise have betrayed to him the whole of a tale which I now, more than ever, wish to have buried in oblivion.
Lady Howard thinks I ought not to disoblige Madame Duval, yet she acknowledges the impropriety of my accompanying her abroad on such an enterprise. Indeed, I would rather die than force myself into his presence. But so vehement is Madame Duval, that she would instantly have compelled me to attend her to town, in her way to Paris, had not Lady Howard so far exerted herself, as to declare she could by no means consent to my quitting her house, till she gave me up to you, by whose permission I had entered it.
She was extremely angry at this denial; and the Captain, by his sneers and raillery, so much increased her rage, that she has positively declared, should your next letter dispute her authority to guide me by her own pleasure, she will, without hesitation, make a journey to Berry Hill, and *teach you to know who she is*.

===Chinese===

她听着信，怒不可遮，声称断不容这样三言两语就打发；她懊悔自己太轻易，竟被劝得把这事交到一班不会办的人手里，并发誓往后要亲自来管、亲自来办。
我劝她打消这主意，求她别去招惹一场除却怨毒一无所获的进攻，全是徒劳——尤其信里似乎隐隐透出，早晚有一天会跟霍华德夫人算更明白的账。她不听：她一股劲儿认定了一个计划，想都不敢想——她要亲自去巴黎，把我也带上，*当面*讨一个公道！
怎样安推她、说服她，我不知道；可哪怕天塌下来，我也不愿这样被拖去赴那样一个可怕的会面——去见一个我从没见过的父亲！
霍华德夫人和米尔文太太眼下的局面都震惊到了极点，她们待我似乎比从前更亲了；亲爱的玛丽亚——我心尖上的朋友——也在尽力安慰我；安慰不了的时候，她便以更大的温柔，陪我一同悲伤。
不过我倒非常庆幸，克莱门特·威洛比爵士在这封信到之前已经离开了我们。不然，满宅的慌乱准会把这桩事从头到尾泄露给他，而我如今比任何时候都巴不得它被永远埋进遗忘里。
霍华德夫人觉得我不该触孴杜瓦尔夫人，却也承认我随她出国去办这种事不合适。说真的，我宁可死，也不愿硬闯到他面前去。可杜瓦尔夫人气势汹汹，若不是霍华德夫人拿出全部威严，声明绝不答应我离开她的家——除非把我交还给您，因为是您的允准我才进来的——她早已立刻押着我上伦敦、取道去巴黎了。
她对这番拒绝大为恼怒；船长又在一旁冷嘲热讽，把她的火气越抽越旺，于是她干脆摊牌：倘若您下一封信再否认她凭自己高兴管束我的权柄，她将毫不犹豫地跑一趟贝里山，*教您认认她是什么人*。

===Original===

Should she put this threat in execution, nothing could give me greater uneasiness: for her violence and volubility would almost distract you.
Unable as I am to act for myself, or to judge what conduct I ought to pursue, how grateful do I feel myself, that I have such a guide and director to counsel and instruct me as yourself!
Adieu, my dearest Sir! Heaven, I trust, will never let me live to be repulsed, and derided by *you*, to whom I may now sign myself, wholly your
Evelina.

===Chinese===

她若真把这威胁付诸实行，没有比这更叫我发愁的了：她那股横劲和那舌头，怕不把您扰得心神不宁。
我既然不能自己做主，也判断不出该行什么路数，那么有您这样一位导师与引路人来给我谋划指点，我心中多么感激！
再会了，我最亲爱的先生！上天鉴佲，必不至于叫我活着被*您*推拒、被您嘲笑——如今我在信末可以这样署名的、整个儿属于您的
伊芙琳娜。

## Letter / 书信
===Original===

XXXVII Mr. Villars to Evelina
Berry Hill, May 21.
Let not my Evelina be depressed by a stroke of fortune for which she is not responsible. No breach of duty on your part has incurred the unkindness which has been shown you; nor have you, by any act of imprudence, provoked either censure or reproach. Let me entreat you, therefore, my dearest child, to support yourself with that courage which your innocency ought to inspire: and let all the affliction you allow yourself be for him only who, not having that support, must one day be but too severely sensible how much he wants it.
The hint thrown out concerning myself is wholly unintelligible to me: my heart, I dare own, fully acquits me of vice; but *without blemish*, I have never ventured to pronounce myself. However, it seems his intention to be hereafter more explicit; and *then*﻿—should anything appear, that has on *my* part contributed to those misfortunes we lament, let me at least say, that the most partial of my friends cannot be so much astonished as I shall myself be at such a discovery.
The mention, also, of any *future applications* I may make, is equally beyond my comprehension. But I will not dwell upon a subject, which almost compels from me reflections that cannot but be wounding to a heart so formed for filial tenderness as my Evelina’s. There is an air of mystery throughout the letter, the explanation of which I will await in silence.
The scheme of Madame Duval is such as might be reasonably expected from a woman so little inured to disappointment, and so totally incapable of considering the delicacy of your situation. Your averseness to her plan gives me pleasure, for it exactly corresponds with my own. Why will she not make the journey she projects by herself? She would not have even the wish of an opposition to encounter. And then, once more, might my child and myself be left to the quiet enjoyment of that peaceful happiness, which she alone has interrupted. As to her coming hither, I could, indeed, dispense with such a visit; but, if she will not be satisfied with my refusal by letter, I must submit to the task of giving it her in person.
My impatience for your return is increased by your account of Sir Clement Willoughby’s visit to Howard Grove.

===Chinese===

第三十七封 维拉尔斯先生致伊芙琳娜
5月21日，于贝里山。
我的伊芙琳娜，不要为这一场与她毫不相干的命运的打击而消沉。你未曾在职分上有丝毫亏欠，招来这番苛待；你也没有因任何一步失检，惹来非难或责备。所以，我最亲爱的孩子，我恳求你拿出勇气来支撑自己——你的清白本该给你这份勇气；你容许自己的哀伤，只应落在他一个人身上：他没有这份支撑，将来总有一天，会痛彻地知道自己多么需要它。
信里暗指我本人的那一句，我全然莫名其妙：我的心，我敢说，完全洗清我于邪恶无罪；可*毫无瑕玷*这四个字，我从不曾僭敢自许。不过，看来他存心日后把话说明白；到那时——倘若果真显出什么，在*我*这一方面也促成了我们为之痛惜的那些不幸，那么我至少可以说：这发现之惊人，连最偏袒我的朋友也及不上我自己的一半。
至于说到我日后还有什么*请托*，也同样超出我的理解。但我不愿在这题目上盘桓，它几乎逼着我生出种种感想，而这些感想，不能不伤着一颗像我伊芙琳娜这般天性纯孝的心。这封信从头到尾裹着一层迷雾，它的谜底，我愿静候。
杜瓦尔夫人这计划，出自这样一位不惯受挫、又全然体察不到你处境之微妙的女人，原在情理之中。你对她这打算的厌恶使我欣慰，因为它正合我的心意。她何不独自去做她计划的这趟旅行呢？那样她连一星半点的违逆也碰不着。而那时，我的孩子和我，便又能重新回到那份安恬的享受里——唯有她一个人搅乱了它。至于她说要到这里来，这样的造访，我实在可以省了；可她若不肯凭一封信就满足于我的拒绝，那我只好勉力当面回她一次了。
你叙述克莱门特·威洛比爵士到霍华德庄园来访，我对你的归期越发望眼欲穿了。

===Original===

I am but little surprised at the perseverance of his assiduities to interest you in his favour; but I am very much hurt that you should be exposed to addresses, which, by their privacy, have an air that shocks me. You cannot, my love, be too circumspect; the slightest carelessness on your part will be taken advantage of by a man of his disposition. It is not sufficient for you to be reserved: his conduct even calls for your resentment; and should he again, as will doubtless be his endeavour, contrive to solicit your favour in private, let your disdain and displeasure be so marked, as to constrain a change in his behaviour. Though, indeed, should his visit be repeated while you remain at the Grove, Lady Howard must pardon me if I shorten yours.
Adieu, my child. You will always make my respects to the hospitable family to which we are so much obliged.

===Chinese===

他如此锲而不舍地殷勤，一心要你对他生出好感，我不很惊讶；叫我痛心的，是你竟被置于那样一番表白之下：那番表白的偷偷摸摸，透着一股叫我震恐的气味。我的爱，你怎样谨慎都不为过：你这头稍有疏忽，都会被他那等性情的人拿去利用。单是矜持，于你已不够：他的行径简直配得上你的愠怒；倘若他再——无疑他必会设法——私下里乞求你的好感，就让你的轻蔑与不快显豁到那个地步，逼得他改一改行止。不过，倘若你还在庄园期间他再度来访，霍华德夫人须得恕我缩短你的行期了。
再会，我的孩子。请始终代我向那好客的一家人致敬意——我们受他们的恩实在太多。

## Letter / 书信
===Original===

XXXVIII Mr. Villars to Lady Howard
Berry Hill, May 27.
Dear Madam,
I believe your Ladyship will not be surprised at hearing I have had a visit from Madame Duval, as I doubt not her having made known her intention before she left Howard Grove. I would gladly have excused myself this meeting, could I have avoided it decently; but, after so long a journey, it was not possible to refuse her admittance.
She told me, that she came to Berry Hill, in consequence of a letter I had sent to her granddaughter, in which I forbid her going to Paris. Very roughly she then called me to account for the authority which I had assumed; and, had I been disposed to have argued with her, she would very angrily have disputed the right by which I used it. But I declined all debating. I therefore listened very quietly, till she had so much fatigued herself with talking, that she was glad, in her turn, to be silent. And then, I begged to know the purport of her visit.
She answered, that she came to make me relinquish the power I had usurped over her granddaughter; and assured me she would not quit the place till she succeeded.
But I will not trouble your Ladyship with the particulars of this disagreeable conversation; nor should I, but on account of the result, have chosen so unpleasant a subject for your perusal. However, I will be as concise as I possibly can, that the better occupations of your Ladyship’s time may be less impeded.
When she found me inexorable in refusing Evelina’s attending her to Paris, she peremptorily insisted that she should at least live with her in London till Sir John Belmont’s return. I remonstrated against this scheme with all the energy in my power; but the contest was vain; she lost her patience, and I my time. She declared, that if I was resolute in opposing her, she would instantly make a will, in which she would leave all her fortune to strangers, though, otherwise, she intended her granddaughter for her sole heiress.
To me, I own, this threat seemed of little consequence; I have long accustomed myself to think, that, with a competency, of which she is sure, my child might be as happy as in the possession of millions; but the incertitude of her future fate deters me from following implicitly the dictates of my present judgement.

===Chinese===

第三十八封 维拉尔斯先生致霍华德夫人
5月27日，于贝里山。
亲爱的夫人：
我想您听说我接待了杜瓦尔夫人的一次来访，不会诧异；她离开霍华德庄园之前，想必早已把来意声张出去了。倘若能体面地避开，我本乐于推掉这次会面；可是跑了这样远的路，再拒她于门外，是不可能了。
她告诉我，她到贝里山来，是为着我写给她外孙女的一封信，信里我不许她去巴黎。接着她便粗声粗气地责问我何以僭越这份权柄；倘若我有意同她争辩，她准会怒气冲冲地同我争这个权。可我拒绝了一切争论。我只安安静静地听着，直听得她自己说累了、巴不得换换也好歇口。然后我才请问她此来的目的。
她答道，她来是要我交出我从她外孙女身上篡夺的权力；并向我担保：事若不成，她绝不离开此地。
不过，这场不愉快的谈话的种种细节，我不想烦扰夫人；若不是为了那结局，我也不会选这么一个不快的题目供您过目。总之，我尽力说得简短，好少耽误夫人的时间，您自有着更好的事情要忙。
她见我在伊芙琳娜随她去巴黎一事上绝不松口，便断然要求：至少也该让外孙女在约翰·贝尔蒙特爵士回来之前，同她一起住在伦敦。我竭尽全力反对这计划；但争执是徒劳的：她丢了耐性，我丢了工夫。她声明：倘若我执意作梗，她立刻立下遗嘱，把全部家产留给外人——虽说否则的话，她原是打算立外孙女为唯一继承人的。
我承认，这威胁在我看来无甚分量：我久已习惯这样想——我的孩子凭着她稳稳可得的那份衣食，尽可以同坐拥百万一样幸福；可她日后命运的无定，使我不能一味听从我眼下判断的指挥。

===Original===

The connections she may hereafter form, the style of life for which she may be destined, and the future family to which she may belong, are considerations which give but too much weight to the menaces of Madame Duval. In short, Madam, after a discourse infinitely tedious, I was obliged, though very reluctantly, to compromise with this ungovernable woman, by consenting that Evelina should pass one month with her.
I never made a concession with so bad a grace, or so much regret. The violence and vulgarity of this woman, her total ignorance of propriety, the family to which she is related, and the company she is likely to keep, are objections so forcible to her having the charge of this dear child, that nothing less than my diffidence of the right I have of depriving her of so large a fortune, would have induced me to listen to her proposal. Indeed we parted, at last, equally discontented; she at what I had refused, I at what I had granted.
It now only remains for me to return your Ladyship my humble acknowledgments for the kindness which you have so liberally shown to my ward; and to beg you would have the goodness to part with her when Madame Duval thinks proper to claim the promise which she has extorted from me.
I am,

Dear Madam, etc.
Arthur Villars.

===Chinese===

她日后可能结下的亲眷、她可能注定的生活方式、她可能归属的那个家族——这许多考量，给杜瓦尔夫人的威胁添了太重的分量。简而言之，夫人，在一场无穷无尽的絮聒之后，我只得同这个全无管束的女人妥协，勉勉强强地答应：让伊芙琳娜陪她住上一个月。
我从不曾让步得这样难看、这样遗憾。这女人的横暴与粗俗，她对体面的全然无知，她所攀附的那门亲眷，以及她将要往来的那路 companions——凡此种种，都强烈反对把这位亲爱的孩子交到她手里；若不是我自己也拿不准我有无权利剥夺她这样大一笔财产，任什么也劝不动我听她的提议。说真的，我们末了不欢而散，彼此一样地不满：她恼我拒绝的，我恼我答应的。
如今只剩下一件事：为我这受监护人从您那里蒙受的慷慨善意，向夫人致以卑下的谢忱；并请您在她认为该来领取这份敲诈去的承诺时，行个好，放她走。
我是，亲爱的夫人，等等。
阿瑟·维拉尔斯。

## Letter / 书信
===Original===

XXXIX Mr. Villars to Evelina
Berry Hill, May 28.
With a reluctance which occasions me inexpressible uneasiness, I have been almost compelled to consent that my Evelina should quit the protection of the hospitable and respectable Lady Howard, and accompany Madame Duval to a city which I had hoped she would never again have entered. But alas, my dear child, we are the slaves of custom, the dupes of prejudice, and dare not stem the torrent of an opposing world, even though our judgements condemn our compliance! However, since the die is cast, we must endeavour to make the best of it.
You will have the occasion, in the course of the month you are to pass with Madame Duval, for all the circumspection and prudence you can call to your aid. She will not, I know, propose anything to you which she thinks wrong herself; but you must learn not only to *judge* but to *act* for yourself; if any schemes are started, any engagements made, which your understanding represents to you as improper, exert yourself resolutely in avoiding them; and do not, by a too passive facility, risk the censure of the world, or your own future regret.
You cannot too assiduously attend to Madame Duval herself; but I would wish you to mix as little as possible with her associates, who are not likely to be among those whose acquaintance would reflect credit upon you. Remember, my dear Evelina, nothing is so delicate as the reputation of a woman; it is at once the most beautiful and most brittle of all human things.
Adieu, my beloved child; I shall be but ill at ease till this month is elapsed.
A. V.

===Chinese===

第三十九封 维拉尔斯先生致伊芙琳娜
5月28日，于贝里山。
我心里万般不愿，万分为难，却几乎是被逼着应允了我的伊芙琳娜离开那位好客可敬的霍华德夫人的庇护，随杜瓦尔夫人去一座我曾巴望她从此不再踏入的城。可是唉，亲爱的孩子，我们是习俗的奴隶、偏见的傻瓜，哪怕自己的判断已把这份屈从判了罪，也不敢逆着整个世界的洪流！然而木已成舟，我们只好尽力往好里将它就。
在你同杜瓦尔夫人同住的一个月里，你将有机会把你能召集的一切谨慎与明断都用上。我知道，她自己认为不对的事，不会来向你提议；可你必须学会不但会*判断*，而且会*行动*：凡有起头的计划、应下的约订，只要你的理智告诉你不合适，便断然避开；切勿因过于顺从的软弱，拿世人的非难、和你日后的悔恨去冒险。
对杜瓦尔夫人本人，你怎样殷勤侍奉都不为过；但我愿你尽量少同她的来往们混在一起，那路人不见得是结识了能给你增光的人。记住，亲爱的伊芙琳娜，再没有比一个女人的名声更精微的东西：它同时是人世间最美、也最脆的一样东西。
再会了，我亲爱的孩子；这一个月不捱过去，我一日不得安生。
A. 维。

## Letter / 书信
===Original===

XL Evelina to the Rev. Mr. Villars
London, June 6.
Once more, my dearest Sir, I write to you from this great city. Yesterday morning, with the truest concern, I quitted the dear inhabitants of Howard Grove, and most impatiently shall I count the days till I see them again. Lady Howard and Mrs. Mirvan took leave of me with the most flattering kindness; but indeed I knew not how to part with Maria, whose own apparent sorrow redoubled mine. She made me promise to send her a letter every post: and I shall write to her with the same freedom, and almost the same confidence, you allow me to make use of to yourself.
The Captain was very civil to me: but he wrangled with poor Madame Duval to the last moment; and, taking me aside, just before we got into the chaise, he said, “Hark’ee, Miss Anville, I’ve a favour for to ask of you, which is this; that you will write us word how the old gentlewoman finds herself, when she sees it was all a trick; and what the French lubber says to it, and all about it.”
I answered that I would obey him, though I was very little pleased with the commission, which, to me, was highly improper; but he will either treat me as an *informer*, or make me a party in his frolic.
As soon as we drove away, Madame Duval, with much satisfaction, exclaimed, “*Dieu merci*, we’ve got off at last! I’m sure I never desire to see that place again. It’s a wonder I’ve got away alive; for I believe I’ve had the worst luck ever was known, from the time I set my foot upon the threshold. I know I wish I’d never a gone. Besides, into the bargain, it’s the most dullest place in all Christendom: there’s never no diversions, nor nothing at all.”
Then she bewailed M. Du Bois; concerning whose adventures she continued to make various conjectures during the rest of our journey.
When I asked her what part of London she should reside in, she told me that Mr. Branghton was to meet us at an inn, and would conduct us to a lodging. Accordingly, we proceeded to a house in Bishopsgate Street, and were led by a waiter into a room where we found Mr. Branghton.
He received us very civilly; but seemed rather surprised at seeing me, saying, “Why, I didn’t think of your bringing Miss; however, she’s very welcome.”

===Chinese===

第四十封 伊芙琳娜致可敬的维拉尔斯先生
6月6日，于伦敦。
我最亲爱的先生，我又一次从这座大城给您写信了。昨天早晨，我怀着最深的不忍，辞别了霍华德庄园那些亲爱的人们；重新见到他们之前，我数着日子过。霍华德夫人和米尔文太太同我道别时，那份殷勤的亲爱叫我无地自受；可同玛丽亚分手，我实在不知怎样才捱得过：她那明显的悲伤，把我的悲伤也加倍了。她要我答应每个邮班给她去一封信；我给她写信，会同给您写信一样自在，几乎一样知无不言。
船长待我很客气；可他同可怜的杜瓦尔夫人一直吵到最后一刻；上车前，他把我拉到一边说：“听着，安维尔小姐，我有件事拜托你：那老婆子发现上了当时，你给我们来信说说她那副样子，还有那法国傻大个儿怎么说，前前后后都写上。”
我答应用遵命，虽说差事不合我的意，依我看也大大地不合宜；可他不是要拿我当*眼线*，就是要我入伙他的恶作剧。
车一驶动，杜瓦尔夫人便心满意足地叫起来：“*谢天谢地*，总算脱身了！我敢说，那地方我这辈子再不想看第二眼。我能囫囵着出来，简直是奇迹；因为打我一路进那门槛起，我的运气就背到了家。我知道，我但愿当初压根儿没去。再说，加上这一层，那还是整个基督世界里最闷的地方：从来没有什么玩意儿，什么都没有。”
接着她又哀叹起杜布瓦先生来；一路上剩下的工夫，她对他那段遭遇猜了又猜。
我问她打算住在伦敦哪一带，她说布兰顿先生会到客栈来接我们，领我们去住处。于是我们一路到了主教门大街一家客栈，由侍者领进一个房间，布兰顿先生正在那里。
他客客气气地接待了我们；见到我似乎倒有些诧异，说：“咦，我没想到您把小姐也带来了；不过，也很欢迎。”

===Original===

“I’ll tell you how it was,” said Madame Duval: “you must know I’ve a mind to take the girl to Paris, that she may see something of the world, and improve herself a little; besides, I’ve another reason, that you and I will talk more about. But, do you know, that meddling old parson, as I told you of, would not let her go: however, I’m resolved I’ll be even with him; for I shall take her on with me, without saying never a word more to nobody.”
I started at this intimation, which very much surprised me. But, I am very glad she has discovered her intention, as I shall be carefully upon my guard not to venture from town with her.
Mr. Branghton then hoped we had passed our time agreeably in the country.
“O Lord, cousin,” cried she, “I’ve been the miserablest creature in the world! I’m sure all the horses in London shan’t drag me into the country again of one while: why, how do you think I’ve been served?﻿—only guess.”
“Indeed, cousin, I can’t pretend to do that.”
“Why then I’ll tell you. Do you know I’ve been robbed!﻿—that is, the villain would have robbed me if he could, only I’d secured all my money.”
“Why, then cousin, I think your loss can’t have been very great.”
“O Lord, you don’t know what you’re a saying; you’re talking in the unthinkingest manner in the world: why, it was all along of not having no money that I met with that misfortune.”
“How’s that, cousin? I don’t see what great misfortune you can have met with, if you’d secured all your money.”
“That’s because you don’t know nothing of the matter: for there the villain came to the chaise; and, because we hadn’t got nothing to give him, though he’d no more right to our money than the man in the moon, yet, do you know, he fell into the greatest passion ever you see, and abused me in such a manner, and put me in a ditch, and got a rope o’purpose to hang me;﻿—and I’m sure, if that wasn’t misfortune enough, why I don’t know what is.”
“This is a hard case, indeed, cousin. But why don’t you go to Justice Fielding?”
“O as to that, I’m a going to him directly; but only I want first to see M. Du Bois; for the oddest thing of all is, that he has wrote to me, and never said nothing of where he is, nor what’s become of him, nor nothing else.”
“M. Du Bois! why, he’s at my house at this very time.”
“M. Du Bois at your house!

===Chinese===

“我告诉你怎么回事，”杜瓦尔夫人说，“你要知道，我想带这姑娘去巴黎，让她见见世面，也长点出息；另外我还有一层缘故，回头咱俩再细谈。可你猜怎么着，我跟你说过那个爱管闲事的老牧师，他偏不放她走！不过我打定了主意，非跟他扯平不可：我要一句话不跟任何人说，直接把她带走。”
我听了这话一惊，实在出乎意料。不过她既露了这个底，我倒很高兴：往后我会格外留神，决不随她出城。
布兰顿先生接着问，我们在乡下过得可好。
“哎呀，表哥，”她叫道，“我成了世上顶顶倒霉的人了！眼下就是拿伦敦所有的马来拖我，一时半会儿也别想再把我拖进乡下去。哼，你猜我吃了什么亏？——你猜猜看。”
“说实在的，表妹，我可猜不着。”
“那我就告诉你。你可知道，我遭了抢劫！——就是说，那坏蛋若抢得着，早把我抢了；幸亏我把钱全藏好了。”
“那，表妹，我想您的损失想必不大。”
“哎呀，你不知道自己在胡说什么；你这话说得没心没肺透了：哼，就因为身上一个钱没有，我才遭了那场大难。”
“这是怎么说，表妹？钱既然全藏好了，我不明白您还能遭什么大难。”
“那是因为你什么都不知道：那坏蛋走到马车跟前，我们什么也没给他——他跟月亮上的人一样没权利要我们的钱——可你信不信，他发起火来那你可见都没见过，把我骂了个狗血喷头，把我塞进沟里，还特意弄了根绳子要吊死我；——要这还不算倒霉，那我就不知道什么才算倒霉了。”
“这案子可真够受的，表妹。可您怎么不去找菲尔丁法官？”
“噢，那个嘛，我这就正要去；只是我想先见见杜布瓦先生；因为顶顶蹊跷的是，他给我来了信，却只字不提他在哪儿、出了什么事，什么都不说。”
“杜布瓦先生！咦，他这会儿就在我家呢。”
“杜布瓦先生在您家！

===Original===

well, I declare this is the surprisingest part of all: However, I assure you, I think he might have comed for me, as well as you, considering what I have gone through on his account; for, to tell you the truth, it was all along of him that I met with that accident; so I don’t take it very kind of him, I promise you.”
“Well, but cousin, tell me some of the particulars of this affair.”
“As to the particulars, I’m sure they’d make your hair stand on end to hear them; however, the beginning of it all was through the fault of M. Du Bois: but, I’ll assure you, he may take care of himself in future, since he don’t so much as come to see if I’m dead or alive.﻿—But, there, I went for him to a justice of peace, and rode all out of the way, and did everything in the world, and was used worser than a dog, and all for the sake of serving of him; and now, you see, he don’t so much﻿—well, I was a fool for my pains.﻿—However, he may get somebody else to be treated so another time; for, if he’s taken up every day in the week, I’ll never go after him no more.”
This occasioned an explanation; in the course of which Madame Duval, to her utter amazement, heard that M. Du Bois had never left London during her absence! nor did Mr. Branghton believe that he had ever been to the Tower, or met with any kind of accident.
Almost instantly the whole truth of the transaction seemed to *rush upon her mind*, and her wrath was inconceivably violent. She asked me a thousand questions in a breath; but, fortunately, was too vehement to attend to my embarrassment, which must otherwise have betrayed my knowledge of the deceit. Revenge was her first wish; and she vowed she would go the next morning to Justice Fielding, and enquire what punishment she might lawfully inflict upon the Captain for his assault.
I believe we were an hour at Bishopsgate Street before poor Madame Duval could allow anything to be mentioned but her own story; at any length, however, Mr. Branghton told her, that M. Du Bois, and all his own family, were waiting for her at his house. A hackney-coach was then called, and we proceeded to Snow Hill.
Mr. Branghton’s house is small and inconvenient; though his shop, which takes in all the ground floor, is large and commodious. I believe I told you before, that he is a silversmith.
We were conducted up two pairs of stairs: for the dining-room, Mr. Branghton told us, was *let*.

===Chinese===

唉，我敢说，这一节才是顶顶叫人吃惊的。不过我跟你说，我看他本来倒可以来接我，跟接你一样，想想我为了他吃的那些苦；老实跟你说吧，我遭的那场事，从头到尾全是为着他；所以他这样，我可不领情，这话我先撂在这儿。”
“可是表妹，把这事的细情给我说几件听听。”
“细情么，说保准你听了头发都要竖起来；总之，起头全是杜布瓦先生的错。可我告诉你，往后他好自为之罢：他连来看我死没死都不来。——想当初，我为了他跑去找治安官，绕了多大的远路，天底下的事都做尽了，落到个猪狗不如的下场，全是为着帮他的忙；如今你瞧，他连——哼，我真是白疼了，傻了。——往后他再叫人抓起来，一天抓一囘，我也再不去寻他了。”
这一来只得把事情说明；说起来，杜瓦尔夫人才听说，她不在的这阵子，杜布瓦先生压根儿就没离开过伦敦！布兰顿先生也不信他进过什么伦敦塔、遭过什么意外。
顷刻之间，这件事的全部真相仿佛*一齐涌上她的心头*，她的怒火狂暴得不可想象。她一口气问我一千个问题；所幸她火气太旺，顾不上看我的窘态——不然那窘态早把我知情的事露了。报仇是她的第一个念头；她发誓明天一早就去见菲尔丁法官，问明白她可以依法给船长那番暴行什么样的惩罚。
我们在主教门大街足有一个钟头，可怜的杜瓦尔夫人只容人听她自己的事；末了，布兰顿先生总算告诉她：杜布瓦先生，还有他全家，都在他家里等她。于是叫了一辆街车，我们往雪山去。
布兰顿先生的房子又小又不方便；铺面倒是占了整个底层，宽绰体面。我想我从前提过，他是个银匠。
我们被领上两段楼梯：因为餐厅，布兰顿先生说，*租出去了*。

===Original===

His two daughters, their brother, M. Du Bois, and a young man, were at tea. They had waited some time for Madame Duval, but I found they had not any expectation that I should accompany her; and the young ladies, I believe, were rather more surprised than pleased when I made my appearance; for they seemed hurt that I should see their apartment. Indeed, I would willingly have saved them that pain, had it been in my power.
The first person who saw me was M. Du Bois, “*Ah, mon Dieu!*” exclaimed he, “*voila Mademoiselle!*”
“Goodness,” cried young Branghton, “if there isn’t Miss!”
“Lord, so there is!” said Miss Polly; “well, I’m sure I should never have dreamed of Miss’s coming.”
“Nor I neither, I’m sure,” cried Miss Branghton, “or else I would not have been in this room to see her: I’m quite ashamed about it;﻿—only not thinking of seeing anybody but my aunt﻿—however, Tom, it’s all your fault; for, you know very well I wanted to borrow Mr. Smith’s room, only you were so *grumpy* you would not let me.”
“Lord, what signifies?” said her brother; “I dare be sworn Miss has been up two pair of stairs before now;﻿—ha’n’t you, Miss?”
I begged that I might not give them the least disturbance; and assured them that I had not any choice in regard to what room we sat in.
“Well,” said Miss Polly, “when you come next, Miss, we’ll have Mr. Smith’s room: and it’s a very pretty one, and only up one pair of stairs, and nicely furnished, and everything.”
“To say the truth,” said Miss Branghton, “I thought that my cousin would not, upon any account, have come to town in the summertime; for it’s not at all the *fashion*;﻿—so, to be sure, thinks I, she’ll stay till September, when the playhouses open.”
This was my reception, which I believe you will not call a very *cordial* one. Madame Duval, who, after having severely reprimanded M. Du Bois for his negligence, was just entering upon the story of her misfortunes, now wholly engaged the company.
M. Du Bois listened to her with a look of the utmost horror, repeatedly lifting up his eyes and hands, and exclaiming, “*O ciel! quel barbare!*” The young ladies gave her the most earnest attention; but their brother, and the young man, kept a broad grin upon their faces during the whole recital.

===Chinese===

他的两个女儿、她们的兄弟、杜布瓦先生，还有一个年轻人，正在喝茶。他们等杜瓦尔夫人有些时候了；可我发现他们全没料到我会同来；我露面的时候，两位小姐想必吃惊多过高兴：她们似乎很不愿意让我看见她们的住处。说真的，若在我力所能及，我本很愿意免了她们这份难堪。
第一个看见我的是杜布瓦先生。“*啊，我的天！*”他叫道，“*这不是小姐么！*”
“天哪，”小布兰顿喊道，“这不是小姐么！”
“哎呀，可不是！”波莉小姐说，“啧，我说什么也梦不到小姐会来。”
“我也想不到，真的，”布兰顿小姐叫道，“不然我说什么也不肯在这间屋里见她：我臊得慌；——本来只当除了姨妈谁也见不着——不过，汤姆，这全怪你：你知道得很清楚，我想借史密斯先生的屋子来着，偏你那么*倔*，说什么也不肯。”
“哎呀，那有什么要紧？”她弟弟说，“我敢打赌，小姐从前也上过两段楼梯的；——是不是，小姐？”
我请他们千万别为我搅扰，并向他们担保，坐哪间屋子我全无所谓。
“那好，”波莉小姐说，“小姐下回来，我们用史密斯先生的屋子：那间可俊了，才上一段楼梯，家什也体面，样样都好。”
“说句实话，”布兰顿小姐说，“我还当表妹说什么也不会大夏天的进城；因为那*根本不合时兴*；——所以我心里就琢磨，她准得捱到九月戏院子开了门再来。”
这便是他们接待我的情形，想必您不会称之为热烈的接待。杜瓦尔夫人把杜布瓦先生狠狠训了一顿疏忽之后，正要开始讲她的苦难史，这下子把全屋的人都占住了。
杜布瓦先生听着，一脸的惊骇之极，不住地抬眼抬手，直叫：“*噢，老天！多野蛮的人！*”两位小姐听得聚精会神；可她们的弟弟同那个年轻人，从头到尾咧着一张大嘴笑。

===Original===

She was, however, too much engaged to observe them; but, when she mentioned having been tied in a ditch, young Branghton, no longer able to contain himself, burst into a loud laugh, declaring that he had never heard anything so *funny* in his life! His laugh was heartily reechoed by his friend; the Miss Branghtons could not resist the example; and poor Madame Duval, to her extreme amazement, was absolutely overpowered and stopped by the violence of their mirth.
For some minutes the room seemed quite in an uproar; the rage of Madame Duval, the astonishment of M. Du Bois, and the angry interrogatories of Mr. Branghton, on one side; the convulsive tittering of the sisters, and the loud laughs of the young men, on the other, occasioned such noise, passion and confusion, that had anyone stopped an instant on the stairs, he must have concluded himself in Bedlam. At length, however, the father brought them to order; and, half-laughing, half-frightened, they made Madame Duval some very awkward apologies. But she would not be prevailed upon to continue her narrative, till they had protested they were laughing at the Captain, and not at her. Appeased by this, she resumed her story; which by the help of stuffing handkerchiefs into their mouths, the young people heard with tolerable decency.
Everybody agreed, that the ill-usage the Captain had given her was *actionable*; and Mr. Branghton said, he was sure she might recover what damages she pleased, since she had been put in fear of her life.
She then, with great delight, declared, that she would lose no time in satisfying her revenge, and vowed she would not be contented with less than half his fortune: “For though,” she said, “I don’t put no value upon the money, because, *Dieu merci*, I ha’n’t no want of it, yet I don’t wish for nothing so much as to punish that fellow; for I’m sure, whatever’s the cause of it, he owes me a great *grudge*, and I know no more what it’s for than you do; but he’s always been doing me one spite or another ever since I knew him.”

===Chinese===

她却讲得太投入，没留意他们；可等到她说到自己被人捆在沟里，小布兰顿再也绷不住，放声大笑，声称他这辈子从没听过这么*逗*的事！他的朋友由衷地应和；布兰顿家两位小姐也抵不过这个榜样；可怜的杜瓦尔夫人惊愕之极，硬生生被他们笑得说不下去。
有好几分钟，屋里简直炸了锅：这边是杜瓦尔夫人的怒、杜布瓦先生的惊、布兰顿先生气冲冲的盘问；那边是姐妹俩抽搐的痴笑、两个年轻人响亮的大笑——那声音、火气与乱劲，谁在楼梯上停一停，准以为自己进了疯人院。末了还是当父亲压住了场面；他们半笑着、半怕着，向杜瓦尔夫人赔了几句生硬的不是。可她怎么也不肯接着讲，直到他们赌咒发誓说笑的是船长、不是她。这才平了气，重新讲起来；年轻人们往嘴里塞着手帕，才算勉强规矩地听完。
人人都说，船长那番欺凌是*可以告官*的；布兰顿先生说，她既然险些送了性命，要多少 damages 都告得下来。
她于是喜滋滋地宣布，要立刻动手偿这口气，并发誓非分他一半家产不可：“因为，”她说，“虽说*谢天谢地*我并不缺钱，一个钱也不稀罕；可我世上最巴不得的就是治一治那家伙：因为不管为的什么，他分明跟我结着大*仇’，为什么我跟你一样不知道；可打我认得他起，他就一直一而再再而三地捉弄我。”

===Original===

Soon after tea, Miss Branghton took an opportunity to tell me, in a whisper, that the young man I saw was a lover of her sister’s, that his name was Brown, and that he was a haberdasher: with many other particulars of his circumstances and family; and then she declared her utter aversion to the thoughts of such a match; but added, that her sister had no manner of spirit or ambition, though, for her part, she would ten times rather die an old maid, than marry any person but a gentleman. “And, for that matter,” added she, “I believe Polly herself don’t care much for him, only she’s in such a hurry, because, I suppose, she’s a mind to be married before me; however, she’s very welcome; for, I’m sure, I don’t care a pin’s point whether I ever marry at all;﻿—it’s all one to me.”
Some time after this, Miss Polly contrived to tell *her* story. She assured me, with much tittering, that her sister was in a great fright lest she should be married first. “So I make her believe that I will,” continued she; “for I dearly love to plague her a little; though, I declare, I don’t intend to have Mr. Brown in reality;﻿—I’m sure I don’t like him half well enough﻿—do you, Miss?”
“It is not possible for me to judge of his merits,” said I, “as I am entirely a stranger to him.”
“But what do you think of him, Miss?”
“Why, really, I﻿—I don’t know.”
“But do you think him handsome? Some people reckon him to have a good pretty person;﻿—but I’m sure, for my part, I think he’s monstrous ugly:﻿—don’t *you*, Miss?”
“I am no judge﻿—but I think his person is very﻿—very well.”
“*Very well!*﻿—Why, pray Miss,” in a tone of vexation, “what fault can you find with it?”
“O, none at all!”
“I’m sure you must be very ill-natured if you could. Now there’s Biddy says she thinks nothing of him﻿—but I know it’s all out of spite. You must know, Miss, it makes her as mad as can be that I should have a lover before her; but she’s so proud that nobody will court her, and I often tell her she’ll die an old maid. But the thing is, she has taken it into her head to have a liking for Mr. Smith, as lodges on the first floor; but, Lord, he’ll never have her, for he’s quite a fine gentleman; and besides, Mr. Brown heard him say one day, that he’d never marry as long as he lived, for he’d no opinion of matrimony.”
“And did you tell your sister this?”

===Chinese===

茶后不久，布兰顿小姐寻了个机会咬耳朵告诉我：我看见的那个年轻人是她妹妹的情人，名叫布朗，是个针线服饰商；又说了许多他家境和家里人的细节；然后声明她一想到这门亲就满心厌恶；又补一句，说她妹妹一点志气、一点想头都没有，至于她自己，宁可死作老姑娘，也只肯嫁个体面人。“说到这一节，”她又添一句，“我相信波莉自己也并不怎么喜欢他，只是她心急，我猜是因为她想赶在我前头嫁出去；不过请便请便；我这个人，嫁不嫁人根本不在乎——对我全是一样。”
过了一阵，波莉小姐又设法来讲*她的*故事。她一面嗤嗤地笑，一面向我担保：她姐姐怕妹妹先嫁，怕得要命。“所以我就叫她信我真要嫁，”她接着说，“我就爱这么气气她；不过说真的，我并不真要嫁布朗先生；——我敢说我不怎么喜欢他，差得远呢——您呢，小姐？”
“我同他全然不识，没法评他的长短。”我说。
“可您看他怎么样，小姐？”
“呃，真的，我——我说不上。”
“可您觉得他俊不俊？有人夸他长得挺不错；——可我自己看，他丑得吓人；——*您*说呢，小姐？”
“我不会看人——不过我觉得他的相貌很——很好。”
“*很好！*——唷，请问小姐，”她懊恼起来，“那您还能挑出什么不好来？”
“哦，一点也挑不出！”
“您要挑得出，那心眼儿可就坏了。你知道，比迪说他不怎么样——可我知道那全是醋。您知道么小姐，我先她有了情人，她气得要死；可她那么傲，偏没人追；我常跟她说，她要死作老姑娘了。可还有一层：她迷上了一楼的房客史密斯先生；可是，天哪，他才不会要她呢：人家是位十足的时鬛绅士；再说了，布朗先生有一天听见他说，他这辈子绝不结婚，因为他看不惯婚姻这回事。”
“这话你告诉姐姐了么？”

===Original===

“O, to be sure, I told her directly; but she did not mind me; however, if she will be a fool she must.”
This extreme want of affection and good-nature increased the distaste I already felt for these unamiable sisters; and a confidence so entirely unsolicited and unnecessary, manifested equally their folly and their want of decency.
I was very glad when the time for our departing arrived. Mr. Branghton said our lodgings were in Holborn, that we might be near his house, and neighbourly. He accompanied us to them himself.
Our rooms are large, and not inconvenient; our landlord is an hosier. I am sure I have a thousand reasons to rejoice that I am so little known: for my present situation is, in every respect, very unenviable; and I would not, for the world, be seen by any acquaintance of Mrs. Mirvan.
This morning, Madame Duval, attended by all the Branghtons, actually went to a Justice in the neighborhood, to report the Captain’s ill usage of her. I had great difficulty in excusing myself from being of the party, which would have given me very serious concern. Indeed, I was extremely anxious, though at home, till I heard the result of the application, for I dread to think of the uneasiness which such an affair would occasion the amiable Mrs. Mirvan. But, fortunately, Madame Duval has received very little encouragement to proceed in her design; for she has been informed, that, as she neither heard the voice, nor saw the face of the person suspected, she will find difficulty to cast him upon *conjecture*, and will have but little probability of gaining her cause, unless she can procure witnesses of the transaction. Mr. Branghton, therefore, who has considered all the circumstances of the affair, is of opinion, that the lawsuit will not only be expensive, but tedious and hazardous, and has advised against it. Madame Duval, though very unwillingly, has acquiesced in his decision; but vows, that if she ever is so affronted again, she will be revenged, even if she ruins herself. I am extremely glad that this ridiculous adventure seems now likely to end without more serious consequences.
Adieu, my dearest Sir. My direction is at Mr. Dawkin’s, a hosier in High Holborn.

===Chinese===

“哦，那还用说，我当场就告诉她了；可她不理会；罢了，她要儍就儍去罢。”
这姊妹俩如此毫无情义、毫无好心，更加深了我本已对她们生的反感；这样一份全不请自来、毫无必要的交底，又同样显出她们的愚蠡和不知羞。
所以到了我们该走的时候，我非常高兴。布兰顿先生说，我们的住处在霍尔本，为的是离他家近些，彼此照应。他亲自陪我们过去。
我们的几间屋子宽大，倒不算不便；房东是个袜商。我确有一千个理由庆幸自己没几个人认得：因为眼下的处境，样样都无可羡慕；米尔文太太的熟人，我一个也不愿叫看见。
今天早晨，杜瓦尔夫人由布兰顿全家陪同，当真去见了附近的一位法官，控告船长对她的欺凌。我费了好大劲才推脱了同去——去了可要叫我为难死了。虽留在家，我也提心吊胆，直到听说控状的下文；因为那样一件事会带给那位可爱的米尔文太太多少不安，我想都不敢想。所幸，杜瓦尔夫人几乎没讨到什么鼓励：人家告诉她，她既没听见那人的嗓音、也没看见那人的脸面，单凭*猜测*指认他，很难告倒；除非她找得到那件事的证人，赢面很小。布兰顿先生把这案子前前后后一掂量，认定这场官司不但花钱，还又拖长又冒险，劝她罢了。杜瓦尔夫人老大不情愿，也只得依了他；但发誓说，往后再受这等羞辱，哪怕倾家荡产也要报这个仇。这段荒唐的遭遇看来可以就此收场、不生后患，我真高兴极了。
再会，我最亲爱的先生。我的通信地址是高霍尔本的袜商道金先生家。

## Letter / 书信
===Original===

XLI Evelina to Miss Mirvan
June 7th.
I have no words, my sweet friend, to express the thankfulness I feel for the unbounded kindness which you, your dear mother, and the much-honoured Lady Howard, have shown me; and still less can I find language to tell you with what reluctance I parted from such dear and generous friends, whose goodness reflects, at once, so much honour on their own hearts, and on her to whom it has been so liberally bestowed. But I will not repeat what I have already written to the kind Mrs. Mirvan; I will remember your admonitions, and confine to my own breast that gratitude with which you have filled it, and teach my pen to dwell upon subjects less painful to my generous correspondent.
O, Maria! London now seems no longer the same place where I lately enjoyed so much happiness; everything is new and strange to me; even the town itself has not the same aspect.﻿—My situation so altered!﻿—my home so different!﻿—my companions so changed!﻿—But you well know my averseness to this journey.
Indeed, to me, London now seems a desert: that gay and busy appearance it so lately wore, is now succeeded by a look of gloom, fatigue, and lassitude; the air seems stagnant, the heat is intense, the dust intolerable, and the inhabitants illiterate and underbred. At least, such is the face of things in the part of town where I at present reside.
Tell me, my dear Maria, do you never retrace in your memory the time we passed here when together? to mine it recurs forever! And yet I think I rather recollect a dream, or some visionary fancy, than a reality.﻿—That I should ever have been known to Lord Orville﻿—that I should have spoken to﻿—have danced with him﻿—seems now a romantic illusion: and that elegant politeness, that flattering attention, that high-bred delicacy, which so much distinguished him above all other men, and which struck us with so much admiration, I now retrace the remembrance of rather as belonging to an object of ideal perfection, formed by my own imagination, than to a being of the same race and nature as those with whom I at present converse.
I have no news for you, my dear Miss Mirvan; for all that I could venture to say of Madame Duval I have already written to your sweet mother; and as to adventures, I have none to record. Situated as I now am, I heartily hope I shall not meet with any; my wish is to remain quiet and unnoticed.
Adieu!

===Chinese===

第四十一封 伊芙琳娜致米尔文小姐
6月7日。
亲爱的朋友，你、你亲爱的母亲、还有那位可敬之至的霍华德夫人，给了我这样无限的恩情，我的感激找不到言语表达；要说我离开这样亲爱、这样慷慨的朋友们时怎样地不忍，我就更寻不出话来告诉你了：她们的好意，既给她们自己的心增光，也给受赠的人增光。但我不愿把写给好心的米尔文太太的话再说一遍；我会记着你的叮嘱，把你们灌满我心底的感激封在自己胸中，教我这支笔改谈些别的题目，免得我慷慨的通信人看了难受。
啊，玛丽亚！伦敦如今在我眼里，已不是不久前我还享有那么多快乐的地方；样样都新鲜而陌生；连这座城本身都换了面貌。——我的处境这样变了！——我的家这样不同了！——我的同伴这样换了！——可你深知我原就不愿做这趟旅行。
说真的，伦敦如今在我是一片荒漠：它不久前那副欢快热闹的模样，换上了一副阴沉、困倦、无精打采的面孔；空气仿佛凝滞，暑气灼人，尘土难当，居民粗鄙少教。至少，我眼下住的这一带是这副光景。
告诉我，亲爱的玛丽亚，你可曾在记忆里重游我们一同在这里度过的时光？在我，它无时无刻不重来！可我觉得，我记起的与其说是一段实事，不如说是一场梦、一个幻梦。——我竟然认得奥维尔勋爵——竟然同他说过话——同他跳过舞——如今看来简直是一场罗曼蒂克的幻境；他那样优雅的谦恭、那样令人心醉的关注、那样高贵出身般的 delicate，使他远远高出于一切男子之上，也叫我那时满心钦叹；如今我追忆这些，与其说是属于一个同我此刻周旋的那些人同样族类、同样血肉的存在，不如说是属于一尊我自己想象捏成的、尽善尽美的偶像。
我没有什么新闻告诉你，亲爱的米尔文小姐；因为关于杜瓦尔夫人，我敢说的都已写给你亲爱的母亲了；至于奇遇，我一件也没有。处在我如今的境地，我衷心希望什么奇遇也别碰上；我只求安安静静、无人理睬。
再会！

===Original===

excuse the gravity of this letter; and believe me, your most sincerely
Affectionate and obliged
Evelina Anville.

===Chinese===

原谅这封信写得这样沉重；并请相信我，你最真诚的
深情而感恩的
伊芙琳娜·安维尔。

## Letter / 书信
===Original===

XLII Evelina to the Rev. Mr. Villars
Holborn, June 9.
Yesterday morning we received an invitation to dine and spend the day at Mr. Branghton’s; and M. Du Bois, who was also invited, called to conduct us to Snow Hill.
Young Branghton received us at the door; and the first words he spoke were, “Do you know, sisters a’n’t dressed yet.”
Then, hurrying us into the house, he said to me, “Come, Miss, you shall go upstairs and catch ’em﻿—I dare say they’re at the glass.”
He would have taken my hand; but I declined this civility, and begged to follow Madame Duval.
Mr. Branghton then appeared, and led the way himself. We went, as before, up two pairs of stairs; but the moment the father opened the door, the daughters both gave a loud scream. We all stopped; and then Miss Branghton called out, “Lord, Papa, what do you bring the company up here for? why, Polly and I a’n’t half dressed.”
“More shame for you,” answered he; “here’s your aunt, and cousin, and M. Du Bois, all waiting, and ne’er a room to take them to.”
“Who’d have thought of their coming so soon?” cried she: “I am sure for my part I thought Miss was used to nothing but quality hours.”
“Why, I shan’t be ready this half-hour yet,” said Miss Polly; “can’t they stay in the shop till we’re dressed?”
Mr. Branghton was very angry, and scolded them violently: however, we were obliged to descend, and stools were procured for us in the shop, where we found the brother, who was highly delighted, he said, that his sisters had been *catched*; and he thought proper to entertain me with a long account of their tediousness, and the many quarrels they all had together.
When, at length, these ladies were equipped to their satisfaction, they made their appearance; but before any conversation was suffered to pass between them and us, they had a long and most disagreeable dialogue with their father, to whose reprimands, though so justly incurred, they replied with the utmost pertness while their brother all the time laughed aloud.
The moment they perceived this, they were so much provoked, that, instead of making any apologies to Madame Duval, they next began to quarrel with him. “Tom, what do you laugh for? I wonder what business you have to be always a laughing when Papa scolds us?”
“Then what business have you to be such a while getting on your clothes? You’re never ready, you know well enough.”

===Chinese===

第四十二封 伊芙琳娜致可敬的维拉尔斯先生
6月9日，于霍尔本。
昨天早晨，我们收到布兰顿家的邀请，去他家吃饭、消磨一天；也在被邀之列的杜布瓦先生，过来领我们到雪山去。
小布兰顿在门口迎接我们；他开口头一句便是：“你们可知道，姐姐们还没穿戴好呢。”
接着便把我们往屋里赶，他对我说：“来，小姐，你上楼去捉她们——保准还在镜子跟前呢。”
他要来拉我的手；我辞谢了这份殷勤，请让我跟在杜瓦尔夫人后面。
布兰顿先生这才露面，亲自领路。我们照旧上了两段楼梯；可父亲一推开门，两个女儿齐声尖叫起来。我们都停住了；布兰顿小姐喊道：“哎呀，爸，你把客人带上来干什么？我和波莉还没穿好一半呢。”
“那就更该害羞，”他答道，“你姨妈、你表妹、还有杜布瓦先生全在下面等着，家里连间待客的屋子都没有。”
“谁想得到他们来得这么早？”她叫道，“我心里还只当小姐向来只惯于阔人家的钟点呢。”
“哼，我这半个钟头也收拾不好呢，”波莉小姐说，“叫他们在铺子里等等不行么？”
布兰顿先生气得厉害，把她们狠狠骂了一顿：可我们还是只得又下了楼，在铺子里给我们搬来几张凳子；她们的弟弟正在那里，他说，姐姐们*被捉住了*，他高兴透了；他又认为理应招待我，长篇大论讲她们如何磨蹭，一家人又如何三天两头地吵架。
好容易等这两位小姐穿戴得自己满意了，才出来见客；可在她们同我们攀谈之前，先同她们的父亲来了一场又长又难堪的对口：父亲那顿训斥虽属应得，她们回起嘴来却尖横之至，她们的弟弟又在一旁放声大笑。
她们一见这个，火气更大，索性不同杜瓦尔夫人道歉，转而同他吵起来。“汤姆，你笑什么？我就纳闷，爸骂我们的时候，你哪来这么多的事要笑？”
“那你穿衣裳要磨蹭这半天，又是哪来的事？你们从来就没ready过，自己心里明白。”

===Original===

“Lord, Sir, I wonder what’s that to you! I wish you’d mind your own affairs, and not trouble yourself about ours. How should a boy like you know anything?”
“A boy, indeed! not such a boy, neither: I’ll warrant you’ll be glad to be as young when you come to be old maids.”
This sort of dialogue we were amused with till dinner was ready, when we again mounted up two pairs of stairs.
In our way, Miss Polly told me that her sister had asked Mr. Smith for his room to dine in, but he had refused to lend it; “because,” she said, “one day it happened to be a little greased: however, we shall have it to drink tea in, and then, perhaps, you may see him; and I assure you he’s quite like one of the quality, and dresses as fine, and goes to balls and dances, and everything, quite in taste; and besides, Miss, he keeps a foot-boy of his own too.”
The dinner was ill-served, ill-cooked, and ill-managed. The maid who waited had so often to go downstairs for something that was forgotten, that the Branghtons were perpetually obliged to rise from table themselves, to get plates, knives, and forks, bread or beer. Had they been without *pretensions*, all this would have seemed of no consequence; but they aimed at appearing to advantage, and even fancied they succeeded. However, the most disagreeable part of our fare was that the whole family continually disputed whose turn it was to rise, and whose to be allowed to sit still.
When this meal was over, Madame Duval, ever eager to discourse upon *her travels*, entered into an argument with Mr. Branghton, and, in broken English, M. Du Bois, concerning the French nation: and Miss Polly, then addressing herself to me, said “Don’t you think, Miss, it’s very dull sitting upstairs here? we’d better go down *to shop*, and then we shall see the people go by.”
“Lord, Poll,” said the brother, “you’re always wanting to be staring and gaping; and I’m sure you needn’t be so fond of showing yourself, for you’re ugly enough to frighten a horse.”
“Ugly, indeed! I wonder which is best, you or me. But, I tell you what, Tom, you’ve no need to give yourself such airs; for, if you do, I’ll tell Miss of﻿—you know what﻿—”
“Who cares if you do? you may tell what you will; I don’t mind﻿—”
“Indeed,” cried I, “I do not desire to hear any secrets.”
“O, but I’m resolved I’ll tell you, because Tom’s so very spiteful.

===Chinese===

“哎呀，呸，我倒要问你与你何干！你最好管管自己的事，别来操心我们。你这么个毛孩子懂什么？”
“毛孩子，哼！也不那么毛：我保准等你们变成老姑娘的时候，还巴不得有我这么年轻呢。”
这样一番对答一直饷销到开饭，我们又上了一回两段楼梯。
路上，波莉小姐告诉我，她姐姐找史密斯先生借屋子来着，想借来吃饭，可他不肯借；“因为，”她说，“有一天那屋子碰巧叫人弄得有点油腻。不过，喝茶还是能借到的，到那时您兴许能见着他；我跟您说，他活脱一位上等人，穿得也讲究，去跳舞会、跳宫廷舞，样样都入时；还有呢小姐，他自己还雇着一个小听差呢。”
饭菜上得潦草，做得糟糕，安排得乱七八糟。伺候的女仆一趟趟下楼去取忘掉的东西，布兰顿一家人只得频频离席自取，一会儿盘子，一会儿刀叉，一会儿面包或啤酒。倘若他们没有那份*架子*，这些本都算不得什么；可他们一心要显得体面，还自以为显得很成功。然而席间最不堪的一幕，是全家不停地争执：这回该谁起身，谁又有资格坐着不动。
饭毕，杜瓦尔夫人照例急于畅谈*她的旅行*，同布兰顿先生、又同满口碎英语的杜布瓦先生，争论起法兰西民族来；波莉小姐这时凑到我跟前说：“小姐，您不觉得坐在这楼上闷得慌么？咱们还是*下铺子*去罢，还能看看过路人。”
“哎呀，波尔，”她弟弟说，“你就爱瞪着眼傻看；你也犯不着这样爱露脸，你丑得能把马吓惊。”
“丑，哼！倒要瞧瞧咱俩谁强。可我跟你说，汤姆，你也犯不上摆这份谱；你要再摆，我就把那件事告诉小姐——你知道是哪件——”
“你告去呀，谁怕你？爱告什么告什么，我不在乎——”
“说真的，”我喊道，“我可不想听什么秘密。”
“噢，可我非告诉您不可，因为汤姆太坏心眼了。

===Original===

You must know, Miss, t’other night﻿—”
“Poll,” cried the brother, “if you tell of that, Miss shall know all about your meeting young Brown﻿—you know when!﻿—So I’ll be quits with you one way or other.”
Miss Polly coloured, and again proposed our going downstairs till Mr. Smith’s room was ready for our reception.
“Aye, so we will,” said Miss Branghton; “I’ll assure you, cousin, we have some very genteel people pass by our shop sometimes. Polly and I always go and sit there when we’ve cleaned ourselves.”
“Yes, Miss,” cried the brother, “they do nothing else all day long, when father don’t scold them. But the best fun is, when they’ve got all their dirty things on, and all their hair about their ears, sometimes I send young Brown upstairs to them: and then there’s such a fuss!﻿—There, they hide themselves, and run away, and squeal and squall, like anything mad: and so then I puts the two cats into the room, and I gives them a good whipping, and so that sets them a squalling too; so there’s such a noise and such an uproar!﻿—Lord, you can’t think, Miss, what fun it is!”
This occasioned a fresh quarrel with the sisters; at the end of which, it was at length decided that we should go to the shop.
In our way downstairs, Miss Branghton said aloud, “I wonder when Mr. Smith’s room will be ready.”
“So do I,” answered Polly; “I’m sure we should not do any harm to it now.”
This hint had not the desired effect; for we were suffered to proceed very quietly.
As we entered the shop, I observed a young man in deep mourning leaning against the wall, with his arms folded, and his eyes fixed on the ground, apparently in profound and melancholy meditation; but the moment he perceived us, he started, and, making a passing bow, very abruptly retired. As I found he was permitted to go quite unnoticed, I could not forbear enquiring who he was.
“Lord!” answered Miss Branghton, “he’s nothing but a poor Scotch poet.”
“For my part,” said Miss Polly, “I believe he’s just starved, for I don’t find he has anything to live upon.”
“Live upon!” cried the brother; “why, he’s a poet, you know, so he may live upon learning.”
“Aye, and good enough for him, too,” said Miss Branghton; “for he’s as proud as he’s poor.”
“Like enough,” replied the brother; “but, for all that, you won’t find he will live without meat and drink: no, no, catch a Scotchman at that if you can!

===Chinese===

您得知道，小姐，前儿个夜里——”
“波尔，”她弟弟喊道，“你要告那件事，我就把你会见小布朗的事全抖给小姐——你知道什么时候！——咱们横竖要扯平。”
波莉小姐红了脸，重新提议：趁史密斯先生的屋子还没收拾好，我们先下楼去。
“哎，就这么办，”布兰顿小姐说，“我告诉您，表妹，我们铺子前有时过的可都是些非常体面的人。我和波莉一收拾停当，总去坐在那儿。”
“可不，小姐，”她弟弟叫道，“只要爸不骂，她们一天到晚没别的事。最有趣的是，趁她们穿着脏衣裳、头发披散在耳朵上，我有时打发小布朗上楼去：然后就是一场好戏！——她们东躲西藏，尖叫嘶喊，疯了一样：接着我把两只猫也丢进屋里，好好抽它们一顿，它们也叫起来；那嗓门，那乱劲！——天哪，小姐，您想不出多逗！”
这又引起姐妹们一场新的争吵；吵完，终于议定我们下楼去铺子。
下楼的路上，布兰顿小姐故意大声说：“不知道史密斯先生的屋子什么时候能好。”
“我也不知道，”波莉答道，“反正这会儿我们再弄不脏它了。”
这暗示没有收到预期的效果；我们安安静静地走了下去。
进铺子时，我看见一个穿重孝的年轻人倚着墙，抱着胳膊，眼睛盯着地面，显然沉在深沉而忧郁的思索里；可他一见我们，便悚然一惊，草草一躬，突兀地退了出去。见他这样全无人在意，我忍不住打听他是谁。
“哎呀，”布兰顿小姐答道，“不过是个穷苏格兰诗人罢了。”
“依我看，”波莉小姐说，“他就是饿得慌，我看不出他有什么可指望的活路。”
“活路！”她弟弟叫道，“他是诗人呀，靠学问就能活嘛。”
“也是他活该，”布兰顿小姐说，“他又穷又傲。”
“多半是，”弟弟答道，“不过话虽如此，你不见他不吃不喝也活不成：不行不行，要苏格兰人不吃饭，你可逮不着——

===Original===

why, they only come here for what they can get.”
“I’m sure,” said Miss Branghton, “I wonder Papa’ll be such a fool as to let him stay in the house, for I dare say he’ll never pay for his lodging.”
“Why, no more he would, if he could get another lodger. You know the bill has been put up this fortnight. Miss, if you should hear of a person that wants a room, I assure you it is a very good one, for all it’s up three pair of stairs.”
I answered, that as I had no acquaintance in London, I had not any chance of assisting them: but both my compassion and my curiosity were excited for this poor young man; and I asked them some further particulars concerning him.
They then acquainted me, that they had only known him three months. When he first lodged with them, he agreed to board also; but had lately told them he would eat by himself, though they all believed he had hardly ever tasted a morsel of meat since he left their table. They said, that he had always appeared very low-spirited; but for the last month he had been *duller* than ever; and, all of a sudden, he had put himself into mourning, though they knew not for whom, nor for what; but they supposed it was only for convenience, as no person had ever been to see or enquire for him since his residence amongst them: and they were sure he was very poor, as he had not paid for his lodgings the last three weeks: and, finally, they concluded he was a poet, or else half-crazy, because they had, at different times, found scraps of poetry in his room.
They then produced some unfinished verses, written on small pieces of paper, unconnected, and of a most melancholy cast. Among them was the fragment of an ode, which, at my request, they lent to me to copy; and as you may perhaps like to see it, I will write it now.

> O **life**! thou lingering dream of grief, of pain,

And every ill that Nature can sustain,

Strange, mutable, and wild!

Now flattering with Hope most fair,

Depressing now with fell Despair,

The nurse of Guilt, the slave of Pride,

That, like a wayward child,

Who, to himself a foe,

Sees joy alone in what’s denied,

In what is granted, woe!

O thou poor, feeble, fleeting, pow’r,

By Vice seduc’d, by Folly woo’d,

By Mis’ry, Shame, Remorse, pursu’d;

And as thy toilsome steps proceed,

Seeming to Youth the fairest flow’r,

Proving to Age the rankest weed,

A gilded but a bitter pill,

===Chinese===

哼，他们上这儿来，图的就是能拼到点什么。”
“说真的，”布兰顿小姐说，“我真纳闷爸怎么儍到留他住在家里的份上，我敢说他房钱是一文也付不出的。”
“付不出倒也是，但凡他能另找着个房客。你知道招租的牌子挂了这半个月了。小姐，您要是听见谁要找房，我告诉您，那可是间好屋，别看要上三段楼梯。”
我答道，我在伦敦没有一个熟人，怕是帮不上他们什么忙：可我对这个可怜的年轻人动了怜，也动了好奇，又问了些他的细节。
于是他们告诉我，她们认得他才三个月。他初住进来时，说好也搭伙；近来却告诉他们他要自己单独吃了——虽说她们全不信，他离了她们家的饭桌之后，几乎没尝过一口肉。她们说，他一向显得很阴郁；这一个月来更比往时*沉闷*；而且他忽然穿起了孝，她们既不知为谁、也不知为何；只猜是为了省便——因为自他住进来，从没有人来看过他、打听过他：而且他准是很穷，最近三个礼拜的房钱都没有付：末了她们断定他要么是个诗人，要么是半个疯子，因为她们先后在他屋里发现过几片写诗的纸。
接着她们拿出了几段没写完的诗，写在小纸片上，前后不相连，一色儿愁苦的调子。其中有一首颂歌的残篇，经我请求，她们借给我抄了；您或者也愿意看看，我现在就把它抄给您。

> 哦**生命**！你这悠长的悲愁与苦痛的梦，

> 这自然所能承受的一切灾殃的梦，

> 奇诡、无常、而狂野！

> 一时以最美妙的希望谄媚，

> 一时以凶残的绝望压排，

> 罪恶的乳母，骄傲的奴隶，

> 你像个任性的孩子，

> 与自己为仇，

> 惟于所不得见欢愉，

> 于所既得惟见悲愁！

> 哦你这可怜、虚弱、倏忽的权能，

> 被恶行勾引，被愚妄追求，

> 被苦难、羞惭、悔恨追逐；

> 而当你艰辛的步履前行，

> 在青年眼中是最美的花，

> 到老年却成最芜的草，

> 一颗镀金的苦丸，

> 一场纷纭、巨大、纠结的灾祸！

===Original===

Of varied, great, and complicated ill!

These lines are harsh, but they indicate an internal wretchedness, which I own, affects me. Surely this young man must be involved in misfortunes of no common nature but I cannot imagine what can induce him to remain with this unfeeling family, where he is, most unworthily, despised for being poor, and most illiberally detested for being a Scotchman. He may, indeed, have motives, which he cannot surmount, for submitting to such a situation. Whatever they are, I most heartily pity him, and cannot but wish it were in my power to afford him some relief.
During this conversation, Mr. Smith’s foot-boy came to Miss Branghton, and informed her, that his master said she might have the room now when she liked it, for that he was presently going out.
This very genteel message, though it perfectly satisfied the Miss Branghtons, by no means added to my desire of being introduced to this gentleman; and upon their rising, with intention to accept his offer, I begged they would excuse my attending them, and said I would sit with Madame Duval till the tea was ready.
I therefore once more went up two pair of stairs with young Branghton, who insisted upon accompanying me; and there we remained till Mr. Smith’s foot-boy summoned us to tea, when I followed Madame Duval into the dining-room.
The Miss Branghtons were seated at one window, and Mr. Smith was lolling indolently out of the other. They all approached us at our entrance; and Mr. Smith, probably to show he was master of the department, most officiously handed me to a great chair at the upper end of the room, without taking any notice of Madame Duval, till I rose and offered her my own seat.
Leaving the rest of the company to entertain themselves, he very abruptly began to address himself to me, in a style of gallantry equally new and disagreeable to me. It is true, no man can possibly pay me greater compliments, or make more fine speeches, than Sir Clement Willoughby: yet his language, though too flowery, is always that of a gentleman; and his address and manners are so very superior to those of the inhabitants of this house, that, to make any comparison between him and Mr. Smith, would be extremely unjust.

===Chinese===

这些诗行粗粝，却透着一股内心的凄苦，我承认，它打动了我。这位青年想必陷在非常寻常的不幸里；可我想不出，是什么使他留在这户无心肝的人家：在这里，他因为穷而被卑劣地轻视，又因为是个苏格兰人而被偏狭地嫌恶。他或许真有为难之处，使他不克自拔、只好安于这般境地。无论是什么，我由衷地怜惜他，只恨自己无力给他一点接济。
谈话间，史密斯先生的小听差来向布兰顿小姐传话：他家主人说，屋子她现在想要就使罢，因为他即刻要出门。
这条非常“体面”的口信，虽叫布兰顿家两位小姐十二分满意，却丝毫没有增添我想结识这位绅士的兴致；她们起身要去的当儿，我请她们恕不奉陪，说我陪杜瓦尔夫人坐着等茶点好了。
于是我又一次上那两段楼梯，小布兰顿非要陪着我；我们在上面一直坐到史密斯先生的小听差来请我们去喝茶，我才跟着杜瓦尔夫人进了餐厅。
布兰顿家两位小姐坐在一扇窗前，史密斯先生懒洋洋地倚出在另一扇窗外。我们一进门，他们都迎上来；史密斯先生——多半是要显显他才是这一亩三分地的主——殷勤过分地把我搀到上首一把大椅子上，对杜瓦尔夫人却不理不睬，直到我起身把自己的座位让给她。
他把其余的人撂下不管，突兀地径自同我搭起话来，那一套情话于我既新鲜又难受。诚然，论恭维之肉麻、辞藻之华丽，谁也比不过克莱门特·威洛比爵士；可他的语言纵然过于浓艳，到底是位绅士的语言；他的风度举止，又远高出这户人家的一切人之上，拿他同史密斯先生相比，未免太不公道。

===Original===

This latter seems very desirous of appearing a man of gaiety and spirit; but his vivacity is so lowbred, and his whole behaviour so forward and disagreeable, that I should prefer the company of *dullness* itself, even as that goddess is described by Pope, to that of this *sprightly* young man.
He made many apologies that he had not lent his room for our dinner, which he said, he should certainly have done, had he seen me first: and he assured me, that when I came again, he should be very glad to oblige me.
I told him, and with sincerity, that every part of the house was equally indifferent to me.
“Why, Ma’am, the truth is, Miss Biddy and Polly take no care of anything; else, I’m sure, they should be always welcome to my room; for I’m never so happy as in obliging the ladies﻿—that’s my character, Ma’am:﻿—but, really, the last time they had it, everything was made so greasy and so nasty, that, upon my word, to a man who wishes to have things a little genteel, it was quite cruel. Now, as to you, Ma’am, it’s quite another thing, for I should not mind if everything I had was spoilt, for the sake of having the pleasure to oblige you; and I assure you, Ma’am, it makes me quite happy that I have a room good enough to receive you.”
